A DROP OF INK. This drop of ink chance leaves upon- my pen, What might it write in Milton's mighty hand! What might it speak at Shakspere's high command! What words to thrill the throbbing hearts bf men t Or from Eteethoi'en soul a grand amen, ; All life and death in one full compass spanned! Who could it's power at Goethe's touch withstand! What words of truth it holds beyond our ken— What blessed promise we would fain be told, t And cannot—what grim sentence dread as death—. ; What venomous lie, that never shall unfold— What law, undoing science with a breath! But—mockery of life's quick-wasted lot— Dropped on a virgin sheet 'tis but a blot!

DAISY AND BUTTERCUP. The. Daisy wooed the Buttercup . Long, long ago, And now he wears her colours gay Upon his shield of snow. True to her love the Daisy is Wherever he may go. Fair Buttercup, a royal maid Of high degree, Lived with her father, lord of all The lovely, broad countrie That reaches from the mountain tops Of Nowhere to the sea. Now Daisy was of lowly birth, But strong and fair, And bolder knight there never lived All noble deeds to dare. He wooed and won the royal maid E'er the father was aware. And when the old king found it out An oath he swore, That if his daughter loved the knight She was his child no more, And with her low-born lover might Go from the castle door. ' Sweet Buttercup was true of heart, And 1.4,ed so well. Would rather wander forth with him Than in the castle dwell, And so she followed where he led Through field, and wood, and And that is why in summer time, Hand locked in hand, They -cylinder through our road-side fields Affd o'er our pasture land; Tellino; their tale of love and trust To all who understand. ;--Leeds Mercury Supplement. HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN ON _HER ENTRANT! INTO THE 50TH YEAR OF HER REIGN.

Queen! more than Queen! Lady of tenderest heart, Gracious as Great! atiTed to that glorious part, To rule o'er: half the Earth and all the Sea imperial mistress of the brave and free, Thou with such homage bast not been content As loyal souls to kingly worth present; But in thy natural goodness, sconiing pride, The founttins of thy love hest opened wide To all thy people, making ;till thine own Such-joys, such sorrows, as Thyself has known! tlo bast Thou won thy people's laeitts; they see _ Wife. Mother, friend, no, Queen atone in thee! Juno 20th, 1886.

, CANDIDATES STILL WANTED.—For the position of "a gentleman who, in proposing a toast, does not wish the same had fallen into better or more able hands. The foundation of ,good labour in any..sphere is a good man, and all that is done 4to give breadth, detth, and fulness to him will react in ultimate improvement upon bis work. _

No serious argument' to make wrong appear right would have half as much effect in sending a youth into evil courses as the careless word that depicts sin of any kind as alight and trivial matter. Never delay till to-morow what reason and conscience tell you ought to be performed to-day. To-morrow is not yours; and though youlshould live to enj4;.y it, you must not overload, it with a burden not its own. The social element in our human nature was implanted in us for mutual assistance and protection. If this natural gift were more cultivated and respected, there would be fewer of the class who describe themselves as" unknown" or "alone."

Little-three-year-old May had a cup of very weak tea given her the other evening, which she stirred for quite a while, and then covered with her saucer. "What's the matter, May ?—is your tea sweet enough ?" asks mamma. "Yes, mamma, thank you. I's waiting for it to draw." Lost wealth may be regained by industry, the wreck of health repaired by temperance, forgotten knolvledge retgred by study, and even forfeite reputation won hick by penitence and virtue; butwho ever again looked upon his vanished hours, recalled his slighted years and stamped them with wisdom, or effaced from Heai-en's record the fearful blot of a wasted life?

The following is an Arabic proverb taken down from the mouth of an Oriental—" Men are four. (1) He who -knows net, and knows not he knows not. He is a fool; shun him. (2) He who knows not, and knows he knows not. He is simple; teach him. (3) He who knows, and knows not he knows. He is asleep; wake him. (4) He who knows, and knows he knows. He is wise; follow him." s • Among the advertisernents in a German paper there . lately appeared the following :—‘. The- gentleman who found a purse with money in the Blumenstrasse is re- quested to forward it to the address of the loser, as he was recognised." A few days afterwards the reply was inserted :—" The recognised gentleman who picked up a purse in the Blurnenstrasse requests the loser to call at his house. , INCEDENTS OF TIM CORONATION.—The Benediction, the Enthroning, and the formal rendering of Homage, now, ensued.. The last of these ceremonies had a singularly feudal character. First, the Archbishop of Canterbury knelt, and did homage for himself and the other Lords Epirituat; then the uncles of the Queen, the Dukes of Sussex and Cambridge, removed their coronets, d, without kneeling, made a vow of fealty in these wo s : w ' . —" Ido become your liege man, of life and limb, an of earthly worship ;• and faith and truth I will bear wit° you, to live arid die, against all manner of,folks. So help me God !" Having toubhed the crown on the Queen's head, they kissed her left cheek, and`retired. The other peers then performed their hothage kneeling, the senior of each rank pronouncing the words. It was at this part of the day's proceedings that an awkward incident oc- curred—an incident, however, which served to bring out an amiable trait in the sovereign's character: As Lord Rolle, then upwards of eighty, was ascending the steps to the throne, he stumbled and fell. The Queen, for- getting all the ceremonieus pomp of the occasion, started forward as if to save him, held out her hand for him to kiss, and expressed a hope that his Lordship was not I hurt. Some rather obvious puns were made on the corre- spondence of the noble Lord's involuntary action with the title which he bore; and even his daughter was heard , to remark, after it had been ascertained that no dainage was done, "Oh, it's nothing I It's only part of his tenure to play the roll at the Coronation."—From Part I. of "The Life and Times of Queen Victoria." MORE CHINESE Alsomaues.—The stranger would find that Chinese titres have no scenery, that perform- ances take place in the open air in the daytime, while the orchestra is on the stage behind the actors ; that the entrance to and exit from the boards aronot from the - sides but from the rear of the stage, and that there is 1 but one of each; the one on the left marking the en- tranee and the one on the right the exit. Furthermore, the stranger would find that although in the. West, those engaged in the business use their own name, in China no one does so. Fancy names are taken, rather such as suit, their fancy, and under them commercial affairs are car- ried on mid involve the same responsibilities without Government interference. It is universally known that in China men wear petticoats and women don the breeches; that the former are never without the fan. A Chinese carpenter planes a piece of wood by bring‘ng , the instrument towards him. In a schoolroom tile scholars study their lessons in a loud voice, which as- sures the tea Cher of attention to their books. Should our stranger ask the length of anything, the reply would be, "Of ten parts three," instead of three-tenths, and if quality he would be told, "Of ten grades three" for the third quality furttead of carrying one watch hidden' in a poeket,u:Chinese gentleman wears Steo outaldo of his' garments attached to a waistbelt of embroidered silk, with their faces exposed. Whereas in the western world it is indecorous to ask another's age, in China it is a com- pliment, and as regards one's name it is the correct thing to be asked, "What is your honourable name?" and the reply, "My unimportant name is Chung." While . the clothing of the Fankwae is stuffed with pockets, that of the Celestial has none His stockings, which are out- side of the trousers, as ;ell as his boots, serve as recep- ---taoles for papers, and in one or the other is thrust the folded fan when not in use while the handkerchief is carried in the sleeve. Fkwers are never planted in the earth, but in pots whic are; arranged- or circular or square steps, or of a pyramidal form, the effect of which , is pretty, with the advantage of being easily moved from place to place for,sunshine or shade. Perhaps, after all, the opposites here described are not so striking as the . relative positions of the family and the doctor. With tlie Chinese the medical man is paid so long as his patrons continue in health, but when sickness occurs payment ceases until recovery takes place; then it re- - coramences.—:Bits of Old China. _By William C. A young gentleman home for the holidays was titling with an old labourer at work in his father's grounds, when the old 'man said: "Ay, ay, sir, 'tis a fine thing is larnin'. There was no such thing when I was a boy; I Was a big fellow, helpin' the family, when all at once school broke out."

A mistake often made by parents is in imagining .that they should be always givers and the children always receivers. Thus the balance is destroyed in each, and both are injured—the children especially, in acquiring habits of selfishness. They ought rather to be accus- tomed to receive gratefully, to give generously, and to do both with gladness, thus learning that they are both duties and both pleasures which should never be entirely separated. Life is filled with trouble, and we must shoulder our share with the best grace we can. We may only seek to make it as light as we can, since to avoid it is impos- sible. There is. one sovereign panacea for this. It is work. Brooding over trouble is like surrounding one- self with a fog—it magnifies all objects seen through it. Occupation Of the mind prevents this; hard work— manual work even—gives the mind other matters of con- cern, and tires the body so that sleep will come. GOBETAN TAPESTRY.—In the famous manufactory of Gobelin tapestry,' which belongs to the French Govern- ment, are produced large and beautiful woven pictures, and the great merit of the work is that it is done en- tirely by hand, no machinery being used. The opera- tion is very slow, each workman putting one thread at a time in itslplace, and faithfully copying a painting _in oil or water colours, which stands near him, as a model. If, in a day, he covers a space as large as his hand, he considers that he has done a very good day's work. Dr. G—, of Edinburgh. was distinguished alike for , his gallantry and good humour. One evening, at a ball in the city, a certain lady of mature age had the mis- fortune to receive some slight mishap to the profuse drapery of her train. "And doctor," she exclaimed, in referring to the inCident afterwards, "it was so very vexing to loose part of my train; I'm afraid I appeared very awkward.' " Midanae," he responded, "by no means—though you did lose a portion of your-train, be- lieve meaou still retain your elegaut carriage." A Western editor of a country newspaper thus an- nounces the acquisition, in his domestic circle, of two "fair, fat, -and flourishing" babies :—" Bring out the brass band and place its noisiest members on the highest- pinnacle of the hencoop. Sound the loud horse-fiddle and let the nation rejoice; for one of the huMblest citi- zens of the commonwealth bath been justly exalted over, his compeers, and we have the honour to be that for- tunate and meritorious individtial. Still, we are not proud; we yet speak to our neighbours o'coasionally ; but at the same time it must be admitted that Nfe feel several:inches taller than 'We did a week ago." A Yankee who had suddenly acquired great wealth by. speculation took it into his head to travel, and finding himself at length in Florence, made a visit to Mr. Powers's studio. Looking over the different statues, his eye rested on the Greek Slave. "What may you call that air boy?" he asked. "The Greek Slave,' replied the sculptor. "And 'what may be the price of it?" continued the Yankee. "Three thousand dollars l'z was the answer, as Powers gazed at the odd specimen of humanity before him. "Three thousand dollars!" he exclaimed; "you don't say so, now? Why, I thought of-buying something on you, but that's a notch above me. Why, statiary is rie ain't it ?"

- - The peril of employing highly educated young men as clerks was again illustrated by the following woman stopped at &greengrocer's the other day, and asked., "Is them lettuce fresh ?" "You mean 'that' lettuce " sug- gested the clerk; "and it is fresh." "Then you'd better - eat it!" she snapped as she walked on. The ,grocer rushed out and asked the clerk what on earth had hap- pened to anger her, and the young man replied, "Why, nothing, h only corrected her grammar." " Ypu have turned away one of my best customers! Only yesterday she came in an asked the how I sold these white sugar, and I got an order for a whole barrel. Hang you, sir! but if them customers want grammar they don't expect to find her in a grocery? No, sir; and if you see she again, you want to apologise in the most humblerest manner." Little Miss Alice Three-year-old has a very unfortunate habit of crying upon the slightest pretext. One day last week she was warned that the next time she cried with- out good and sufficient cause she would be punished. Soon after she bawled lustily. "Why,are you crying?" she was asked. "Becauthe Bridget wbuld not let me go out to*play." The punishment followed, and then this dialogue: Do ,you know why you were punished ?" " 'Eth mamma." "Why wa§l it? , " Becauthe Bridget wohld not let me go out to play." One day she an- nounced to her father her intention to grow up with as much haste as possible, in Order to be a music man and play on a hand organ." "And what will your poor papa do ?" that fond parent inquired, "while you are going about with your hand organ far away_ from home ?" Miss Alice looked perplexed. She is very fond of her father. She turned the matter over in her mind before she made answer; then she saidi "Oh, dat'll be all right. Y,u shall be my monkey, and go and get all the pennies." . A woman who opened a small millinery shop engaged a painter to paint her a sign. When it came home the other day she saw that it. read, " Mris. J. (Prolonged cheers.) Mr. GEORGE MELLY, who was received with much en- thusiasm, then addressed the meeting. He thought there had been a great deal too much said aboat him or his pre- eeace there that night, but he would add one word to all that had been said about him. In looking into his political history that morning he found, for he had almost forgotten it, that it was the Liberal party of Warrington who first gave him the idea of entering into political life.' (Cheers.) On the 29th April, 27 years age. he visited Warrington with the intention of standing for tee borough. He was met by Mr. Alderman Bargess—(cheers)—and by Mr. Peter Ryl ands. (Renewed cheers.) The negotiations came to nothing, and he was afterwards invited to stand for the borough of Preston. Defeated there, he found at last a haopy political harm in a vast constituency of Radical workirg-men—(hear, hear)—advanced by the Suffrage Bill of 1868 from 3,000 to 30,009, and whom he represented for three consecutive Parliaments. In those days it was not possible to free ireland from the yoke of the Church or from the yoke of the landlords until the franchise had been extended to the boroughs of England, Scotland, and Wales. It was not until after the franchise had been extended to the people of Great Britain and Ireland, that we were brought face to face with the democracy of Ireland, and knew what she wanted, and to give it to her. (Cheers.) And that was the great question which the people of England had to decide. He brushed aside in a moment all question of what were called Unionist Liberals. "The ?Times" well said that day that it did not enter into the imagination at man to con- ceive Lord Illertington, Mr. Goschen. or Mr. Chamberlain having a working majority in Parliament." (Hear, hear.) Thera were still only two parties in this great country (hear, hear)—in spite of the cabal of Birmingham, of the weak-kneed Whigs of Rossendale—(laughter and cheers)— and of the miserable calculating prudence of West Edin- burgh—that was Mr. Goschen. (Laughter.) They were not broken up like the French into groups. There were two policies and there were two leaders as he would show• them. The one question asked then was " Will you govern Ireland by force or will you govern Ireland by her own consent. Willyou allow the destinies of this great empire to he wielded by the Tory party and Lord Salisbury— (cries of "No, no ")---or shall it remain in the hands of the Liberal party and 11,Ir. Gladstone. (Cheers.) The ,single, question was, would they have coercion and civil war in Ireland now, or would they grant the Irish people the power to govern themselves with due and proper restrictions in Parliament assembled. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) Alluding to the address of Lord R. Churchill and its reference to " One men power," Mr. Melly said three years ago the extension of the sfafftage to householders in the counties was under consideration. Lord Hartington objected to giving the vote to the Irieh cottager on the distinct ground that if the votes were redistributed in Ireland, and a large Home Rule majority was sent to the House of Commons, they would have to grant its request. That was the beginning of our present troubles with Ireland. Last May Mr. Chamberlain, taking into consideration the difficulty of passing any por- tion of coercive acts then about to disappear in course of law, made some arrangement with Mr. Parnell as to having four councils in Ireland, to whom were to be granted the management of their own affairs. This plen, to which Mr. Chamberlain was deeply attached, ,was brought before the Cabinet, as we now knew, by one of those open secrets by which one got behind the scenes. It was objected to by the Cabinet, of which Lord Carling/ord, Lord Derby, and Lord Hartington were mem- bers, and at that moment Lord R. Churchill entered into negotiations with Mr. Parnell. He promised that if the Irish members would join the Tories in turning out Mr. Gladstone on the queetion of Egypt, the Budget, or any other question,they would make some arrangement,not stated, and at any rate would abolish coercion in Ireland. Mark that, for all this led up to where they stood that day. (Cheers.) Upon this arrangement the Liberal Government was dismissed from office and went into the cold shade of opposition. At once it was announced Lord Carnarvon, a Home Ruler, was sent to govern Ireland without coercion, and night after night Lord Spencer was held up to abuse and opprobrium and misrepresentation—(hear, hear, and cheers) —for having coerced the Irish people. Time went on and an arrangement was arrived at between Lord Carnareeon and Mr. Parnell,.ofwhich they knew this, that it was sufficient to convince Mr. Parnell that the Tory party, having abolished for ever the principle of 'force and coercion•in Ire- land, were gaing to grant Home Rale, and he directed the whole great Irish bode' of our fellow-citizens in England, in Wales, and in Scotland to cast in their lot with the Tory party. Notwithstanding these influences the result of the election was declared to be that Mr. Gladstone- was in a majority of 85 over the Tory party, but that- the Tory party•a-nd Parnellites combined,were only in a minority of one. It was an open secret that Mr. Gladstone communi- cated with Lord Salisbury, expressing the hope that be would jpin in solving for ever the Irish question., (Cheers.) "An old man tn a harry" said this puny vehipster, Lord Randolph Churchill—(hear, hoar, and laughter)—who re- presented the very dregs and follies of the Tory party, and for whom every respectable Tiny blushed every time they read his speeches or his addresses. (Hear, hear, and cheers) At that moment Mr. Gladstone was so little ready to take office,, but so anxious that this great question having reached this point in its history, should be solved, that he was prepared to join with Lord Salisbury, probably in the manner of the arrangement of the Seats Billawith a view of carrying out a policy which would put an end to six hun- dred years of strife, and which would avert an immediate civil war. (Cheers.) When Parliament met, this arrange- ment was still in suspenee, but with the appearance of Mr. Parnell and his 85‘ followers a change came over the spirit of the Tory dream. Mr. W. H. Smith was sent to Ireland to make inquiries„ and on the 26th of .7anuary the statement was made that coercion was to be at once applied, and that the National; League was to be suppressed by force. This assuciaticn was to be blotted out of existence by the most oppressive laws; but the attempt would have been met by ane rent proclamation and within a few days or a few weeks thecountry would have been plunged in a civil war. (Cheere ) It was not until the Tory party had.proved faithless to their engagements with the leader of the National peaty; not till the Conservative patty were about to use the power of that great democeacy of the newly enfranchised 25'4 mil- lion of county electors in England; Scotland, and Wales for the coercion (4 the democracy of Ireland; not until they had shown to, America, te Austealia, and to our own United Kingdom that they could not, and would not, preserve the Union, that they would not listen to the elected represents- tives 86 of them, in the claims they were about to bring forward to, govern themselves; not until then did Mr. Gladstone step forward and say iithey had no prescription to save this trouble, no suggestion by which clvil war could be averted, then be would take the helm and try to guide the ship. (Applause.) Bat more, they had been told that Mr. Gladstone must be wrong, for he was deserted by Lord Hareington, was deserted by Mr. Goschen, by Mr. Chamber- lain,. by Mr. George Trevelyan, and by fifty or sixty, or seventy sound Liberals. It was not for him to say a word against those gentlemen. ' He be- ijeaed them to be mistaken. He believed most of them were mistaken from the highest possible motives. (Hear, hear.) But when they put the authority of these men before him, he answered that he preferred the author- ity of the last Lieutenant but one, Lord Spencer—(hear. hear)—he preferred the authority of the Tory Lord Lieu- tenant, Lord Carnarvon, and the present Lord Lieutenant, Lord Aberdeen, of Sir William Bara-Dyke, and the widow of Lord Edward Cavendish. He believed that list of au- thorities, aad would add to them the name of Sir Robert Peel— (ehaers)—who had been Secretary for Ireland, and who, by reason of his secretaryship of Ire- land and his experience of the country, had been turned out for Blackburn because he was a Home s Ruler, (Cheers.) Where were they now? They had the

A CENTRIFUGAL MILK SEPARATOR in the creamery at Burlington, Illinois, burst recently,. One of the frag- ments struck the foreman, cutting off a leg, aed causing his death in a short time. This is the second accident in the vicinity in one week from separators. FEEDING Miten Cows.—Food, and the condition of the cow, have a great influence on the 'quality of the milk ; but there is a wide difference in the quality of the milk of cows of different breeds, and those of the same breed. Nothing will make the milk of an Ayrshire or a Dutch cow as rich as that of the little Jersey, any more than it will make the flow of the Jersey as large as that of the other breeds named. But this, by the way, is no argument wing., liberal. feeding, nor against feeding rich, nutritious foods to milch cows. They have their influence in the increase-of both the quality and the quantity of the milk. - SHEARING Mecnnsa—According to the. Engineer, a machine for shearing sheep is said to be in successful operation in Victoria. It is made of brass, in the shape of a small trowel. The motion .is actuated by a small turbine wheel, about 3m. in diameter, geared into another wheel, on which is fixed a; cutter. In front is a comb, serving as a guard against cutting the skin. The steam is conveyed from the boiler byan indiarubber tube, which is double, having One inside the other. The inner one is the injection, and the space between the two the ejec- tion. The machine is used in the same fashion as the shears, but cuts, it is stated, much quicker and far cleaner, without the least danger of injuring the fleece or sheep. MILKING Comimmow.—Details of the milking compe- tition at the last dairy show appear in the journal of the British Dairy Farmers' Association. Two. prizes were offered for pure-bred shorthorns, two for shorthorns not eligible for the Herel 13ook, two for Jerseys and Guern- seys, two for other pure or cross-breeds, add a champion cup for the best of all the breeds. Forty-six cows and heifers were tested, comprising three in the first division, fifteen in the second, nineteen itt the third, and nine in the fourth. Two mifkings on the day of competition were taken, and the points were awarded in considera- tion of age, number of days since calving, yield of milk, percentage of cream, and analysis of solids'and fat. The champion cup was taken by the shorthorn cow exhibited by Mr. Birdsey's executors. The winner of the first prize in tile fourth division was an Ayrshire' cow, and the second prize winner was a cross between shorthorn and Ayrshire. The fifty-five shorthorns, seventy-eight days on an average after calving, gave the good average , yield of 42-891 b., or about 17 quarts of milk in 24 hears, of high enough quality to contain 12-69 per cent.:of solids, of which 3-62 per cent. was fat. CitEmsx.—The most difficult 'part of dairy workis the manufacture of cheese, as it inv6lvps avast amount of

unceasing care and skill. The number of different kinds made is almost legion, and even in our own island each dairy district has its own special niake.k Perhaps the most important variety, as being the ode made most extensively, is the Cheddar, so named from the district where it wasfirst reduced to a system by Harding; and this we may take as typical of the whole. Shortly stated, the manipulation is as follow:—The evening's and the morning's milk are mixed together, and heated up to 80 deg. Fahr. To this is added rennet, or some of the arti- ficuoltubstitutes, sufficient to coagulate it in 20 minutes, though some prefer the time to be an hour. After it is " set ' sufficiently it is cut up, slowly with a breaker,, composed of thin sharp blades, into little cubes of half- inch size. Next it is further broken with the ordinary shovel-shaped wire breaker; some of the whey which has now separated is drawn off with a syphon, heated • up to boiling point. and returned to the vat, the object being to heat upithe whole to 100 deg., so that the curd may, by contracting and hardening, expel the whey out of its mass. The curd must be kept well stirred during the whole of the time of the heating up, and continued until it has acquired a proper degree of consistency and acidity. The whey is ttien all run off, the lumps of curd piled up' to drain in thd bottom of the vat, then put into a large chessat " (cheese-bat), pressed with half a ton weight, taken out:l'mA ;broken fine in a curd mill, salted with 11b. of salt to 561 b. of curd, put up into vats the size the cheeses are to be, and pressed with one ton for four days—the covering cloths to be changed frequently, during that time. They are afterwards stered in a room kept at 60 deg to 65 deg., turhed daily, the bandages kept on until hard enough to keep shape themselves, whenithey will be ripe enough for eating at three months Old.—Primrose .711C.Connell, THE VALUE OF ENSILAGE.—INTERESTING EXPERIMENTS. —Onefaf the most interesting and valuable features in connection with the recent show of the Bath and West of England Society, at Bristol, was the exhibition of six kinds of ensilage, made under as many different condi- tions. It appears that under the auspices of the society several experiments have been conducted in the manu- facture of ensilage, the object being to ascertain the loss or gain of nutritive qualities incurred in the process of ensiling crops as compared with hay made from the same herbage. Another point raised in the inquiry was as to the comparative value of sweet and sour silage, and the comparative advantage of pitting the fodder in a chaffed and unchaffed state. ' Summing up his reference to the work undertaken by the Committee, Professor Ramsay says there is a loss 9f nutrition in converting grass into silage, and also a loss of nutrition in converting grass into hay, though it is smaller in the latter case, and this would seem to.show that the feeding qualities of good hay are greater than those of silage. With regard to the superiority of sweet or sour silage, it is remarked that the question Is not settled by these experiments. Science and practice are the best guides, and not the laboratory alone. With regard to sweet ensilage it is observed that probably the care and attention necessary to Make it will'prevent its being .generally manufactured. As to- the advantage or disadvantage of chaffing the fodder, that is a matter which rests with the, farmer himself. By chaffing more moisture is retained, and in the ex- periments in question there was, so far as could be seen, but little difference in the space occupied by respective weights of chaffed and unchaffed fodder. In a conversa- tion upon this matter with Sir John Lawes at Rotham- sted, Sir John clearly stated his opinion that when heated to a high temperature for making sweet silage, there is without Any doubt, a great waste of feeding matter; but he prefers to withhold any definite opinion upon the feeding value of silage in general until he has sufficient Material from his own experiments to afford the. means of showing in- a -fairly _ conclusive manner what its capacity is. Sir John's silos are brick buildings partly above and partly below ground, the depth being some 20 feet. He intends to fill with chaffed Mdder as befcire, it being absolutely essential to chaff' for the pur- pose of analysis. At the same time, there is a great question as to whether it is as easy to make sweet silage from chaffed as from unchaffdd 'fodder unless consider- able time is expended in the filling. At the present moment chemical analysis affords little practical infor- mation to the general public, and the formula usually- adopted by chemists is decidedly unsatisfactory. I be- lieve that the great point, or one of the great points, with which we have to deal in estimating the relationship of the value of silage to that of hay is with reference to the moisture. It is asserted by some that water in the plant is identical with that which is unmixed with any substance, but that there is virtue in the water of a feed- ing plant there can be no doubt. For instance, if a ton of grass is given to an animal, and'the results are noted, it will be found that it has a greater feeding value than the same ton reduced to a perfectly dried food to which the equivalent in the water which has been evaporated is again added. It is just the, same with turnips or swedes, wWch, as Sir John Lawes remarked,lire abso- lutely tuid entirely food without any waste. In a long conversation upon` this question with Professof-Arna, of Arnerica;'who has recently attended the Dairy Con- ference this opinion was expressed in a very able man- ner by the PrordssOr. He holds that there is,a difference in value between', a mechanical mixture of food and a chemical mixtureosnd that, in other words, the water held by the plant or the root is chemical and natural, while that which -bas been added to it when it has bieen dried is merely, mechanical, and is therefore of consider- ably less value. This is a very pertinent point, and con= firms the belief of feeders in general; who infinitely prefer the peen or raw natural food to the dried-one given in conjunction with water.—JAMES LONG.

div.p: 'WRY HAS THE SALE OF " GORDON'S " EXTRACT GROWN SO MARVELLOUSLY? BECAUSE there was a demand for such a medicine Bemuse there was a crying want for a remedy on which the people might depend in their hour of need, and "Gordon' s Extract" has supplied that want, and is filling the aching void that existed before its advent. Because "Gordon's Et" enables the sick person to regain health, and the well one to keep it. Because health to the people—to heel who have to work with their brains or their hands to earn the bread they eat—is a vital neeessity. Because ill-health means to them inability to labour; inaptitude for work means lack of wages; want of money means the parting one by one of the Possessions of the household, the ornaments from the mantel, the best furniture from the parlour, the watch from the fob, the chain from the neck, and the rings from the finger. These and the Sunday clothes and the best boots, aiike of man, wife, and children, are taken one by one to the sign of the three brass balls, and are there mortgaged for the breal which ill-health prevents from being earned. They are fol- lowed by the blankets from the bed, the sheets from under tied sick person. the tablecloth from the table; for even though sickness be in the house, hunger must be appeased.. Alt the pages of this paper would be sadly insufficient to tell of the woes and misery, the pangs of hunger, the despondent minds, the broken hearts, and the Immature deaths which preventable sickness (preventable by the use of "Gordon's Extraet ") has caused. Because Ill' health is the bane and poison of life, and "Gordon's Ex- tract" is its antidote. Because "Gordon's Extract" ensures health, imparts health, regains health, and keeps health when gotten. And because health means strength; strength means work; work is synenymoos with wages; with wages come the comforts and enjoymente of life, decent clothing for the Children, and the ability to pay their school fees, likewise en- abling people to pay their way, "to look the whole world in the face," and to "owe not any man," thereby securing the respect and gaining the esteem of friends and neigheours ; and because health secures all this, "Gordon's Extract" owes its Phenomenal success ; because " Gordon's Extract" is ft health giver, a health imparter, and a health keeper; And be- cause the ills "Gordon's Extract" can remedy are many. Be- Cause it relieves sick headache, disperses biliousness, is a Curative for dyspepsia, a foe to liver complaints, and an enemy to kidney diseaees ; because of these " Gordon's Extract" has a place high in the bead roll of the world's fame. Row can it he wondered at—the aching limbs, the pains in the Sibs and under the shoulder blades, the loss of appetite or the teething of food, thes bilious vomit, the acidity and heartburn, the pain ,tter meals, the weight at the stomach, the dragging down of the intestines, the deficient bile, the deranged bowels, the impaired digestion, the failure to assimilate food, the in- ability of ',he orgees to extract nourishment, the wasting away of flesh, the decrepitude of confirmed ill-health, the despondent and despairing mind, the fierce fits of temper, the unnatural gloom, the fear of irripendlitg danger, and the cores of other Painful, confusing, untoward, end disagreeable symptoms, have, one and all of them been found to be amenable to the curative power of "Gordon's Extract." Because" Gordon's Extract " disperses, referee, and cures the strangest, the most Severe, and the most contradictory symptoms, and the worst complications of disease. And because "Gordon's Extract" does all this—and is a blessing to humanity nerd the natural 'enemy to disease—beeause Of these things the sale of " Gor- don,. txteact " has grown marvellously, and is still in- creasing, and in bottles at Two Shillings is sold at all chemises.

TOOMALS, 74, Boston-street, Brafford, writes July 24th, 1885.—Gentlemen,—Permit me to attest my unsolicited and humble testimony to the healing and curative properties of Your EXTRACT, not only in restoring the weak and debilitated but in the curing of Epilepsy in its most aggravated form; not only do I speak from information, but personal observation in one special 05s—viz., that of a woman subjected to the above disease for upwards of twelve years; not so severe at first, but as time went on the fits became mare frequent, until the patient was seldom a week without the recurrence, until she was reduced to sheer helplessness, and almost to a state of idiocy; for over three years not able to do her own household Work, and the family had tried anything and everything that doctors and patent medicines could do without effect; in fact. she gradually became worse, until the doctors said i there was no cure, and the patient could not sur- vive long. They had tried many patent medieines, one preparation to the amount of £7 This for a time seemed to have a little effect, and the family had hopes of a cure, but 20 soon as the system became used to the medicine, the medi- cine became useless and all hopes again blighted. The family, In fact, became seriously impoveri bed in expending money With hope of a cure, but all to rio purpose; besides, the hus- band's health became enfeebled for want of rest for such a length of time that he was laid aside for long, until the family Was reduced to a tsitiful condition indeed. however, as the last effort your EXTRACT was resorted to, and with surpris- ing effect! six or seven bottle, regularly taken successively Until the fits, became less frequent and the health became im- preyed, until the woman was enabled to attend her household duties; and now, though she has not used the EXTRACT for many months, she hos not had fits for twelve months, and is now in her usual health. Any party wr.ting me for proof, I will gladly unswer and give the full name and address of suf- ferer-, and at my expense; they will most gladly reply to any inquiry, but for reasons -which are justifiable, they would rather not have their name come before the public. Yet you are at perfect liberty to make what use of my statement you like, and, believe me, yours respestlully, DAVID TEIOXEAS, Bookseller and Stationer.

• FIGHTING IN BURMAH. RANOOON, SuNDAy.—On the 12th inst. Captain Duns- ford, of the Bengal Infantry, and Lieut. Wyneyard, with 40 Rifles of the King's (Liverpool Regiment), attacked 500 Dacoits at Salon, on the western bank of the river, 50 miles north of Minhla. Tne Dacoits were driven out, but Cap- tain Dunsford was 010, and three men of the Liverpool Regiment were wounded. These awaits formed part of Boh Shway's force, who recently killed Mr. Phayre. Lieut. Huggins, of the 21st Madras Infantry, on the 12th inst. routed a large body of insurgents at Geu, 20 miles to the north of Salon. Ninety-two insurgents, including five bobs, or officers, were killed, and many prisoners, incluiing four bobs, were captered. The country is disturbed. The pre- sent condition of Upper Burmah is largely due to the want of sufficient civilian staffs. DISTURBANCES IN ALBANIA. CORFU, SATURDAY.—Intelligence has been received here from Janina. Disturba.nCeS have occurred at that place owing to pillaging of some shops by Albanian volunteers. Ahmed Eyoub Pasha has despatched reinforcements to Janina to restore order. FUNERAL OF THE KING OF BAVARIA. Mtneees, SATURDAY.—The funeral obsequies of the late King Louis took place this afternoon. The funeral proces- sion was headed by the troops under the command of Baron Horn, General of Infantry. Preceded by the veterans of the Bavarian army, marched deputations trom the Prussian Hussars, the Austrian lufantry, and the Russian Dragoon Regiments, of which the late King was honorary colonel. Immediately in front of the coffin came. in accordance with ancient custom, 25 so-called Gugsloaenner, who were clad from head to foot in black monks habits, which completely covered their faces, leaving only the eyes visible. Follow- ing the great crucifix, which was cerried just behind the coffin, walked the Prince Regent, all the foreign and Bavarian Princes, and special Envoys from foreign States, including Sir Edward Malet, repro- sentbig Queen Victoria. The act of consecration was per- forme a by the Archbishop of Munich, after which the body was conveyed to its final resting place, and deposited in the ancestral vault. THE POPE AND DON CARLOS. RoetE, SATURDAY.—The Pope, when receiving on the 16th inst. a person possessing influence with Don Carlos, expressed strong disapproval oi any eventual attempt of the Spanish Pretender to dieturb the peace and tranquility of Spain. THE EXPULSION OF THE FRENCH PRINCES. Paws. Seercoenev.—ln the Senate to-day M. Beranger read the report of the Committee on the Expulsion Bill. The report recommends the repction of the measure on the ground that it was incompatible with liberty, and preju- elicial to the existence of good relations with foreign Powers. It further declares that the question of expulsion is not a matter to be dealt with by a Legislative Assembly, but one the decision of which must be left to the judicial authorities. Pains, MoNDAT.—The discussion of the Expulsion Bill commenced iu the Senate to-day. M. Jules Simon opposed the measure on the ground that there was nothing to justify it. He declared that the Republic had nothing to fear ex- cept from its own mistakes, and that the real danger lay not ia the Princes, but in the Commune. PARIS, liVEDNEsnave—The law expelling the Fretrch Princes is officially promulgated here to-day. The Comte de Paris and his son will leave for England to-morrow. After receiving their friends in the morning they will embark at Treport at four o'clock, accompanied by the Comtesse de,Paris. The Comte's manifesto will be published on Friday. The Due d'Aumale arrived at Eu yeeterday. Prince Napoleon will leave for Geneva to-day, and his son Prince Victor for Brussels. It is not expected that they will issue any manifesto, but a demonstration of Prince Victor's adherents will probably take place at the Northern Railway Station. It is stated that Count de Bon- neva!, Colonel of the 12ch Regiment of Chasseurs, stationed at Rouen, has reeigned his cornifeand. THE PANAMA CANAL. Palm, SATURDAT.—The preamble of the bill authorising the Panama Canal Company to issue a lottery loan points out that although the report of M. Roueseau, the delegate sent by the French Government to ascertain the prospects of the canal, admits the possibility of success, the under- taking is dependent upon contingencies of a serious nature. The Technical Commiselon of the canal, however, while not . denying the difficulties attending the scheme, had expressed the conviction that the obstacles which were apprehended would be overcome. In conclusion the preamble makes some formal reservations concerning the possible delay in carrying out the work anti obtaining the necessary funds for its completion. TURKEY. CONSTANTINOPLE, TUESDAY.—Sir E. Thornton has made fresh representations to the Porte requesting the ratification of the Egyptian Financial Convention of 1885, but has not yet received a reply. The Porte's ratification is, however, considered certain.

VLEIINA, WEDNESDAY.--fhe Upper House of the Ans. trian Reichsrath to-day passed the measures mentioned on the order of the day, including the NIP enacting a sPecial judicial process for dealing with anarchist offences. The Reichsrath was afterwards prorogued by Count Taa i ffe n She name of the Ealperor.

The revenue was estimated .at £72,328,000, and it would prob- ably amount to £73,601,000, while the expenditure, estima- ted at £71,681,000, would probably be increased to £76,453, 000. The Revised Estimate was, therefore, worse than the Budget by £3,409,000. The capital outlay on buildings and irrigation was put at £5,516,000, giving a total expen- d?turf, in excess of revenue of £8,368,000, which had been met by borrowing to the extent of £2,924,000. Under "Political charges," there was an increase of £164,000, due to extra subsidies to the Ameer, to the expenses due to the Rawnl Pindi Durbar, and to the cost of the delimitation of the Afghan frontier; and under the Army there was an in- crease of £3,053,000, mainly owing to the cost of the mili- tary preparations in connection with the Afghan frontier dispute. As to the coming year, the revenue is estimated at £75,799,000 and the expenditure at £75,617,000, which was only about half a million below that of the previous year, both years being swelled by the extraordinary charges due to political events. The Budget for 1836.7 is altogether better than the revised Estimate of 1885-6 (which contem- plated a deficit of over two millions) by £3,034,000. The year would close with a small surplus of £182,000; and, in spite of tbe difficulties in Upper Bursnah, there was no reason to apprehend that this would not be realised. The great increase in the estimated revenue is due to the fact that the revenues of Upper Burrnah are included for the first time, and the accounts of the Scinde Railway are also included. Under the head of opium there is a net improve- ment of nearly three quarters of a million. As to the ex- penditure, the most important items are nder the head of Army and Railways. The British troops have been increased in the last and this year, and the establishment is to be brought nil to 69,761 men of all ranks, excluding officers, and the total cost of the additional British troops will be £675,000 in India, and £150,000 at home. The native army is to be increased by 11,968 men, and the total in- creased cost will be £360,000. In addition, a sum of £244, 000 is to be spent on coast and harbour defences. The total expenditure on railways is £5,336,000, of which over three millions is for frontier railways, and the total amount spent on irrigation is £Bll,OOO. The present amount of the debt is £175,500,000, which is £14,500,000 more than in 1884.5. But in the same period the debt incurred for railways and irrigation works has in- creased by £22,000,000, so tbat the uncovered debt has ab- solutely decreased £7,500,900. Putting assets in the shape of public works, railways, &c at £208,179,000, and our total liabilities in the shape of debt at £245,556,000, our un- covere.l liabilities only amount to £51,377,000. The net percentage of the earnings of public works gives a return of 5-79 per cent. on the £150,346,000 of capital spent up to March 31 on railway construction, and the net return on irrigation works is 3.42 per cent. On the whole, be was of opinion that the financial condition of India was not en- tirely unsatisfactory. In the discussion which followed this statement, Lord R. CHURCHILL thought there was nothing in it to cause grave anxiety ; the expenditure was not excessive, nor would it be necessary to resort to extra taxation. He complained that changes in the form of accounts were so often made, and hopedsthat no further change would become necessary. Sir G. CAVPHELL dealt at considerable length with the question of Indian finances generally, and agreed with Lord R. Churchill that the increased expenditure would be per- manent. Mr. F. W. Maclean, Mr. S. Smith, Sir Fergusson, Sir R. Fowler and Mr. Everett also spoke; and Mr. HOWARD having given a general reply, the usual resolutions were agreed to. t.,...THE PATENTS AMENDMENT BILL passed through Com- mittee and was read a third time. Tns IRISH MUNICIPAL FRANCHISE.—On the motion to go into Committee on the Municipal Franchise (Ireland) Bill, Mr. Limo; opposed it; and Mr. H. Fovann having pointed out the impossibility of the bill passing this session, the motion was carried on a division by 66 to 17.—1 n Committee, Mr. BRODRICE moved to report progress, but the motion being negatived without a division, the Conser- vative members protested against the bill being proceeded with, and no further opposition being offered to it, it passed through Committee without amendment. Titn LORDS AND THE IRISH LaBOM:LIIRS.—On the con- sideration of the Labourers' (Ireland) Acts Amendment Bill, Mr, PARNELL move i to disagree with the Lords' amend- ntents.—Mr. BRODRICS defended the Lords' Amendments. —Mr. FOWLBE stated that Clause 11, which was described as the most vital in the bill, was struck out by the Lords, and he agreed with Mr. Parnell that the bill would be worthless without that clause.—After some discussion the amendments were gone through, and the most important of them were disaareed with.---Mr. STANSFELD an- nounced that the House would Meet at three o'clock on Thursday. The anise adjourned at 1-35. i HOUSE OF LORDS.—TVESDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 4-15. IRISH LABOURERS.—A message was brought from the Commons, announcing that they bad agreed to certain of their lordships' amendments to the the Labourers (Ireland) Act Amendment Bill, but disagreed with others. BILLS DEALT TlL—The Married Women Maintenance in Case of Desertion Bill went through Committee, and was read a third time and passed, after a lorotest by Lord Den- man against the manner in which legislation was being turned out. The Parliamentary Elections (Returning Offi- cers) Act (lea) A.lllolldalei2t Bill passed through Commit-

tee, clauses 2to 6, both inclusive, being omitted on the motion of the Marquis of Salisbury. The Report of Amend- ments to the Medical Act Amendment Bill was received, and other bills were advanced a stage. SHOP Houes' REGULATION.—On the motion for going into Committee on the Shop Hours' Regulation Bill, the Earl of Weems objected to a measure of such importance, af- fecting, as it did, the whole of the retail trade of the country, being shuffled through Parliament at the eleventh hour of the fe!ssion.—The ARCHBISHOP of CANTERBURY believed that the moral effect of the bill would be vety considerable indeed. A large number of shopkeepers were merely through carelessness cruel to the attendants in their shops.—The Marquis of SAIestoRY observed that the principle that legislative protection should be afforded to young persons who were unable to protect themselves was enshrined in our own law, but that was no excuse for the slovenly form in which the bill was prosecuted.—The Duke of ARGYLL expressed e.nphatic approbation of the general principle of the bill which concerned life, health, and morality.—The bill passed through Committee with some amendments, one of which was the omission of the clause requiring shop- keepers to display in their windows the hours of employ- ment of their assistants.—A. proposal by the Earl of LIMERICK IO exempt licensed refreshment-rooms and public- housterfrom the operation of the bill was rejected by 20 votes to 5. A DRINK I:hue—Lord FITZGERALD moved the second reading of the Intoxicating Liquors (Sale to Children) Bill. —Lord HARRIS objected to it, but the Marquis of. SALIS- BURY did not think it worthy of serious opposition, as he did not suppose eny attention woula be paid to it if it be- came law.—The bill was read a second time. The Consolidated Fund (Appropriation) Bill and the Pub- lie Works Loans Bill were also read a second time. The House adjourned at 8-10 till Wednesday. HOUSE OF LORDS.—VEDNESDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at three o'clock. THIRD READINGS.—The reports of the Committees on the Parliamentary Elections (Returning Officers) Act 1885 Amendment Bill, the Land Tax Commissioners' Names Bill, and the Returning Officers' Charges (Scotland) Bill were considered and agreed to, and the Standing Orders havine been suspended, were read a third time.—On the report of the Tithe Rent Charge Extraordinary Redemption Bill, Lord HARRIS protested against the alterations which had be ads in the bill since it had passed through the Corn- ta-ee of the House of Coremons.—The report was agreed to. and the bill read a third time. THE SHOP HOURS BILL.—On the 'report of the Shop Hours Regulation Bill, the Earl of WEMYSS moved that it was not desirable to proceed with the bill until the evidence taken 'before the Select Committee of the House of Com- mons bad been presented to this House.—Lord ELLEN- BOROUGH objected to the bill on the ground teat it would press heavily on shopkeepers in the poorer districts.—The nuke of ARGTLL characterised the opposition to Lord Wemyss at this stage as that of a fanatic.—The amend- ment was negatived.—On the motion of the LORD CHAN- CELLOR a clause was inse-ted recliairing a notice for the shop hours to be exhibited.—The report was agreed to, and the bill read a third time. INTOXICATING LIQUORS (SALE TO CHILDREN) BILL In Committee on the Intoxiceting Liquors (Sale to Chil- dren) Bill, on clause 1, which prohibits the selling or supplying of intoxicating liquors to children, Lord COL- CHESTER snored to omit the word " supplying." After some discussion the amendment was agreed to, and the bill passed through committee, and was read a third time. IRISH LABOURERS, dIC —The Commons' reasons for dis- agr:eing with some of the Lords' amendments to the Labourers (Irelend) Acts Amendment Bill were considered. Some were agreed to, but others their Lordehips insisted upon.—Several bills were read a third time, Their Lordships adjourned at 5-45. HOUSE OF LORDS.—THIIIISDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter-past four o'clock. In the case of the Oldham Corporation Bill the Stand- ing Orders were dispensed with, and the bill was read a third time. ADJOURNMENT DURING PLEASURE.—On the motion to adjourn " during pleasure," Lord DENMAN again pretested against the dissolution of Parliament at the present time.— The Earl of FEVERSHA.M thought the dissolution uncalled fer. Her Majesty's Ministers, after their defeat in the House of Commons, should have tendered their resign Itions, and Lord Hartington and those who acted with him might have carried on the government of the countrve—Their lordships adjourned during pleasure. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THCIRSDAY. The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. In the case of the Accrington' Clitheroe, and Sabden Railway Bill, the Manchester Ship Canal Bill, and the Mid- land Railway Bill the Lords' amendments were considered and agreed to. MISCELLANEGUS.—Mr. BRYCE, stated, in reply to Mr. S. Smith, that there had been some unavoidable delay which would prevent the consent of the Spanish Cortes being ob- tained in time to allow of the Convention with this country coming into force on the Ist of July, the day fixed. It would therefore be necessary to fix a later date, and it was hoped that an early day in July would be named.—Upon consideration of the Lords amendments to the Parliamentary Elections (Returning Officers) Act Amendment Bill, Mr. LABOUCHERE thought it a monstrous thing that the representatives of the nation shculd be placed in the position of slaves to the Conserva- tive leader of the House of Lords.—Some of the Irish mem- bers were in favour of throwing out the Lords' amendments, , but ultimately they were agreed to.—The Municipal Fran- chise (Ireland) Bill was read a third time, on the motion of Mr. SEXTON.—The resolutions of the committee on the East India accounts were agreed to. The House was counted out at fire minutes past eight o'clock.

FERRYBOAT DISASTER IN BOHEMIA.-50 LIVES LOST. PRAGUE, WEDNESDAY.—lntelligenee received here from Kozerad reports that a ferryboat capsized at that place yes- terday while crossing the Sazava river. Fifty persons fell into the water, many of whom were drowned. Twenty- live bodies had been recovered up to this morning. THE LATE 160 BART PASHA. CONSTANTINOPLE, WEDNESDAY.—The Sultau has ordered the gunboat Nesgo to proceed to Genoa to take on board the remains of Hobart Pasha, which are to be interred with great pomo in the Scutari Cemetery at the expense of the Imperial Civil List. The gunboat will start at once under the command of the captain and manned by the crew of the vessel of which the deceased admiral was formerly com- mander.
IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT_ -

HOUSE OF LORDS.- The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 4.0. MANCHESTER SRI? CANAL Btu. —The report of the Com- mittee on the Manchester Ship Canal Bill was read, and, the Standing Orders being suspended, the measure was passed through all its remaining stages. THE GOVERNMENT OF INDIA ComurrrEs —The Earl of KIMBERLEY moved to discharge the orders of the 11th and 16th of March last respecting the Select Committee on the operation of the Act for the Better Government of India (1858) and certain ether Acts relating to India. He ex- plained that his reason for so doing was the objection which had been taken to the Committee in the House of Commons, particularly by Lord R. Churchill, both on account of its numbers and the unofficial character of its members. He pointed out that Lord Randolph Churchill had himself sug- gested an inquiry.—Lord SALISBURY objected to the very unusual course taken by Lord Kimberley.—The motion was then agreed to. RETURNING OFFICERS' EXPENSES AND THE RATES.— Earl SPENCER moved the second reading of the Parliament- ary Elections (Returning Officers) Expenses Act (1875) Amendment Bill. In explaining the provisions of the Bill be pointed out that they all tended to the reduction of the cost of elections, and as to that section throwing the return- ing officers' expenses on the rates he submitted that it was no new principle, having been adopted in connection with the election of sanitary boards, school boards, and municipal councils.—Lord SALISBURY offered to withdraw his opposi- tion to the second reading if the Government agreed to restore the bill to its original shape. There was no evidence before their Lotdships that the returning officers' charges were new too high, and he had received a number of letters from returning officers stating that the scale laid down in the schedule was insufficient. If the Government did not accept his offer, be would move the rejection of the bill.— Lord SELBORNE thought the proposals objected to by Lord Sa4isbury required careful consideration.—After some con- versation between Lord KIMBERLEY and Lord SALISBURY, in which the latter declined to withdraw his opposition unless both the proposals to which he objected were withdrawn from the bill, Lord KIMBERLEY reluctantly con- sented to withdraw them.—The bill was then read a second

time. THE MEDICAL ACTS AMENDMENT Committee on the Medical Acts Amendment Bill, the Duke of RICH- MOND and GORDON moved an amendment to give the Uni- versity of Aberdeen and the University of St. Andrews each a representative on the Medical Council instead of one repre- sentative for those two Universities, which was the proposal In the bill.—On a division the amendment was carried by 44 to 41, and a number of verbal amendments proposed by Lord SPENCER in various clauses were agreed to without a etivi- sion, and the bill passed through Committee. A number of bills were advanced a stage. Their Lordships rose at 8-10. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. Trut DISSOLUTION.-011 the motion of the CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER, it was agreed that the House at its rising adjourn until Thursday, and he stated that the Proro2,ation would be on Ftiday and the Dissolution on Saturday. Tun NEW HEBRIDES.—On the third reading of the Ap- propriation Bill, Sir W. 13.itarrELoT asked whether any far- ther information could be given in regard to the action of France in the New Hebrides, to which Mr. BRYCE replied that he`was Rot able to add anything to what had been al- ready stated. INLAND REVENUE OFFICIALS —There was also some conversation as to the position of the Civil Service writers and Lower Division officials of the Inland Revenue Depart- ment, in which Mr. Puleston, Mr. Gregory, Mr. Pickerszill, and Sir H. Holland took part, an". Mr. H. FOWLER 'aid, with regard to the Civil Service writers, that certain sug- gestions were being considered, and when the Treasury had given its judgment on them they Would be embodied in a Minute.—The Appropriation Bill was then read a third

WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. There were present Mr. Brown (vice-chairman) presiding; and Messrs. Voisey, Forster, Isherwood, ,Ratcliffe, Clarke, Jolley, Grange, BonnM, Blaoklahrst, Woods, 3. Houghton, Eckersley, Kilshall, Owen, Humphries, Strange, Jones, Harrison, John Houghton, Wright; J. C. Sutton (clerk), and S. Sutton (deputy clerk). LETTER FROM THE CHAIRMAN. The CLERIC said he had received a letter, dated Carnar- von, front the chairman (the Rev. (ir. F. Roberts), stating that the sudden and unexpected death of his brother pre- vented him from attending that meeting. THE SCHOOLS. In the minutes of the Padgate Schools Committee it was stated that Mr. Henley, inspector, and Dr. Mouat, medical officer of the Local Government Board, met the committee • at the schools on Tuesday afternoon, and held a consulta- tion with them regarding the new dietary tables recently submitted for the apprcval of the Local Government Board. These gentlemen, together with the schools medical officer (Dr. Jack), afterwards visited the homes and schoolrooms, and found everything in a satisfactory condition. The medical officer reports the children to be in excellent health and the hospital empty. A vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Joseph Houghton, of Woolston, for his present of nuts and sweets, and his kindness in lending the children a field for their sports on "Valking Day."--On the motion of Mr. JorxisT, seconded by Mr. RATCLIFFE, these minutes were confirmed.

'THE WORKHOUSE. The Matron of the Workhouse (Mrs. Mackay), on behalf of the school inmates, begged to kindly.thank Mrs. Wil- kinson for the illustrated Dapers she sent them; Dr. Mackie for a number of periodicals, and the Rev. B. B. Prescott for two hampers of flowers; and also Mr. R. Isherwood for the oranges he sent for the children on Walking Day.— The CHAIRMAN said it was very kind of the persons who made these presents, which they might be sure would be appreciated.

WALKING DA.Y. The Superintendent of the Padgate Schools (Mr. Mines) reported that everything in connection with Walking Day passed off satisfactorily, and that as the children passed through the streets there were frequent congratulatory re- marks as to their appearance. c&c.—The CHAIRMAN said he believed the appearance both of Padgate Sckool and the Workhouse gave entire satisfaction to the whole of the in- habitants who had the opportunity of witnessing their pro- cession.-Mr. JOLLY said that was also the case with regard to the Blue Coat School boys, and indeed all the institutions of the town were well represented.—The matter then dropped.

A.FP3INTMENT OF MEDICAL OFFICER. There were three applicationslor the post of medical effi- cer for No. 1 district, in place of Dr. Joseph who has re- signed. The applicants were Dr. Cannel!, Dr. Adams, and Dr. Jack.—Mr. JOLLEY said that personally he thought all the applicants were eligible and good men, but inasmuch as Dr. Jack already held the office of medical officer of the Padgate schools under the Guardians, and bad performed the duties of that office in the best way he would move that he be appointed.—Mr. ISHERWOOD said that as one of the School Committee he had great pleasure in seconding•the proposal. When the committee had gone round the schools and made inquiries they always got the most satisfactory answers with respect to Dr. Jack.—Dr. MAMIE and Mr. VOISEY supported the proposal, and it was stated by Mr. JOLLEY in reply to Mr. Ratcliffe, that the remuneration of the post he proposed to appoint Dr. Jacks to was £lOO a year, and that it had cost Dr. Joseph something like IGO a year for medicines.—The proposal that Dr. Jack be appoint- ted was then carried unanimously, the CHAIRMAN express- ing his approval of the appointment. The relief cases were then proceeded with.

TRAGIC SUICIDE UT PIRESI% PARK, DUBLITC-011 Tues- day the police found in the Horse Shoe pond, Phccnix Park, Dublin, the dead body of a gentleman' aged 35 years, about five feet nine inches in height, dressed in dark tweed. Be- side his hat was the following letter, unsigned :—" For this act which I contemplate, no one is directly or indirectly re- sponsible. It is my own act. I have not even been thrown over by my friends. They know not where lam or how situated. For the past thee days I have been wandering about. sleeping in the parks at night, and as I see no prospect of this dreary.outlook clearing up, I think it well to end it thus. It would be worth while opening my head. lam certain there is something wrong, not insanity, but some sort of derangement which produces effects not dissimilar to those of insanity. If anyone who knows me living should see me now, it would be a Last act of kindness—certainly the last I should have an opportunity of seeking for on this occasion—to cut me dead."

MEETING AT BURTON WOOD. A meeting of the Liberals of Buttonwood was held in the National Schoolroom, Buttonwood, on Thursday evening when there was a large attendance. The chair was ocea- pied by Mr. G. W. Rawlins, of Rainhill, who was supported by Messrs. C. A. Luffman (Newton), J. Prescott (Earks- town), F. Broadbridge (election agent), J. tewton ("Collins Green), Sze. The CIIIIII3iAN sal:: they were passing through a . crisis more important than any other crisis of the present cen- tury. The House of Commons was to be dissolved and the people of the country had to decide upon the policy to be adopted with regard to Ireland. (Hear, hear.) Party dis- sensions were what they must always reckon upon on such occasions, for the Liberal party were not led by the nose like the Tory party, Liberals had a healthy habit of think- ing for themselves, and be would much rather they had honest opposition than opposition based upon selfish obedi- ence to orders. (Applause.) They must regret those who had left their ranks, and they respected their honest scruples and convictions, but they could not but regret that they looked upon the ques ion of the Government of Ireland in a different light to that in which they (the Liberals) did. (Applause.) They were now face to face with a general election, and the Newton Divieion could not have allowed Sir Richard Cross to have a walk over. It was the duty of the Liberal party to have a fight and see what was the opinion of the voters upon the Irish qnestion, and they thought they were going t 4 win. (AppAase.) The Tories thought they were going to win because they hoped to be backed up by a certain number of Liberal dissentients, but his (the chairman's) inquiries lead Lim to the conviction that the Liberal party was strong and united, and that it would be polled for Mr. Gladstone in its full strength. (Ap- plause.) He thought in Sir George Errington they hea a man more likely to win the seat than any other they could think off, and that the country would vote Liberal and Gladstonia.n, white they had every appearance of being able to return Sir George Errington. (Applause.) Mr. C. A. LIIFFMAN proposed "That this meeting COl- dually approves the Irish policy of her Majesty's Govern- ment, and earnestly hopes that the elections now impend• ing will result in the return of a majority to the House ot Commons pledged to give to Ireland a fair and complete system of self-government." lie aaked, why should not the Irish people govern themselves ; and said when they found a difficulty in saying Irishmen. should govern Ire- land, it was not because the thing itself was wicked and elate], but it was because of the prejudices clinging around the question. (Hear, hear.) Ha thought niany• of the prejudices were due to the acts of rapine and violence which bad accompanied the aeitation, bot there had never been a movement towards liberty in this century which had not been accompanied by similar acts--.-(bear, hear,)—which seemed to be the acts of the most ieretrant men, and their rough mode of expressing their opinion. They were agitating for that which Liberals had striven for veers to obtain. and that was government for the people by the people—(applause)and let the Liberals as reasonable men give it to them. (Renewed applause.) The antagonism to Home Role was principally found in the Orange ranks, and if they were excluded they could scarcelg find a Protestant in Ireland who was opposed to the measure. (Hear, hear.) The question .was, in what spirit d,d they intend to apprcach the matter? Was it to be Lord Salis- bury who should deal with it, or Mr. Gladstone? (" Mr. Gladstone," and applause.) Then be urged them to support Sir George Errington. (Applause.) Mr. MEHERS (Burtonwood) seconded the resolution, and

NEWTON ELECTION- SIR GEORGE ERRINGTON'S CANDIDATURE. The announcement in our columns last week that the Executive of the Newton Liberal Council had de- cided to recommend the adoption of Sir George Errington, Bart., as the Liberal candidate, to oppose the return of Sir Richard Cross at the forthcoming election appears to have excited a most enthusiastic feeling among the Liberal classes in every part of the division, and it would seem by the satisfaction which has been expressed that it would have been difficult to select a more Aular candidate. The Liberal "300" met at the Co-operative Hall, Earle-street, on Monday night, and there was a very large attendance, including representatives from every part of the division. The chair was occupied by Mr. Charles Pilkington, J.P., who explained the steps taken by the Executive in selecting a candidate, and announced, amid much .applause, that that body had unanimously decided to recom- mend. the "300" to adopt Sir George Errington as their candioate.—A short conversation followed, after which Mr. G. W. RAWLINS (Rainhill) moved, Mr. JOHN UNSWOHTII, junr. (Golborne) seconded, and Messrs. F. A. R. NEILL (Bold) and P. HALL (Earlesto-wn), supported a motion to the effect that Sir George Errington, Bart., be the Liberal can- didate.—The resolution, on being put to the meet- ing, was carried unanimously and with enthusiastic cheers. Various arrangements were then made for -carrying on the campaign in a vigorous manner, and the meeting concluded with a vote of thanks to the Chairman. On Tuesday afternoon Mr. Charles Pilkington, J.P., issued an explanatory address to the electors of the division in reference to the qualification of the Liberal candidate. A copy of this appears in our advertising columns to-day. It will be seen that Sir George is on his way from the United States, and may be expected any hour. Though Sir George Errington at the time of writing had not arrived in England there is great enthusiasm among Liberal workers, and a determination to put forth every effort to bring the contest to a successful issue. The candidate is expected to arrive in Liverpool from America to-day (Saturday), but arrangements had been made for a deputation to meet him at Londonderry on Friday, in order to obtain his for- mal consent to his nomination, the offer of the Candidature having been made to him and accepted through his representative in England. The cam- paign will be begun immediately upon the candi- dates arrival in England, and it is understood that his election will be conducted by Mr. F. Broad- bridge, who displayed great energy and personal activity as the election agent last, year for Colonel McCorquodale. MEETING AT HAYDOCK. A public meeting in support of the candidature of Sir George Ertington Bart., was held in the Colliery School, Haydock, on Wednesday evening. Considering that the meeting had only been announced in the morning, and that a heavy shower fell immediately before the commencement, there was a large attendance, and the proceedings were marked with great unanimity. The chair was occupied by Mr. Charles Piikington, J.P., Chairman of the Liberal "300," who was supported on the platform by Messrs. T. Shepperd Little, barrister, Liverpool; T. H. Richmond, barrister, Liverpool ; S. W. Rawlins, Rainhill ; F. Broad- bridge, election agent; Taylor, Bailey, &c. The CHAIRMAN commenced by remltking that they met under rather peculiar circumstances. They had begun their , campaign while their candidate was away; but, of course, they expected as soon as he returned to England they would have another meeting there, and the people of Hay- dock would have an opportunity of hearing and seeing him He referred to the action ot the Ex,cutive of the Liberal "300" in securing a candidate, and on the previous Mon- day night the "300" unanimously accepted Sir George Errington. One of the first recommendations was that if possible they were to get a local man. Sir George Errington was a local man. He was of an old Yorkshire family, and owned estates in the south of England and in Ireland, and he was the trustee of the late Mrs. Stapieton-Bretherton at Rainhill. A great deal of his time had beets spent in Lan- cashire, he was thoroughly well known, and he was a great personal friend of Lord Granville's and Mr. Gladstone. (Applause.) Those two recommendations alone ought to recommend him. (Loud applause.) Sir George Errington was also well acquainted with political life, and accustomed to all its details, and represented Longford county for six years. Besides being well known in London and elsewhere, he was the trusted agent of the Liberal Government. In choosing Sir George Errington to oppese Sir Richard Cress, be thought the Council had acted very wisely, and they could not have selected a better or a stronger man. (Hear, hear.) As a Roman Catholic, he was in favour of denominational *cation, one of the strong points in that division, an if elected he would go to Parliament as a thorough-going Liberal and a strong supporter of Mr. Gladstone's Home Rule Measures. (Cheers.) He (the chairman) was a strong Unionist, and he thought they were all Unionists, but while he believed it would be a great disaster to Great Britain to completely separate Ireland from England, he thought none the less that a separate Parliament, or government of Ireland's own affairs, was equally necessary. (Applause.) If they allowed the Irish people to manage their own affairs things would be better in this kingdom. (Cheers ) Mr. T. SHEPHERD LITTLE proposed—" That this meet- ing cordially approves the Irish policy of her Majesty's Government, and earnestly hopes that the elec- tist now impending will result in the return of a majority to the House of Commons pledged to give to Ireland a fair and complete system of self government." He remarked that he was what might be described as an Irish Protestant; awl some might think it strange that he was supporting an 'English Catholic, but the Liberal party, as a party, had entered upon a period superior to religious bigotry and intolerance. (Applause.) Sir George Errington claimed their support on a question' of the most vital importance to the wetl-being of England. and he thought the (proposals of Mr. Gladstone to allow the Irish people to manage their own domestic affairs, at

said the principle of Home Rule was one in which he had long believed. (Hear, hear.) Not only did he be- lieve in it as a matter of justice to Ireland, but he believed in it as a matter of policy, outside its justice, for the sake of the benefit of the two countries. (Applause.) If they gave the Irish people the liberty of governing themselves, he be- lieved it would be one of the greatest blessings, not only to Ireland, but to this country, for both peoples would be benefitted by it. (Applause.) Mr. JOHN PRESOOTT, in supporting the motion, said Mr. Gladstone now appealed to the Eliglish people and he wanted them to say yes or no to the great question he had laid before them. He' (Mr. Prescott) urged that it would be better for them as a great nation to grapple with the ques- tion at once. Ifeland was the diseased limb in the British empire. The Tories said let it alone, but it woald not do to let it alone. (Hear, hear.) The wisest course was to apply the remedies calculated to heal it and to restore it to its proper health and strength. (Hear, hear.) The Tories claimed to be the friends of the country, but they should not claim the monopoly of patriotism. (Applause.) He loved his coun- try, and he would not submit or support a single measure which he thought was calculated to injure her or rob her of her prou4 supremacy among the nations of the world. (Ap- plause) He was heartily glad to support Home Rule for Ireland because he believed England would be no worse but rather petter if they granted suc.n a bill. (Applause.) The resolution was then enthusiastically carried. Mr. NEWTON moved, and Mr. BROADBRIDGE seconded, vote of thanks to the chairman, which was passed and the meeting terminated.

Th Queen and Princess Beatrice left Balmoral Castle on Thursday afternoon for Windsor, It Is 'announced that Mr Home, the well-kaown Spiritual- ist, has died at Anteuil, aged 53 years. Sir Charles Ed. Trevelyan, Bart., died on Saturday. He is succeeded to the baronetcy by Mr. George 0. Trevelyan, M.P. It is staed that the marriaze of Earl Cairns (better known as Lord Garnloyls) and Miss Adele Grant as teea broken off. A Parliamentary paper issued shows that the late ()onset, vative Government appointed no less than 328 magistrates in Ireland during their brief tenure of office. SNOW ON BEN NEVIS.—Snow in midsummer is a rare phenomenon. On Thursday, however, it fell almost con- tinuously on Ben Nevis, the total fall amounting to about an inch and a half, and on Thursday the weather was cold in the north. The national testimonial to Mr. Schnadhorst has already reached the large sum of £9,000, and it has been arranged to kcep the fund open till it is raised to £lO,OOO. One of the principal subscribers to the fund is Mr. Chamberlain, who has given :f:250. EIGHT PERSONS BURNED TO DENTH.—A fire occurred on Monday night in the repairing shops of the Metropo- litan Horse Railway, Boston, U.S. Eight persons ale known to have perished in the jiames, and others are missing. The fire is believed to have been the work of an loom- diary.
