div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, JUNE 26, 1886.

THE Addresses of the various Liberal can- tlidates in this part of Lancashire and Che- shire will be found in our advertising col- turins to -day, and we commend them to the tareful consideration of our readers of all Shades of political opinion. It will be seen that they are one and all sin favour of the Drineiple of Home Rule for Ireland. Mr. JOHN CROSFIELD from the first gave an em- Phatic support of Mr. GLADSTONE'S scheme Of self-government for Ireland; and he has tot grown lukewarm as the days have rolled by. Sir GEORGE ERRINGTON declared him- Self some time ago to be a Home Ruler; and he is not likely to. flinch now that the stone which the Tory builders have rejected has become the chief stone of the corner. qeaking on his behalf in a circular issued the other day, while Sir GEORGE was yet on the sea, Mr. CHARLES PILKINGTON, Liberal chairman of the Newton Division, said : "Re will ask for your suffrages as a staunch supporter of the principles of Mr. GLAD- STONE'S Home Rule policy for Ireland, as an advocate for a thorough reform of the Land Laws, and as a Liberal whose sympathies are:strongly enlisted in the general policy of his party." We heartily endorse the , !xpression of regard for Sir GEORGE as a Liberal. He has been of great service to the Party in the past, and we are glad to know, /low that the Irish voters and the English Catholics are standing side by side with the Liberals, that he has an excellent prospect of being returned by a substantial majority. The Tories of the Division have professed to have great doubt as to whether he would stand a contest. They may now set themselves at ease—if they can—for Sir GEORGE arrived at Liverpool yesterday afternoon. He at once approved of all that had been done on his be- half, and his address—a thoughtful and effec- tive one—will be found in another column. Mr. AUGUSTINE BIRRELL is in the thick of the fight in the Widnes Division; and his re- turn is regarded as a matter of course by the Conservatives, as well as by the Liberals. There is a large preponderance of Irish elec- tors in the Division ; and, as Mr. T. C. 13-cvARDs-Moss was swallowed in November as a bitter pill, they are going to enjoy them- selves this time by putting Mr. Moss in a hopeless minority. Mr. BIRRELL declares himself in his Address to be "a warm sup- Port,n- of Mr. GLADSTONE." He is not blind to the facts of the situation; on the contrary, he looks at them at all sides, for he says : Difficulties there may be ahead of us, but it is Surely better to pass through these than to dwell ianiongst them for ever. Mr. Gladstone's policy may '3e difficult: Lord Salisbury's is plainly impossible. .T3he twenty years of firm government Lord Salis- My advocates would be twenty years of bullying and. coaxing, and of constant and discreditable in- tligue with the Nationalist Party in the British varliament. Such a policy, so far from strengthen- ing the Imperial Parliament, would disgrace and ihight destroy it. Home Rule has never failed yet, and I rejoice that the only available course open to us is one which has so fair a chance of success. Mr. J. T. BRUNNER, M.P., as the accepted candidate of the Liberals of the Northwich Division, has a comparatively easy task be- fore him. The Conservatives are so dis- heartened by the beating which he gave them in November last that they have not been able to "screw their courage to the sticking Place." Unable -to induce Mr. W. H. VER- 15IN to try another fall as a Conservative, they have persuaded his brother, Mr. ROBERT YERDIN, to enter the lists as a Liberal Unionist, hoping thereby to create disunion amongst the Liberals. This is "a weak invention of the enemy." and it is doomed to miserable failure. Mr. BRUNNER'S Address gives a brief summary of the events which have led up to the present crisis, and it is throughout Pervaded by a fine spirit. He quotes the following passage from one of Mr. GLAD- 1 STONE's speeches made in November last-1 a passage which ought to stop the mouths of those who erroneously assert that no warn- had been given of what was likely to happen : If (said Mr. Gladstone) su.ch a matter comes for- Ward at the outset of the proceedings of the new arliament as I have described, namely, a demand bade constitutionally by the vast majority of the Topresentatives of Ireland. for the concession of large local powers of self-government, accompanied Z9hth the admission that the unity of the Empire 18 not to be impaired, the magnitude of that sub- ject will sweep into the shade for the moment, all those subjects of ordinary legislation on which I, or Others, have addressed you, and the satisfactory Eettlement of that subject, which goes down to the l'ory roots and foundations of our whole civil and

political constitution, will become the first duty of Parliament. MR. ARTHUR SINCLAIR stands a good chance of defeating Mr. SETON-KARR at St. Helens, where, as at Widnes, the Irish vote is exceedingly strong. Mr. SETON-KARR denies that the alternative policy "is a policy of coercion," but he cannot deny that Lord SALISBURY has talked of twenty years of coercion; or that the Tory leader in the House of Commons announced, on the 26th January last that the policy Lord SALISBURY'S Admini- stration had decided on was the "suppression of the National League." The Tory can- didates may juggle with words ; but their tricks are childish—they can be seen through. Mr. SINCLAIR does not thus dodge the issue; 'he faces it manfully, for, as he aptly observes in his address, he does not "see any reason, why the principle of local autonomy, which has been so successful in other countries, I should be inapplicable to the United King- dom." And with regard to the particular form of the application of the principle, he. gives good reasons for the faith that is in him. Speaking the other day at the de- monstration in the Engineer Hall, he said : Mr. Gladstone with his great genius has proposed a plan which has one great advantage, and that is, that it has been accepted cordially by the 85 mem- bers who represent the bulk of the people of Ire- land in the House of Commons. Some people say that a great many Irishmen did' not vote for the 85 representatives who follow Mr. Parnell. But when we for the first time have let all the householders vote, an we find them return out of seven-eighths of the area of Ireland, 85 members to Parliament, all holding one view, on this question, if representa- tive government is not the most complete farce possible, we ought to listen carefully to what these men say. Mr. GLADSTONE himself, it may be noted, used the same argument in his great speech at Glasgow, on Tuesday, and he pressed it home, for it is an argument which is un- answerable. It is due to Mr. SINCLAIR, as to the other Liberal candidates, to say that while he is in favour of Home Rule, he looks to it as a means to an end—as a means, in the first place, of satisfy- ing the aspirations of the Irish people, and of bringing to their doors the blessings of self- government. The Irish question once dis- posed of, English Liberals would have the English Parliament do something for Eng- land, and Scotland, and Wales. There is a , reform yet to be effected of the land laws—a' reform which by setting free the soil of this country will find employment for surplus capital and surplus labour ; which will take off some of the pressure, in our great towns, in the hard struggle for existence, and at the same time add to the wealth of the nation by doubling the produce of the land. A reform is needed ih the procedure of Parliament itself; there is too much sham talk and too little real work. The House of Commons has too much to do, and those who would block the path have too much of their own way. It suits the Tories to have a dead-lock in legislation ; for they do not want anything to be done. Let Liberals , who may have their doubts as to some features of the Home Rule Bill, ask themselves if they are prepared to sacri- fice all their hopes of future legislation by giving the Tories support—either directly or indirectly. The case of the Dissidents would be different if there were any hopes of either Lord HARTINGTON Or Mr. CHAMBERLAIN forming a Government, or of either of them entering a Coalition Ministry. But there is not the slightest ground for any such expec- tation ; the electors are called upon to de- cide between Lord SALISBURY and Mr. GLADSTONE—between Coercion and Con- ciliation ; and the issue is so great—the con- sequences may prove to be so tremendous— that we trust reason and not prejudice will hold sway—that there will be a disposition to let bye-gones be bye-gones—to inaugurate an era of peace—to offer a warm hand, rather than an iron shackle, to our brethren across the Irish Sea,

ON Monday evening the Liberals of Warring- ton showed their enthusiasm for the Liberal candidate and for the cause which he repre- sents. Wycliffe Hall was crowded to excess; and a considerable number were content to stand during the whole of the proceedings. Mr. JOHN CROSFIELD met with a hearty reception, and, responding with equal heartiness, he touched the right chord when he said he hoped that the same sympathy which they showed to him they would show to their Irish brethren across the sea. He dealt effectively with the statement, made at the Tory meeting in War- rington last week, that he had made a foul charge against Lord SALISBURY in saying that his policy was a policy of twenty years more of coercion ; . he proved his statement up to the hilt by quoting Lord SALIS- BURY himself. All he had to do was, as he said, to "state simple facts and state them plainly." He ridiculed the opposition of the London " Times " as something they need not fear; the outaitne of past experience was that the cause which the " Times " op- posed was "as good as won." Mr. GLAD- STONE had gone forth with the cry of "Jus- tice to Ireland;" the hearts of the People were with him, and it was inevitable that he should win in the end. Mr. CROSFIELD said he had no fear that any wrong would be done to Ulster, if Ireland were given a Parliament of her own. Protestants in Ireland had no cause for alarm, with England as a nation of Protestants behind them. He then pro- ceeded to point out that we really owed it to Lord CARNARVON that there was a dissolu- tion at the present moment. If his lord-- ship had not had his memorable inter- view with the leader of the Nation- alists, the Tory party would not h:...ve gained forty seats at the last election, through the Irish vote; and the result would have been not a dissolution, but a majority of fifty for Mr. GLADSTONE'S Home Rule Bill. Mr. CROSFIELD concluded a vigorous address by a stirring appeal to all sections of Liberals to march under the banner of the PRIME MINISTER, and march as of old to victory Mr. GEORGE MELLY afterwards delivered a powerful speech, in which he showed by irre- sistible arguments that there was no halting place between the policy of Home Rule ad- vocated by Mr. GLADSTONE and the policy of coercion adopted by Lord SALISBURY and the Tory Party as far back as January last. The meeting was throughout in keen sym- pathy with the various speakers, ; and if there is as much thorough work as there is thorough earnestness, there can be no ques- tion that Warrington will, on Friday next, reverse the verdict which was given at the last election.

MRS. TOMKINSON AS A SPEAKER.—" The Man- chester Evening News" says :—One of the most interesting features in connection with the Cheshire contests is the plucky way in which Mrs. Tomkin- son, the wife of the Liberal candidate for the Eddisbury Division, is helping her husband. She attends all his meetings, and usually speaks for about 20 minutes. Mrs. Tomkinson, who is a bar- onet's daughter, is a remarkably eloquent and logical speaker, and full of enthusiasm for Home Rule. .

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY,' JUNE 26, 1886.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY,' JUNE 26, 1886.
"TOUCH AND GO."
Lord Randolph Churchill some time ago advocated a Committee on Indian affairs; but when a Committee is proposed by the Liberals he opposes it. He is consistent only in his inconsistency.

"The London Times" referring to Lord Randolph Churchill's address, regrets that he should have lapsed "into his earlier contro- versial style." This is one way of putting it; the scriptural way would be to say—" The dog is turned to his own vomit again."

The Irish electors of St. Helens have held a large meeting and pledged themselves to work heart and soul for the Liberal candidate. Liberals of all sections have but to do their duty, and Mr. Sinclair will win by a large majority.

There is a block on the line so far as the St. Helens Railway Bill is concerned. It has passed the Commons and also the second reading in the House of Lords ; but, as it is now opposed, it will be shunted into a siding for the rest of the present Parliament.

At the Tory meeting held at Newton, on Monday, in support of Sir Richard Cross, the audience tried to sing "For he's a jolly good fellow." But they couldn't do it; and no wonder; he is anything, as a speaker, but "jolly." The poet Gray must have had "a Cross in his eye" when he said—" Melan- choly marked him for her own."

This is how Mr. John Morley, in his Address, hits the Irish nail on the head : " The crying need of Ireland is a strong Government, and no Government Will be strong which is not national in the first place, which is not responsible for the consequences of its action in the second, and which is not able to exercise a large and liberal measure of real power in the third."

Mr. Gladstone has, by exposing his mis- representation, punished Mr. Caine for assert- ing that as Prime Minister he had made a solemn declaration that the Land Bill and the Home Rule Bill "must be taken both as one." The member for Barrow has, like' a mischievous schoolboy, been careless, or something worse, and he has, very properly, been "cained " by the master.

Lord Salisbury, under a threat of moving the rejection of the Returning Officers' Ex- penses Bill, has caused the clauses to be struck out which proposed to throw the return- ing officers' expenses on the rates. He doesn't want poor men to have a fair chance of being returned to Parliament. And why should he ? Does he not regard them, especially if they happen to live in Ireland, as little better than Hottentots?

Sir George Errington has been unani- mously adopted by the Liberal "300" as the candidate for the Newton Division. It is much to the credit of the party that they can brush aside sectarian feeling in the present great crisis. The Irish and Catholic electors will, of course, work as hard as the rest; and we trust that Sir George will be able to say— "l came, I saw, I conquered."

NIINOORN VOLUNTEERS FOR WIMBLEDON.—The Runcorn detachment of the 2nd C.R.V. will be represented at Witnble- don this year by Lieut. A. Timmins, Sergeant W. H. Har- vey, and Colour-Sergeant Mort. RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.-A Sitting of this court was 'held on Tuesday, before his honour Judge Wynne Ffuulkes. The list comprised 13 adjourned summonses, 48 original plaints, and 10 judgment summonses. There were no cases of interest. RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD ELECTION - A ratepayers' meeting for the purpose of electing three members to serve on the Runcorn Burial Board was held in Bettr-sda Sesool- room on Thursday evening. The retiring members. Messrs. Coleburn, Rooerson, and Littler, were unanimously re- elected. Mr. William Brookes presided. AOCIDENT AT WIDNES.—On Fiiday night George Wil- liams, a carpenter employed at Messrs. Hutchinson's Chemical Works, and who lives in Widnes-road, met with an accident. While following his employment he fell a distance of IS feet and fractured three of his ribs. Under the care of Dr. Cooper he is now progressing very satisfac- torily. LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOt.RD INQUIRY AT WIDNES.— Major Tulloch, of the Royal Engineers, held an inquiry at the offices Of the Widnes Local Board in reference to the application of fhe Board to borrow £8,900 for works of private street improvement. Plans and details of the pro- posed works were produced and appeared to satisfy the in- spector. There was do opposition. FOUND DROWNED AT WIDNES.—Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, on Tuesday held an inquest on the body of Thomas Clarke, who. was a labourer at Messrs. Pilking- ton's works, add lived at 32, Davies-street. He had been missing since Whit-Monday, and on the 21st inst. bis dead body was found floating in the St. Helens Canal. A verdict of "Found drowned" was recorded.

HILTON PARISH CHURCH.—In honour of the anniversary of the accession of Queen Victoria to the throne, special sermons were held at Hilton Parish Church, on Sunday. In the morning the F and G (Runcorn) Companies of the 2nd Cheshire Rifle Volunteers were present, and there was a good congregation. 'Die appointed accession service was gone through, and the National Anthem was sang. SeruvicEs AT CRONTON.—The anniversary of the Cronton Wesleyan Sunday School was celebrated on Sunday. Mr. J. Catterall, of Liverpool, preached in the chapel, morning and evening, to good congregations, and in the afternoon a'i address to parents, teachers, and scholars was given by Mr. Frank Lawriuson. Special hymns were sung by the scholars at each service. The collections realised the sum of £9.

WIDNES WESLEYAN CIRCUIT.—The liarterly meeting has been held this week, under the presidency of the Rev. R. Burdon, The invitation to the Rev. James Bryant, of Chorley, to labour in the circuit after next conference was confirmed; and Mr. James Hothersall was cordially- thanked for his three years' service. A large company p took of & sumptuous repast, generously provided by Mr. and Mrs. B. Brown. THEFT FROM A Sr. HELENS TRAM CAR CONDUCTOR At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday William Clark, having the appearance of a tramp, was charged with steal- ing a cape worth 3s Gd, the property of Thomas Fishwick, of Prescot, who is a driver in the employ of the St. Helens Tram Car Company. The prisoner pleaded guilty and stated that he slept in a tram car in the King's Arms-yard on Sunday night and took the cape next morning. The prisoner was sentenced to a month's hard labour.

RUNCORN NATIONAL SCUOOLS.—The annis ersary sermons were preached on Sunday at the Parish Church, in the morning by the Ray. Canon Morris, D.D , chaplain to the Duke of Westminster' and in the afternoon by the Rev. T. M. Armson, curate. The services were fully choral, Mr. J. Johnson presiding at the organ. In honour of the anni- versary of the accession of her Majesty Queen Victoria to the throne, " God save the Queen " was sang as a proces- sional at the m*raing and afternoon services, and as a reces- sional in the evening. ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT WIDNES.-011 Thursday morn- ing Mary Pincers, aged 48, wife of Samuel Pincers, a fur- naceman at the Tharais Copper Works, Lugsdale, and living at 25, Warrington-road, attempted to commit suicide. For about three months she has suffered from rheumatism and been low spirited. At half-past six she left the house with the object, as she stated, of taking a walk over Lugsdale Bridge. A quarter of an hour later she was found in the yard with her throat cut. Her daughter made the discovery. She is under the care of Dr. MacLennan, and is expected to recover. PRESENTATION TO A CUSTOMS OFFICIAL AT RUNCORN. —Mr. F. &mons, formerly the collector of H.M. qustoms at the port of Runcorn, has been presented with a hatdsome sight-day dining-room timepiece, and a pair of eiquisite vases, as a token of the respect and esteem in which be was held. The various shipowners, merchaats, shipbrokers, customs officials, and others connected with the shipping interest had subscribed. Mr. Meadowcroft made the pre- sentation, and Messrs. George Summerfield, G. H. Taylor, Rawlinson, and W. Shaw made a few remarka, eulogistic of Mr. Samons, who suitably responded.

LIBERAL ELECTION AGENTS. The following gentlemen are the appointed Liberal agents for the boroughs and divisions named : Warrington Mr. Henry Roberts; St. Helens: Mr. Henry Lindon Riley (solicitor) ; Widnes Division: Mr. H. B. Shores ; Newton Division: Mr. Fred. Broadbridge (solicitcr) ;. Nortltiviell Division: Mr. Algernon Fletcher (solici- tor), and Mr. William Handley for Runcorn Dis- trict; .Eddisbury Division : Mr. E. Brassey (solicitor). THE PROPOSED NEW RAILWAY.—The Parliamen- tary agents for the St. Helens and Wigaii Juctions Railway Bill attended before the Examiner on Thursday week, and proved that no further stand- ing orders were applicable to the amendments made in this bill, which was therefore read a second time in the Lords on Monday night. Thursday was the last day of presenting petitions. It is stated that two were presented—one by Colonel Gamble and the other by Mrs. A. Heywood, of West Derby. The last named was expected to be amicably settled, but the promoters could not accede to the requirements of Colonel Gamble, and no further progress can be , made with the bill during the present session. TILE QUEEN'S REIGN.—The fiftieth anniversary of the reign of the Queen was specially marked ia some of the churches in Warrington on Sunday. At the Parish Church the choir sang "God save tho Queen," and at the conclusion of both morning and evening service the organist, Mr. W. S. Woods, played Handel's Coronation Anthem ; and at Holy Trinity the choir and congregation joined in Singing the National Anthem at the close of the evening's service. Prayers were recited in the differ- ent Cathdlic churches of the town. The prayer "Vic- toria Regina" was sung at Buttermarket-st. Church after the last Mass. Her Majesty succeeded to the Throne on the 20th of June 1837, on the death of her uncle William IV. The length of her Majesty's reign has been exceeded by three English Sov- ereigns, namely, Henry • 111., Edward 111. and George 111 whose jubilees were celebrated in 12,65,

' ably over two millions of gallons. At Stockswell pumping station thefe are considerable alterations in progress. Mr. Timmins, of Runcorn, had at work men engaged in lower- ing the pumps of No. 1 well, in order to meet the increased consumption of water. There will also be made great im- provements in the engines "Virginia" and "Mary," and when pumping operations are resumed the yield of water will be increased from 900,000 gallons a day to one and a half million gallons. Accompanied by Mr. W. W. Gossage, who met them at Srockswell, the party drove op to Netherley, where a somewhat lengthened stay was made. The handsome buildings -were in capital attodition, and their appearance has been enhanced by the planting of about 60 trees, and a thorn edge which marked the boundary • while the gardens attached to the cottages were artistically laid out. It may be said that the gas and water works are conducted very profitably for the rate- payers. During the past year the profits on the gas manu- facture was £1,320, and upon the water works upwards of £BOO, which, considering that during the last few years there has been a reduction in the price of water amounting to the sum of about £2,000, while during Mr. Cart's control. the water rents have been reduced 25 per cent., speaks well for the committee in charge. At both establishments em- ployment is given to 70 men. Upon completing the business at Netherley the horses heads were turned towards Hunts Cross on the way home. The palatial residence of the Chairman of the Board' Wa.l3 on the route, and Mr. Gossage gave the party a cordial 'invita- tion to walk through his grounds, and it was as cordially accepted. Mr. Gossage. acted as cicerone to his guests. He pointed out .the fine-view that was to ba obtained- from the lawn, described the objects of interest in the garden and in his conservatories and hot-houses, and gave* the members the treat of visiting his stables, and inspecting the fine horses there. Subsequently he entertained the party in his residence, and he was heartily.thanked for the kindness and urbanity he had shown by Mr. Brown and Dr. O'Keeffe on behalf of the me mbers.. Widnes was reached about seven o'clock in the evening.

Mr. Seton-Karr says that Mr. Gladstone's Home Rule Bill would place "the legisla- tive and executive power in the hands of the Irish National League." There are 86 Nationalists in the. House of Commons; but the Irish Parliament would be composed of over 200 members. He has _ forgotten the first order, and, very unkindly, he ignores Ulster altogether. Mr. Seton-Karr is not good at ordinary figures ; he should confine himself to figures of speech.

• Warrington Liberals, in particular, will be delighted to hear that Mr. William Crosfield, the late Liberal candidate for the borough, has been invited to contest Lincoln as a Gladstonian candidate. Mr. Joseph Ruston, the sitting member, who is a " Unionist " Liberal, has decided not to oppose him ; and this means that Mr. Crosfield may count on an easy victory over Tory opposition. At the General Election in November, the Liberal candidate was re- turned by a majority of 1,025. Mr. Crosfield has gone further and not fared worse.

Mr. Gladstone is doing all that can be reasonably expected of him to satisfy the the Dissidents of the Liberal party. He admitted in his speech at Manchester, last night, that in view of the strong feeling of the country it would be necessary to retain Irish representation at Westminster, for Im- perial.purposes. And now let Liberals of all classes fall in, close up, and charge the enemy until victory is won all along the line.

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

2ND RUNCORN STARR-BOWICETT BUILDING 'SOCIETY.— An appropriation took place on Thursday at Frodsham under the presidency of Mr. S. Hope, of Runcorn. Mr. W. Stanway, of Lowlands-road, Runcorn, was entitled by the result of the ballot to an appropriation of £2OO. RuNcoAN BOARD OP GUAUDIANS.—The members of the Runcorn Board of Guardians held their usual fortnightly meeting at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday afternoon. The chair was occupied by Lieut.-Colonel Ashton, and there were also Present the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, J. J. Lock- wood, and Messrs. Stokes, Lewis, Mclntyre, Knowles, Had- field, Weir, Fisher,‘ Whitlow, Hewitt, Brandretb, Hall, Forster, Percival, Bagulay, Farrell, Fisher, and H. Linaker (clerk).—The Rev. J. J. Lockwood proposed the adoption of the minutes of the Finance Committee, which, he said, recommended the payment of the sum of .221 Us 7d to the Royal Exchange Assurance for repayment of interest in con- nection with the hospital and of other accounts amounting to i total of £36. There was also, Mr. Lockwood said, the an- nual statement of the clerk of the Board, which gave the number of removal cases as being eight. It had been the custom to allow two guineas for each case, one with another, and he new proposed that the sum of sixteen guineas be pied to the clerk fer his services regarding removals. There was now a diminution in the number of cases, and, it ap- peared that the Act of 1818, which conferred a residential settlement by three years' residence, had reduced the num- ber of removal cases. Formerly a twelve months' residence, without receiving parochial relief, would confer the status of irremovability, but not a settlement, as in case the resi- dence was broken the pauper could be removed.—Mr. Mclntyre seconded the confirmation of the minutes, which motion was then oarried.—The Local Government Board wrote saying that they had been informed by their inspector that he had called the attention of the Board of Guardians to the want of proper accommodation for the girls and younger children; the Board inquired if the matter had received the consideration of the Guardians, and, if so, with what result. The matter was left in the hands of a commit- tee:—Mr. Fisher said that some time ago it was suggested by Mr. Dansey, Local Government Board inspector, that some alteration should be made in regard to the bath room for the girls and infants. At the previous Board meeting Mr. Lockwood, Mr. Speakman, and he (Ar. Fisher) were appointed a committee to go into the matter. On the pre- vious Wednesday they met Mr. Davis, of Frodsham, the architect, and asked him to draw up a plan. Mr. Davis had drawn up a plan which, Mr. Fisher thought, would meet in every respect the requirements of the Local Govern- ment Board. The estimated cost was 275, but he thought that the work could be done for less. A discussion followed, in the course of which the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner objected to the expense of the proposed alteration. The Rev. J. J. Lockwood proposed that tenders be asked for; he thought that the Board could have what was required at far less cost than the one submitted. After further conversation Mr. Weir proposed, and the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner seconded, a motion to the effect that the old system be continued.— Finally it was resolved that no alterAtion should be made further than the provision of an additional " tub " for bath- ing. Relief business was then taken. CHEAPEST HOUSE in the city for Glass, China, Oriental Wares, and Fancy Goods.—l7s, Oxtord-street, Manchester.— Advt.

OPEN-AIR CONCERT AT RUNCORN.-011 Wednesday evening the Mill Brow Brass Band, which is making itself a name as a set of musicians, gave a concert in the Runcorn Market Place. Although a strong cold wind prevailed, a capital audience assembled and listened with pleasure to the following programme :—March, from "II Trovatore," Ver- di; fantasia, " Myosotis," C. Lowthian ; vales, My Queen," Bucalossi ; grand selection (with solos for cornet, euphonium, and trombone), "I. Puritani," Bellini ; mor- ceau, "Maid of Athens," Allen; polka, " Figaro," Schiller; finale, "God save the Queen." For intelligent and skilful execution "I Puritani " and "Maid of Athens" are deserving of special mention. Mr. Tom Outhwaite conducted. Another concert will be givbn on Wednesday evening next, when selections from the "Bohemian Girl " will be performed. THE 'AMOUR OF A RUNCORN INSURANCE AGENT. At Runcorn Petty sessions on Monday, Martha Savage, a young woman, who lives at Weston Point, made application for an affiliation order against William Palin, an agent for the Royal Liver Assurance Society, residing at 6, Clarence- street, Runcorn. Mr. Lake appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Knowles (Widnes) for the defendant. The case was heard a fortnight ago, but the defendant upon oath then denied in toto all the affirmative evidence, and the Bench de- clined to make an order. Additional evidence was then ad- duced, and it was stated that the defendant was married on Whit-Monday. On the present occasion the defendant was not put into the box, and no other witnesses were called. The Bench (Messrs. J. Brundrit and Alfred Thomas) made an order upon the defendant to pay 3s per week until the child attained the age of 16 years. A WIDNES PUBLICAN FINED.—At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday John Lynch, landlord of the Commercial Inn, Appleton, was summoned under two informations with hav- ing, on the Ist March, at the Drill Hall, Widnes, sold spirits and beer without having an excise license authorising him so to do —Mr. Heal, the superviser of ex- cise, prosecuted, and stated that on the day in question there was a ball held at the Drill Hall and the defendant sold spirits and beer there without an excise license. He obtained the magistrates' cons,:nt to apply for such a license, but he did not do so. His excuse was that he was unaware that it was necessary.—The defendant pleaded guilty, but said he was ignorant that he needed an excise liaise.—Mr. Gasket', junr., said the defendant had rendered himself liable to a penalty of £7O, but as this was the first case that bad been before them they would impose a tine of only 5s and costs in the first case and order th'e payment of costs in the second.

A RUNCORN WILL CasE.—ln the Probate Division, on Wednesday, Sir James Hannan and a common jury had before them the suit of " Frodsham v. Ffodsham." It had reference to the testamentary depositions of the late Mr. James Frodsham, a farmer, bite of Chester, who died on the 19th of February, 1886. The will, dated the 15th January, 1886, was propounded by the plaintiff, and 'probate was op- posed by the defendant on the ground of undue execution, unsound mind, and undue influence. It appeared that in January, 1886, the deceased wanted to alter his will, and sent one of his sons to his solicitor, Mr. Linaker, to whom he stated that he wanted to leave his property amongst his children. The deceased was twice married. By his first wife he had six children, and after her death be married the defendant, his present widow. By the will she was left £2O only.—William Henry Linaker, in practice at Runcorn, gave evidence as to the circumstances attending the making of the will in question.—On Thursday, Sir James Hannpn and a common jury resumed the hear- ing of the case.—After the defendant, the widow, had been shortly examined, a consultation took place between the parties engaged in the case, and ultimately a compro- mise was arrived at by which a weekly allowance was made to the widow upon the will in question being admitted to Probate, with costs out of the estate.—The jury thereupon found for the will, which was pronounced for by the learned judge, who said that the arrangement was a 'eery proper one to make.

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AIITYORITY.—The usual fortnightly meeting of this Authority was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday afternoon. The chair was occupied by Lieut.-Colonel Ashten, and there were also present the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner and J. J. Lockwood; Messrs. Knowles, Hadfield, Stokes, Mclntyre, Weir, Percival, Whit- low, Hall, John Ashton, Lewis, Brandretb, H. Linaker (clerk), and J. Farrington (nuisance inspector).—The Local Government Board wrote saying that, having now received from Dr. Joseph Adams; medical officer for the Rural Sani- tary Authority, a copy of the annual report of the district for the year ending 31st December last, they sanctioned until March, 1887,, his re-appointment as medical officer for the district.—Mr. H. Booth, contractor for Overton drain- age, wrote saying that as more than six months had elapsed since he completed his contract he should, he said, feel obliged if he could have a cheque for the balance due, £49 103 Bd. The completion of the work bad been certified by the engineer, and he had put the roads in what he considered to be satisfactory order, under the direction of the surveyor. He had, he remarked, lest fully £340 on the contract.—The Clerk said that he had no doubt that the contractor had lost every shilling that he said he had, but as the necessary cer- tificate as to the satisfactory completion of the work had not yet been received the Board were consequently not in a position to at once pay the amount due. No action was therefore taken on the matter.—Mr. Farrington, inspector of nuisances, dic., then submitted his usual report, which con- cluded the business of the meeting. BREACH OF THE PEACE. Isabella Melling, a married woman, was charged at Warrington Occa- sional Court, Bank-street, on Tuesday, before Mr. Edward Greenall, with committing a breach of the peace by assaulting Sarah Robinson, at Newton, on the 31st July, 1885, and was bound over to keep the peace for six months, and to pay the costs, 19s.

1376,-and 1809. MR. RYLA.NDS' CONTEST AT BURNLEY.-Mr. 11,37-lands is in good spirits, and so are his supporters, who, with the solid help which they expect from the tdonservatives, are sanguine of victory. The Irish have also begun to stir themselves in favour of Mr. Jas. Greenwood, the Gladstonian. candidate. On Tuesday evening a general meeting of the Conserva- tive canvassers of Burnley was held at the Lecture Hall, Literary Institute, to hear the decision of the committee as to the steps to be taken by the Conservative party at the coming election." The chair was occupied by Mr. J. 0. ''S..Thursby. The Chairman, in introducing the business, said that in deciding to give their support to Mr. Rylands they were only following the advice of their leaders, and he quoted Lord Salisbury, who had said that no Liberals in voting against Home Rule ought to suf- fer by it.--Mr. J.lnowles proposed the following resolution :—" That this meeting approves of giving a hearty support to Mr. 'Viands after the gallant and patriotic spirit evinced by that gentleman, and this meeting pledges itself to use every legitimate means to.secure'his return."—Mr. J. Folds seconded the resolution, which was put and carried unani- mously. MR. LEICESTER, M.P., AND LORD SALISBURY.— Mr. J. Leicester, M.P., sends for publication the fol- lowing copy of a letter addressed to Lord Salisbury: —" I see by the papers that you intend to throw out the Returning Officers' Fees Bill. As a labour repre- sentative, I regard such an act as little less than an infamy, and I know that should you venture upon the patience and forbearance of the people in this matter you will hasten the doom you so richly merit. I have no words of contempt or scorn bad enough to paint such an enormity. The record of the act will for ever be the monument of its villany. What this bill has to do with you or yours I cannot tell. I only know that it would enable the people to send to Parliament those they thought fit. Your impertinent interference with this sacred right is a flagrant violation of every principle of justice, and shows to what depths of meanness and degradation a noble lord can descend. I regard this impertinence therefore as a challenge to the people to . do their worst for the wrongs they "aye suffered from that black and loathsome despotism, the House of Lords—an institution the removal of which would be hailed with joy from thevery centre of the land to its circumference.—Yours, in deepest disgust, JOSEPH LEICESTER." div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

_ A special meeting of this Board was held at the Gas Works on Tuesday morning, under the presidency of Mr. F. H. Gosiage. ,Present—Messrs. Handley, Heves, Mid wood, Wright. Gaskell, jun., Brown, Cook, Taylor, Houghton, Alltn (clerk), Carr (engineer), and Higginson (surveyor). Trim harm-nous DISBASKS HOSPITAL.—Tbe Clerk said be had written to the Local Government Board informing them of the Board's decision to erect administrative huts for the Infectious Diseas•is Hospital instead of the admini- strative block shown on the plan. On his own responsibiliiy be stated that if the period of repayment of loan were ex- tended from 30 years to 50 years the Board might seem their way to put up the structure according to the original plan. The Local Government Board replied that they regretted the decision at which the Board had arrived, but they were not prepared to extend the period of repayme:it.—On the motion of Mr. byes, seconded by Mr. Cook, it was decided that the tender of Mr. Rothwell for the erection of the boundary wall and fever ward and administrative huts be accepted. The amount was £2,199. It was further re- solved that £2.600 be borrowed for the purpose. THI MARKIIT FOR POLITICAL PIIRPoSES.—Mr. Allen said applications had been made for thu hiring of the Market Hall for political purposes.— Ifter some discussion, in which the undesirability of allowing the hall to be used for this purpose was commented upon, it was resolved with- out dissent, on the motion of Mr. Houghton, seconded by Mr. Cook, that the hall should not be used for political meetings.

HILL CLIFFE BAPTIST CHAPEL.—On Sunday, the anniversary. of ' the Sunday school in connection with this place of worship was celebrated. Sermons were preached in the afternoon and evening by the 'Rev. James Parker, M.A., of Halifax; and in the morning a special service was held for teachers and friends, and conducted by Mrs. Parker. The con- gregations were large, and the collections in aid of the school and church funds amounted to about £37. .

THE SUDDEN DEATH IN THE PAILK.—On Satur- day, Mr. W. T. Husband held an inquest at the White Hart Hotel respecting the death of a labourer named Seamy, a middle-aged man, who died sud- denly early on Friday morning under circumstances reported in our last issue. He was standing near the Town Hall, smoking his pipe, when he suddenly fell down. When he was picked up he was dead. Deceased was in the employ of the Corporation. He had previously complained of illness, but had not been attended by a doctor. The jury brought in a verdict to the effect that deceased died 'from natural causes.

CHARGE AGAINST A WATCHMAKER. At the Borough Court, yesterday, a watchmaker 'named George Tomlin, of Buttermarket-street, Ntae charged that, being the bailee of a watch belonging to Thomas Holding, file. manufacturer,. Kerfoot-street, he appropriated it to his 'own use, thereby stealing it. From particulars given by Chief Constable Hunt it appeared that on the 9th June Holding sent a person with the watch to repair. A few days afterwards he called for - watc,h, but neither it nor the defendant could be fpund. lIS called several times afterwards with the same re- sult. It was found, afterwards that defendant_ had given the watch to some one else to pledge. He had, however, subsequently sent money to redeem it, but by that time the watch had come into the possession of the police.—The Bench fined defen- dant 'los and costs. AN ORDERLY WALKING DAY.—There were only three cases an the sheet at the Bordagh Court on Saturday—two men and a woman being charged with drunkenness—and on the conclusion of the business Alderman Burgess, who sat on the Bench in conjunction with Alderman Chandley, remarked that it was very creditable to Warrington that after I a great holiday such as Walking Day there should have been so small a number of persons charged with drunkenness and disorderly conduct. He asked were there any other charges? Chid Con- stable Hunt replied that there were two ox three persons to be charged. Everything on Friday was very peaceable and orderly up to eight or nine o'clock in the evening. , Alderman Burgess then made a passing allusion to the fact that on Friday evening the streets of the borough were almost in darkness; he presumed that there was something , wrong at the Gas Works. Chief' Constable • Hunt said that there were two or three lightS in different ' parts of the town, and Alderman Chandley remarked that on a holiday like Walking Day it was a strange thing that the lamps were not lighted. The subject then dropped.. A FIGHTING FAMILY.—At the Borough Court on Tuesday, before Alderman Chandley and .Mr. R. Garnett, a woman named Dinah Gl4ave was charged on a warrant with having assaulted her sister, Annie Mills, on the 20th of the present month. She was defended by Mr. A. Browne. The case for the cOm- plainant was that on Saturday last she received a telegram from the prisoner stating that her mother was dead. She came to Warrington on the follow- ing morning and found that her. mother was alive. In the evening prisoner andcomplbinant quarrelled, and, it was alleged, prisoner bit complainant on the hands, shoulders, and other parts of the body. In cross-examination complainant denied that a quar- rel arose about a feather bed and the sum of .£lBB which was in the County Court; she also denied that she struck prisoner first. Inspector Berry said `that he received a warrant for the apprehension of the prisoner, and went three times to the house. He found the doors barricaded, and it was a difficult matter to get inside. On reading the warrant to the prisoner she said that she was guilty. For the defence Mr. Browne did not contend that an assault had not been committed. The quarrel,'he d, arose about a feather bed Which the mother had promised to give to one of the children. There 'was also a sum of .2188 in the County Coil* in the name of the complainant, and there had always been a dispute about the money. The two quarreled about these things, and called each other bad names. They then had a fight, in which one was as much to blame as the other. The mother gave evidence in support of the prisoner. The magistrates intimated that they gave credence to the story of the complainant, ana fined prisoner 20s and costs, in all .C 1 15s 6d. IlayNns's, for Goloshes, from is 4d to 2s, cheapest in the trade.—Adet. • . .

; SANE:EY Wrnx MiLLs' TRIP.—On Sturday the , workmen of Sankey Wire Mills had their annual excursion. The annual outing, which is a very popular one, has usually been to some watering place at a distance, but this year the increased attractions that Liverpool is able to put in the way of visitors secured that busy city a visit, and the excursion that was arranged to leave Bank Quay at 7-45 in the morning, and return from Lime-street, Liverpool, at 9 o'clock in the evening, carried no • insignificant number of passengers. The train was timed to stop at Sankey Bridges and Fidlers' Ferry. It will be seen that those who had the s 'arrangements in hand made sure of a long day in • the city for the visitors, but provision had also been made for their spending it in an enjoyable manner. Reduced charges for the excursionists had been se- cured for visiting the Great Eastern, and crossing , the water to New Brighton, where cheap facilities ' were also arranged for admission to the Winter Palace and to the Baths. The railway tickets in- cluded admission to the Exhibition, and the excur- sionists nearly 'all paid a visit there. The many ob- jects of interest were inspected with pleasure, and the local exhibits were particularly noticed. On the whole an exceedingly enjoyable day was passed. The number of people who availed themselves of the trip were no fewer than 616, and on their re- turn universal satisfaction was expressed at the way in which the arrangements had been carried out. Mr. W. Bramhall was the secretary. WALLING DAY.—In addition to the particulars we gave last week with regard to the -procession of school children on Walking Day, we may add the following ;—Ladies' School: Number of scholars on books, 210; average attendance, 165; number of teachers, 6; Mr. Beamont is the sole manager. There is no Sunday school in connection with the Ladies' School. The girls assembled at the school at 9 am., and proceeded to Bank Park, and took part in the general procession to the Parish Church. Games were engaged in at St. Elphin's College field in the afternoon, followed by tea in the school. at 4 p.m. The games were renewed in the evening until 8 p.m. Miss,M. Jones is the head mistress.— St. Mary's, Great Sankey: The Penketh scholars, ri numbeng over 100, assembled at the Penketh Con- skrvative Club at eleven o'clock; under the super- intendence of Mr. Jonas Foster, to await the arrival of the Sankey scholars, about 350 in number, and under the management of the Rev.. E. S. Jackson and Mr. W. Ray. Mere they fell into ranks two deep, and, headed by the Great Sankey Brass Band, and with banners and colours gaily flying, they paraded the principal lanes of the village until one o'clock, when they went iaito a field kindly lent for the occasion by Mr. Skelton, and there feasted on buns and milk, while the teachers went for lunch provided by Mr. Jeans. About half-past four the scholars sat down to tea in groups, and made a hearty meal. Later on the first-class scholars, teachers, and parents, who had now assembled in large numbers, went to Sankey School, where a. splendid tea had been prepared. Games were in- dulged in by teachers, scholars, and parents, until about 9-30, when oranges were distributed to the infant scholars, and then they began to slowly dis- perse, having spent an enjoyable day. VOLUNTEER CONCERT.—On Monday evening a concert promoted by the members of the Warrington (9th Lancashire) Rifle Volunteers was given in the Drill Hall, in aid of the families of two recently deceased comrades, Sergeant Adam Hill and Cor- poral-Bugler James Buckley Mellor. Therq was a good attendance, amongst those present being the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), who presided, Colonel Thackwell, C.P., Major O'Leary, Major Bolton, Cap- tain Gooch, Captain Buckton, Lieut. Baines, and several officers from Orford Barracks. The hall and neatly improvised platform were tastefully decorated with plants and shrubs. The Mayor said he had pleasure in presiding on that occasion, although his pleasure was considerably modified by the circum- stances which had led to the concert, for it was to render pecuniary assistance to the widows and 'young children of two of their late comrades, who .aad been bereft of their dearest and best friends. 'Hear, hear.) The musical portion of the pro- gramme was then probeeded with. The volunteer band, under the leadership• of Bandmaster Arm- strong, won much praise by.their performances, and. deservedly 80. Corporal George Wright, of the 19th L.R.V., sung three songs, "The gallants of England," "Forward," and "Jack's Reward," and was very Warmly applauded. Miss Cavanagh was equally successful in "Kathleen Mavourneenr and "Sun- beams," as was also Miss Rose, who contributed "The Gates of the West," and "The Old Loch." Mr. Cavanagh was down for "The Skipper," and "The Desert,' and in response to a recall gave an equally' good rendering of N" The Friars of Order Grey.' "My sweetheart when a boy," and "I seek for, thee in every flower," received, as might be expected, ex- cellent treatment from Mr. Dell, who was recalled to bow his acknowledgments. Several selections were admirably rendered by a glee party composed of Messrs. F. J. Dell, R. Grounds, H. Atkinson, W.. Knight, and (1 Monks. The legerdemain perfOrm- a.nces of Professor Acton very materially contributed to the enjoyment of the evening, and showed indeed. remarkable cleverness. The accompaniments were ably played by Mr. G. Riley. At the conclusion votes of thanks were, passed to the Iklayor and per, I formers.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held on Thu—r-s—day. Present— Mr. T. S. Tiinmis, J.l'. (chairman), the Rev. Fathers Clarke and Finegan, Messrs. John Brock, J.P., Bradshaw. Glover, Deacon, Itnison, Robinson, Dr. O'Keeffe. and Danby (clerk.)—The minutes of the District Education Committee, passed on the motion of Mr. Deacon, stated that during the month of May (three weeks) there had been 110 applica- tions for the payment of fees, and they were recommended to be paid in 103 cases. 243 persons appeared before the committee for contravention of the Education Act. Forty- two persona had been convicted by the magistrates, and one boy had been sent to an industrial school.—On the recom- mendation of the Finance Committee accounts amounting to £636 17s were passed for payment. The receipts for the month amounted to £1,166 03 6d, including £l,OOO re- ceived from the overseers on account of precept.—On the proposition of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. Bradshaw, it was unanimously resolved "That the state of health of Mr. R. Houlden Davies necessitating a sea voyage, his absence be approved in accordance with section 14, second schedule of the Elementary Education Act, 1870."—The Chairman said that the cause of Mr. Davis's absence was explained at the last meeting, and in order to prevent the seat becom- ing vacant, it was necessary to pass this resolution.

WIDNES LOCAL BOARD INSPECTION. The annual inspection by the Local Board of those im- portant properties of the town, the Gas and Waterworks took place on Tuesday. For the first time for a considerable number of years, Mr. F. H. Gossage, J.P., the chairman, honoured the occasion with his presence, and the other members who took part were Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. D. Wright, F. Heyes, B. Gaskell, jun., B. Brown, J. Taylor, J. Houghton, T. Handley, Cook, and E. Carey. Mesers. Allen (clerk), Carr (engineer), Higginson (surveyor), and Dick- son (nuisance inspector) accompanied the party. The gas works were first inspected. Mr. Carr acted as guide and in the progress through the works it was noticeable that every- thing was in the neatest and cleanest order. The greatest interest was centered in the plant for the formation of sul- phate of ammonia from the residual products of the gas manufacture. This process was foreign to the gas works until last October, when it was commenced owing to the low and unprofitable prices at which the ammoniacal liquor. could be dispesed of, and has been continued with very satisfactory results under the direction of Mr. Carr, the engineer. This plant cost £4OO and has been a very profitable investment. When the year has been completed about 130 tons of the chemical will have been manufactured, and so far it has realised les per ton after paying all expenses of interest and capital. It may be of interest to state that on an average the works produce about 80 millions cubic feet of gas per annum, which is distributed at net prices ranging from 2s 3d to large consumers to 2s 9d for householders. Entering a largo waggonette from the stables of Mr. Lea, of Victoria-road, the party shaped their course for Pea Hill. En route various highway questions were discussed, andthe particular spots to which they referred were inspected. At Pea Hill the immense covered reservoirs were apparently in good order, and a depth of water of upwards of 20 feet was registered. The storage capacity of the reservoirs is 12 million gallons, and the daily consumption is now consider-

div.head: SHOCKING IMMORALITY IN RUNCORN.
div.p: SHOCKING IMMORALITY IN RUNCORN.

At Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday, bdore Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. James Handley, John West, landlord of the Duke of Wellington Hotel, Per- cival's-lane„ was charged with having, on the 20th May, knowingly permitted his premises to be the habitual resort and place ot meeting of women of ill-fame. Mr. Superintendent Leah prosecuted on behalf of the police, and Mr. F. A. Lake appeared for the defendant. Mr. Leathwaite watched the case on behalf of Messrs. Greenall and Company, thel owners of the house.—The case had been adjourned' on several occdOons in consequence of two. wit-1 nesses named tlizabeth Mulloy, 15 years of age, and Emily 'Aldridge, 17 years of age, both girls who earned theirliving in an immoral fashion, who ab- sconded to Scotland when summoned as witnesses. They were apprehended at Birkenhead and brought to Runcorn by Sergeant breild.—Sarah .Roscoe, wife 'of James Roscoe, of English-row, Runcorn, deposed to a sailor and a youngwoman being drunk in the house on the afternoon of the 20th May. She saw grossly immoral conduct carried on in the bar par-, Jour. Margaret Langley, whose husband had charge of West's stables, corroborated.—The girls previously mentioned admitted that they were in the house all day, and that a woman named Bentley was very drunk there. They admitted that the house was the habitual resort for women of their class, and that the greatest immorality was car- ried on.—Sergeant Neild described the finding of drunken persons in the house on the day in ques- tion.—Mr. Leathwaite said prior to this offence the defendant had been served with notice to leave the house; and he had since left the premises. He hoped, therefore, their worships would not endorse the license.—For the first offence the defendant was fined .£5 and costs £3 14s, or two months' hard lahour, and for the second offence .E 1 and costs 9s 6d, or 14 days.—Mr. Brundrit remarked that he did not think such things could exist in the town of Runcorn. The owners had no idea how the house was being conducted or they .would have en- dorsed the license. But in future the fact that a person had left the house would not prevent the endorsement-of a license.

div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.

OCCASIONAL COURT.-At an Occasional' Court held on Monday, at the office in Winwick-street, Sarah Ellen Wilkinson was fined lOs and costs for being drunk at Little Sankey.--A man named William Jackson was charged with sleeping out at Arpley, and was dismissed on promising to leave the town. Mr. Edward Greenall was the magis- trate.

div.head: ij –
div.p: ij -

There were no charges down for hearing by the borough magistrates on Wednesday and Thursday 'mornings. Music IN TM3 PAIM.—The band of the Ist Bat- talion The King's (Liverpool) Regiment (stationed at Dublin) will perform in the Bank Park on Mon- day evening, from 6.-30 p.m. An excellent pro- gramme has been prepared.

- A RESTIVE Hoist—On Thursday afternoon a Mr. and Mrs. Stainer, who came from Martel, near Knutsford, were driving through Mersey-street with a horse and trap, and the horse plunged when at the corner of Mersey-street leading into Irlam and Church-streets. The occupants of the trap were both thrown out, and the lady was severely shaken.

NEM,' SCHOOLS. —lt is stated that the designs sub- mitted (in a limited. competitica.i)bT Messrs.--Thos- Beesley and John Ed. Wright, as joint architects, have been unanimously selected for the new ele- mentary schools to be erected in flamilton-street, Battersby-lane. Accommodation will be provided for about 550 children, and it is expected that the work will be commenced early in July. THE SHOCKING ASSAULTS ON CHILDREN. - At the Borough Court, on Monday, the young man Pat- rick Hart, forge labourer, Silver-square, who was last week remanded oh a charge of -having crimin- ally assaulted Martha Ellen Wilcock, Elizabeth Law- ton, and Mary Barber, each of the age of eleven years, was again brought up and committed to the next assizes for trial. Mr.-J. L. Whittle appeared for the prosecution. .

ExcuisioN To REYL. The annual excursion in , connection with Bank Quay Soap Works took place on Saturday, and was well patronised by the work- men and their friends. Rhyl was the destination • chosen, and the trippers visited various objects of interest in that delightfui neighbourhood. The ex- cursion train left Bank Quay station at seven o'clock in the morning, leaving Rhyl a few minutes before eight o'clock in the evening. The weather was fine and a day of much eiijoyment was spent. A CHILD RUN. ON/ED.—Early on Thursday after- noon a boy' named Hill, about three years of age, the son of an out-porter .at Bank Quay Station, who lives off Church-street, was knocked down and run over in Church-street by a lurry. One of the wheels 6f the limy went over the head of the child, who was taken to the Infirmary in an unconscious condition. The child died from its injuries on the " evening of the same day.

VEGiTARIANIS3I AT THE LIVERPOOL EXHIBI- TION.—The vegetarian dining-room at the Liver- pool Exhibition, of which our townsman, Mr. W. H. Chapman is manager, continues to be very- largely patronised. On Whit-Monday, we under- stand, no fewer than 1,640 persona sat down to din- ner between the hours of 11 and 7, this number ex- ceeding by 150 the number supplied id the similar room at the Heaitheries, in 1884. This Nroom, it may be explained, has been established for the pur- pose of practically demonstrating the simplicityand general meriteof a vegetarian diet. THE BIRTH AND DEATH RATE Or WARRINOTON. —For week ending Saturday, June 19th, 1886.—The Mean temperature was 528 Fahr., and therefore 4.7 deg. colder than the preceding week. The maxi- mum temperature 61 Fahrenheit. was recorded on the 14th inst., and the minimum temperature. 44 Fahrenheit, on the 14th inst. The rainfall measured -32 in. The general direction of the wind was N. During the week, which was the 25th of the current year, 23 births and 'l2 deaths were registered.. The death rate from all causes was equal to 13.4 per 1,000, against 21 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 19.4 the cor- responding week of last year. The deaths included' 1 from diptheria, 2 from diarrhcea, 1 from measles; 3 from phthisis, 1 from premature birth, 1 from heart disease, 1 from lung disease, 1 from brain disease. Three cases of diptheria and two 'of whooping cough were reported under the require- ments of the Act of Parliament.—JNo. H. GORN A Tx,. Medical Officer of Health..

div.head: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATUBDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess and Alderman Chandley. thatTNICENNESS.—For this offence Michael Loftus was fined 55 and costs, Gronway Jones 5s and costs, and Mary DicCane lOs and Costs. MWDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Alder- __ _

man Chandley, and Councillor Greening. ASSAULTING AN "INFORMER."-Margaret Fleming was charged with assaulting Annie Duffy, on the 15th June.— Complainant said that Fleming hit her three times and then took her by the head. She said that prisoner called her an informer in connection with a case in which a man was sen- tenced to twelve months' imprisonment.—The Bench ordered prisoner to find bail in £lO to keep the peace for six months, or in default, to ao to prison for six months. WIFE ASSAULT.—WiIIiam Lewis was charged with assault- ing his wife on the 6th inst.—Complainant, whose face was much disfigured, proved the assault. Defendant said he was very sorry, and such a thing would not happen again.—He was ordered to be bound over, himself in £2O, and two sureties of £lO, to keep the peace for six months, in default of finding sureties to go to prison for a month.—William Bailey, for being drunk and disorderly in the Market-place on Saturday night, and for assaulting his wife at the same time and place, was sent to prison for a month, with hard labour. A VIOLENT Fartow.—Thomas Rowan, for being drunk and disorderly in Percivars-fold, and for assaulting P.C. Corcoran, on Saturday night, was sent to prison for a month. DatxxaNNEss.—Michael Hardwick. charged with being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket street, wa& dis- missed on promising to leave the town.—William Plinston was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Queen's-court, on the 14th inst. He was fined 103 and costs.—Mary Dagnall, charged with being drank and dis- orderly in Rose-yard, was fined 5s and costs.—Ann Walker, who was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Irlam- street, on Saturday night. was dismissed on promising to leave the borough. UNREGISTERED LODGING-HOUSE--Martin Cunliffe, whOse wife appeared, was charged with keeping lodgers in St. 1 James's-street, Latchford, without havigg the house regis- tered.—A fine of 103 and costs, or 14 &Sys' imprisonment in default of payment, was imposed. FIGHTING.—Brian Flaherty and Thomas Critchley were summoned for causing a breach of the peace by fighting in Dial-street, on the let inst.—They were each bound over to keep the peace for six months. STONE-THROWING.—Patrick McLoughlin, charged with throwing stones in Jackson's-yard, was fined 10s and costs, and ordered to nay for two windows that he had broken. Prrca AND Toss —Levi Bebbington. Thomas Cox, Jos. Cox, and John Henry Williams were charged with playing at pitch and toss at Lodge-lane Bridge, on the 14th inst.— P.C. 35 proved the case, and Chief Constable Hunt said that many complaints had been received of this offence.— Williams was ordered to pay the cost of the summons, and the others were fined 5s and ~osts, 7s, each. FRlDAY.—Before Captain Reynolds and Mr. John White. A MARRIED COUPLE'S DISAGREEMENTS.—Martin Dooley was charged with stealing various articles of furniture, value 40s, belonging to his wife, Julia Dooley. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the wife, aid Mr. H. L. Riley (St. Helens) for the husband. The couple are separated, and it was alleged that the husband bad taken away several articles of furniture that were the property of the wife. The case was adjourned for a month to see if a reconciliation could be effected. WILFUL DAMAGIB.—Martha Johnson, charged with doing wilful damage on the 22nd June to property rented by ker husband, was ordered to pay the damage, 108, and costs, or go to prison for fourteen dAys. For throwing a stone at her husband in Winwick-street, on the 23rd just, she was sent to prison for fourteen days.
RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MoNDay.—Before Messrs. Brundrit and Thomas.

MISCEILA—NEOUS.—IIary Ann Gough. Patrick Glavin, and Catherine McCoon were each fined for drunkenness.—A fine of 103 and costs was imposed upon Felix McCoan for using obscene language.—John Worrall, charged with committing a breach of the peace was dismissed with a caution.

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT.

MONDAY.—Before Messrs J. Brock and T. S. Timmis. DE —For drunkenness James Doyle, George and Ann Cartwright (husband and wife), Edward Con- nolly, John Doherty, Frank Flatley, and Henry Burrows were each fined. A DRSERTER.-Thomas Smith, a private in the 2nd Bat- talion Sonth Lancashire Regiment, stationed at Warring- ton, was charged with being an absentee from his regiment without leave. The case was proved by P.C. Porter, and the prisoner was handed over to a military escort. FELONIES.—James Smith, 13 years of age, was charged with having on Saturday evening stolen a shawl, worth 12s, from the dwelling-house of Patrick Kegan, 11, Dark. street. After a brief absence of Mrs. Kegan from the house the shawl was missed, and the prisoner was subsequently advanced 2s 3d upon it at Mr. Svred's shop. He alleged it was his mother's. The prisoner, who had been twice con- victed as a thief, was sentenced to seven days' imprison- ment, and afterwards to be detained in a reformatory four years.—Eliza Brocklehurit, a middle-aged woman, was Charged with stealing, from the dwelling-honse,33, Sankey- street. a pair of boots, the property of Mary Alice Heyes. Ike prisoner, who bad lodged at the house, offered the boots in pledge at the shop of Mr. Charles Neil, Ann- street, on Saturday. She was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour.
WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS._
.THIJESDAY.—Before Mr. H. Gaskell, jan., and Mr. George

Pilkington. DRUNKENNESS.—For being drunk John Byrom, Thomas Ragan, Patrick Martin, James Arnold, Martin Grady, Catherine Cummins, John Lally, John Mailer, John Malone, Peter Grady, John Palino and William Kilroy, were each fined.

BREACHES or Tlia PEACE.—Annie Martin was convicted of fighting Rose Kelly on the 12th Jane, and was bound over to keep the peace for two months. For causing a dis- turbance in Back James-street on the 14th • inst., Richard Johnson, an elderly man, was dealt with in a similar manner; and so also was an elderly woman named Margaret Connolly, for cursing and swearing and shouting in Hale- road, Ditton, on the 11th inst. YOUNG GAMALEns. —P a t r chargedick O'Ne with I ,i t h plJamesPlaying iMn gu Murray, andb by John Murray, youths, were way of gaming in the public place, Back Caroline-street, on the 13th inst. It was alleged that the boys were playing for money, and half a pack of cards and 11d was picked up from the ground by the constables.—The defendants denied the allegation, but the Bench fined each of them is and costs. Doziso.—John Nolan, a young man, was charged with, being asleep whilst in charge of a horse and cart in Vic- toria-road on the 10th inst.— The defendant, who said he was dozing, was fined 5s and costs. WOMEN'S WRANGLES—Margaret Fay was summoned for assaulting Winifred Carney. The defendant was fined 6d and costs 155.---For assaulting Catherine Dillon, Mar- garet McWilliams was fined 2s 61 and costs.--Annie Gateby and Elizabeth Hunt harl summoned each other for threatening to commit an assault.—Mrs. Runt was bound over to keep the peace, and the summons agaiest Mrs Gateby was dismissed.
LYMM PETTY SESSIONS. FarneY.—Before Messrs. G. C. Dewhurst, S. Stanton, and

C. Lister. A VIOLENT FARMER.—Thomas Morris, a farmer, High Leh. was charged with having been drunk and disorderly on the 3rd of June.—P.C. Arthern said that on the 3rd inst. he saw the defendant coming down Swanhead-lane, High-lane, in a trap. He appeared to be whipping the horse very severely, and on his return he stopped the horse and examined it, after which he allowed defendant to go on his way. The latter, however, did not go far till he turned back and need very violent and threatening language to witness. He also said the horse was his own, and he should do as he liked with it.—Richard Shakeshaft and Ann Cook gave corroborative evidence, and Mr. Jenkins, solicitor, of Warrrington, having spoken in defence, a fine of 5s and 18s 6d costs was imposed. • A WELL-ENOWN VOICE.—Mary Ann Platt, fustian cutter, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly at Lymm on the 12th inst. P.C. Dutton proved the case.— Sergeant Barrington said that on the day referred to he heard defendant's voice at about a quarter of a mile die- tant,—Defendant : How could you know it was my voice at a quarter of a mile distant ?—Sergeant Harrington: I have heard your voice too often not to know it.—A fine of 5s including costs was imposed. CARELESS DRIVERS.—For having been drunk whilst in charge of a horse and carriage on the 8,11 instant, at High Legh, John Blackledge, farmer, was fined 5s and costs.— John Brundrett, for a similar oflencea B )11ington on the 18th inst., was fined 5s 6d costs —Samuel Dawson, a wag. goner, for driving without reins at High Legh, was fined 58 and costs.

THE ELECTION CAMPAIGN. Sir James Gibson Maitland (C) has retired in favour of a Unionist candidate for Stirlingshire. The Executive Radical Union at Birmingham have re- solved to raise a guarantee fund of £20,000. The Conservatives will not bring forward a candidate for East Edinburgh, but will support Mr. Goschen. The Divisional Council of West Birmingham have selec- ted Mr. Chamberlain as the Liberal candidate by 147 votes to 27. Sir Charles Dilke has spoken at Chelsea and advocated Home Rale for Ireland. A vote of conadence in him was paned. Mr. Chamberlain addressed a meeting at Barrow on Thursday evening in support of the 'candidature of Mr. Caine.

Mr. Charles Williams, war correspondent, will oppose Mr. Herbert Gladstone at West Leeds as an Independent Unionist. Mr. Broadhurst has been unanimously chosen as the Liberal Home Rule candidate for the Western Division of Nottingham.t On Thursuav night Mr. Goschen addressed a large and lively meeting of his constituents in the Music Hall. Edinburgh. Mr. Parnell has consented to address a meeting at Ches- ter on Tuesday next, in support of the candidature of of Dr. Foster, M.P. At Carlisle Mr. Ferguson, M.P. (Unionist Liberal), on Wednesday retired, and Mr. Gully, Q.C. (Ministerialist), has issued his add,ress. Mr. J. W. Lowther (Conservative) will contest Mid- Cumberland against Sir Wilfrid Lawson (Ministerialist), Mr. Howard having withdrawn. • The Liberal Council of the North-West Division Of Man- chester have selected Mr. Hy. Lee as their candidate. Mr. Lee is a supporter of Mr. Gladstone. Mr. F. S. Powell, the sitting member for Wigan, has con- sented to seek re-election in the Conservative interest. Mr. C. M. Percy is the Liberal candidate. It is announced that Mr. Bright, nephew of Mr. John Bright, will contest East Glamorganshire against Mr. A. Thomas, Gladstonian, the sitting member. The writs for the new House of Commons will be issued simultaneously with the publication of her Majesty's pro- clamation dissolving the present Parliament. Mr. Arthur Arnold addressed a large meeting of electors on Wednesday evening at Higher Broughton, and a resolu- tion in his favour was carried by an overwhelming majority There was great indignation on Thursday at Wednesbury upon its becoming known that Mr. Wilson Lloyd, the borough member, and Mrs. Lloyd, had been badly assaul- ted. _ _ _

A a meeting of the Liberal Executive Council of the Central Division of Birmingham, Mr. John Bright was selected, with only four dissentients, as the Liberal candidate at the ensuing election. Mr. A. B.,Rowley, Liberal candidate for Ashton-under- Lyne, addressed a crowded meeting of electors at Ashton- ander-Lyne en Wednesday night, and a resolution in his favour was adopted almost unanimously. Mr. Gladstone has informed Mr. Kitson that, in view of other heavy engageemts, he finds it impossible at present to visit Leeds and deliver a political address. The right hon. gentleman spent Thursday quietly at Hawarden. Mr. T. Crosland, who contested Huddersfield at the last election as Conservative candidate against Mr. Leatham, has again come forward to oppose Mr. Summers, the Gladstonian Liberal, in whose favour Mr. Leatham has retired. Mr. A. B. Forwood, the sitting member for Ormskirk, has accepted an invitation to again contest the constituency in the Conservative interest. Colonel Blundell, the sitting member for [flee, will seek re-election as the Conservative candidate. Sir Hsrace Davey, Q.C. (Solicitor-General), and Mr. Joseph Leigh, the selected Liberal candidates for Stockport, on Wednesday night, addressed a public meeting of the electors, and subsequently a vote of confidence in them was passed. The "Globe " urges the conservative leaders not to be jockeyed by the Unionists. It points out that the Tories will secure the return of about 100 candidates, and asks what advantage the Conservatives are to receive from their self-abnegation. The Council of the Eccles Division Liberal Association have unanimously invited Mr. E. D. Gosling to become a candidate for the Eccles Division of South-East Lancashire. Mr. Gosling has accepted. He approves Mr, Gladstone's Irish proposals. Mr. Goschen addressed a crowded meeting in the Circus at Newcastle-on-Tyne on Tuesday night. He said he had had a personal attack made upon him by tha Premier. He Iwould repel that attack where he ought to repel it, and in terms which it deserved. The Chancellor of the Exchequer (Sir W. Harcourt) ad- dressed his constituents at Derby on Thursday night, and

_ replied to .some recent speeches by Liberal seceders. Sir William remarked that it was nonsense to deny that the in- terview between Lord Carnarvon and Mr. Parnell "meant business." The Blackburn Liberal Council on Wednesday night, after an animated discussion, resolved not to bring forward any candidate at the impending election, and the Conserva- tive candidates, Mr. William Coddington, M.P., and Mr. William Henry Hornby, will be returned without op- position. At a full meeting of the Executive Parliamentary Com- mittee of the Preston Liberal Association held on Wednes- day night, Mr. George Potter, of London, was unanimously chosen to contest the representation of the borough as a Gladstonianeand it was also decided to invite Colonel Goodair to tome forward as second candidate on the same principles. The Executive Committee of the Liberation Society has
_ issued a circular in view of the General Election, in which it says :—Wherever the circumstances of the case justify

. - such a course there should be resolute efforts to secure the choice and the return of candidates who are desirous of furthering the society's objects ; and more especially in Wales and Scotland. Mr. T. Healv has received the following ominous texts from Scripture from a correspondent: "Two of the Chamberlains were wroth and sought to lay hands on the king, and when inquisition was made ef the matter they were both hanged on a tree." (Book of Esther ii., 21, 23. A. V. condensed.) "Woe unto them! for they have gone in the way of Cain and perished." (Catholic Epistle of St. Jude, 11). • _ _

Mr. Childers, in addressing his constituents on Saturday, remarked that' the Government had noc considered the Irish land adequate security on which to base their Pur- base Bill, and bad therefore taken the whole taxable value

of Ireland as security. He described himself as unreservedly pledged to Mr. Gladstone's Home Rule Bill, but said the Government were tot bound now to stand by the Land Pur- chase Bill. A London correspondent says :—At the office of Lord Hartington's Committee in Spring Gardens there. is a much larger wealth of candidates than of constituencies. Yoang men, many of them barristers of fortune, go there in hopes of finding an open door to Vaa.House of Commons, and they are met with abundant courtesy, but with no constituency. As a matter of fact, the demand for what Mr. Gladstone calls "Paper Unionist" candidates is already exhausted. An address has been issued by Mr. Joseph Arch, M.P., and Mr. Leicester, M.P., representing labour in the House of Commons, calling on the British democracy to attend a demonstration in Hyde Park, this (Saturday) afternoon, "in order to prove to the world at large that Mr. Gladstone has the heart of England with him. Contingencies from Scotland, Ireland, and Wales will be present, and resolutions be proposed approving of the policy ef Home Rule for Ire- land. This, we submit, is a powerful and practical method of giving effect to our recent manifesto." A London correspondent says :—Sr Robert Peel has added a new chapter to tho history of his remarkable poli- tical career. He has formally joined the Liberal party. For some weeks he has absented himself from his once familiar place on the Tory benches. To-night (Monday) he boldly crossed the floor, voted against his old party on the Belfast Main Drainage Bill, and announced lais adhesion to the Radical programme. He now proposes to contest the Inverness burghs against Mr. Finlay as a Home Ruler and advocate of disestablishment and a Crofters' candi-. date.

Mr. Herbert Gladstone attended a meeting on Monday i night n support of the candidature of Mr. J Kitson Presi- dent of the National Liberal Federation, for. Central' Leeds. Mr. Gladstone said that the long-expected declaration of the Tory policy showed that if they came into office Ire- land was to have immediate renewal of coercion. He twitted Lord Salisbury with inconsistency in Irish policy, according to being in or out of office, and described the manifesto of Lord Randolph Churchill as the product of a mountebank statesman, which would be ridiculous if it did not emanate from one who had been one of her Majesty's Secretaries of State. At a meeting of the Barrow Conservatives on Monday night, it was unanimously resolved.....-' That this meeting fully recognises that t .he one issue before the country on the present occasion is the separation proposals of the Prime Minister, and that, as our present member, Mr. Caine, has courageously resisted them, both in the House and be- fore his constituents, considers that the wisest course to pur- sue will be to bring out no Conservative candidate, but give a general support to the sitting member. .This meeting, however, expresses eat...nest hope that Mr. Caine will not during next Parliament take any hostile action towards the Church of England." Mr. Chamberlain, addressing his constituents on Saturday night, said that at the time he took office he to.d I‘lr. Glad- stone exactly what his opinions were upon the Irish ques- tion; that he did not believe it would he possible to estab- lish a Parliament in Dublin, and at the same time to maintain.the conditions Mr. Gladstone bad himself laid down as necessary and essential. Quoting from his address issued after accepting office last February, he claimed .that I he stood now upon the same platform in regard to the Irish question as at that time. If he had consulted his personal ambition he would have remained in the Cabinet, but he ob- jected to the Home Rule Bill because he considered the conditions Mr. Gladstone had affixed to any measure of the kind were not fulfilled in the measure, and, therefore, he resumed an independent position by resigning office.
