resolution approving Mr. Chamberlain's candidature was carried, there being about a hundred dissentients. On Wednesday there was a demonstration in St. James's Hall, London, under the auspices of the British Home Rule Association, in support of the Metropolitan candidates who 'favour the Irish policy of the Government. Lord Sandhurst I presided. The principal speaker was Mr. Sexton, M.P., who, referring to the Parnell-Carnarvon controversy, said Lord Carnarvon was too sedate and experienced a I,9litician to send for the leader of the Irish people merely for idle curi- osity. The Irish party knew that immediately before the interview Lord Carnarvon saw Lord Salisbury,and that he saw him again immediately after. He had no doubt that if Lord Salisbury had won 30 more seats, as many as would have made him independent of the Hibernian Orange Frankens- tein, he would before this time have brought forward a Horne Rule Bill of his own. The moment he saw the result of the elections he resolved upon a policy of "Jim Crow." Now Irishmen were more fervently and heartily with the Liberal party than ever they were heartily against them. He declared that the Liberals could win 15 seats in Lon- don, and thus they had it in their power to extinguish at a single blow the majority by which the Prime Minister was defeated.

Mr. John Morley, the Chief Secretary for Ireland, on Saturday, attended a large and enthusiastic meeting of Liberals in Bradford. In responding to a vote of confidence in the Government, he criticised the recent utterances of Lord Salisbury, who denied at Leeds that he had advocated coercion except against murderers, burglars, and mutilators of cattle; but why, then, did he say he would repeal those repressive laws at the end of twenty years? Liberal sece- ders would find that if they prevented the Government from dealing with the Irish question, Lord Salisbury would go to the root of the matter and settle it once for all, and no one could blame him. If the Irish were nbt given what they wanted, coercion Must again be resorted to. Lord Salisbury and tne seceding Liberals would attempt to enlist English sympathy in favour of some policy that would lead to the government of Ireland according to English ideas of what was best and most fitting, but the benignant effort made in this direction some 40 or 50 years ago showed how futile such a polio- would be. No measure that might henceforth be proposed to deal with this question could go behind the large liberality of Mr. Gladstone's bill ; for the Liberal party, in its main body, would never assent to a narrower scheme than that which had been proposed by the present Government. Until this question was settled Great Britain could scarcely again enter into a great foreign en- terprise. He was persuaded that there was in Ireland all the material out of which, with time, freedom, and respon- sibility, there might be built a solid nation worthy to take its place among the other nations that have the British flag waving over them.

He told them nant's, drove to the Central Station, which he left that he wrote to Mr. Gladstone, and entreated him to pay shortly before six h'clock on his way to Hawarden to attention to his old friend Mr. Chamberlain, and that if amidst the greatest enthusiasm. he would only take the advice of Mr. Crosfield and his fel- low patriot's in Warrington he guaranteed that there would be a glorious return as soon as the election was over. Mr. Crosfield said some time ago that how Lord Salisbury could "stand upon a platform to advocate the banishment of a million of Irish people and 20 years' coercion passed his comprehension." Those were his words at Earlestown on the 22nd May last. He repeated them almost word for word in his address last week, and yet he was astonished at his Dr. Mackie's remarks that such a charge was "foul," and called Mr. Gladstone to witness that they were true. air. Crosfield dwelt unnecessarily, as he thought, upon his putting such a strong word as "foul" upon his remarks. He, however, meant to 'say that it .was and very painfully true, and that in this coun- try we should not let our great men, upon either side, be maligned as Mr. Crosfield had maligned Lord Salisbury without raising an instantaneous and power- ful protest. Mr. Crosfield's charge was, not that Lord Salisbury wished the Irish to "emigrate," but to " banish " them. He used a phrase, and stuck to it, which from their earliest days they had looked upon as a mark of shame. He heard Lord Salisbury say that it would be better to spend £50,000,000 of the £150,000,000 proposed to be spent on the landlords in sending out one million of labourers from the parts of Ireland where there was congestion, and that practically gave £5O to every man, woman, and child who went. (Applause.) Sir GILBERT GREENALL, who was received with ap- plause, said he was grateful to Mr. Crosfield for the cour- teous manner in which he had spoken of him. (Hear, hear.) He could assure Mr. Crosfield that he would say nothing in that content which would for one moment be dis- pleasing to him or to any of his friends, and that he should regard with all respect and confidence the kindness which be (Mr. Crosfield) had expressed. (Hear, hear.) Proceed- ing, Sir Gilbert said he believed they all knew his political creed. They knew his religious feelings and religious senti- ments. They knew that he was a Churchman—a tolerant Churchman. (Hear, hear.) He believed that the Church had so broad a base that she could receive into her fold all those who loved God and kept His commandments, and the Church would, and in his opinion did, receive into her body such people. With respect to Ireland. he was no separatist, he was no repealer, and he would keep the integrity of the Empire, and never, never should he be doing or assisting in any measure which in the least degree appeared to him to threaten the continuity of the union of Great Britain and Ireland. (Cheers.) Would he coerce Ireland? No; quite the contrary. His feeling was that Ireland required pati- ence, careful and liberal consideration and treatment. There was nothing that he ,would withhold that could be given to Ireland safely with regard to the union. There was nothing he would withhold from Ireland with ressitect to her domestic and social matters which would make the people more united and happy and give them more liberty to cultivate those interests which were most advantageous to their happiness. (Cheers.) • The resolution was then carried amidst applause. Mr. It PIERPOINT moved " That this meeting pledges Itself to use all legitimate means to return Sir Gilbert Greenall as member for the borough at the approaching general election." (Cheers.) Mr. GEO. WOODS seconded the proposal, which was agreed to. A vote of thanks to the Chairman, moved by Sir GILBERT GREEN/a; and seconded by Mr. ISIEERWOOD, brought the meeting to a close.

ATHLETIC SPORTS AT ASHTON. The annual sports in connection with the Ashton Recreation Society, which were postponed from Whit-Monday in consequence of the wet weather, were held on Saturday, on the ground of the Re- creation Society, the weather, with the exception of a sharp thunderstorm, being delightful. There was an attendance of 2,000 spectators, but, as usual with postponed meetings, the entrants mustered in very small numbers for each event. J. Ellison, of I the Earlestown F.C. (5 'yards) got the best of the starter in the 100 yards handicap, which he w m rather easily from E. Lever, St. Helens (3-1). Elli- son also landed the 220 yards hurdles from the 10 yards mark, beating H. Hall, Handforth (6), by half a yard. The mile handicap was won by J. Massey, of Warrington (15), who also ran second in the half mile to J. C. Samuels, Chorley (scratch). The 440 yards handicap was won by H. Hall, Handforth (15), from J. C. Samuels (scratch). In the open wheel event only two men turned out—J. Birch, St. Helens (110), and J. Clarke, Widnes (scratch), who finished in the order named. PRESCOT. PRESCOT BOARD OF .GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians was held at the Union Workhouse Whiston, on Thursday forenoon. There were present—Mr. J. Lowe (chairman), Rev. C. W. Wool!, Messrs. J. Jackson, W. Birchall, J. Buckley, T. Eatock, W. Gerrard, J. Kenwright, J. Griffiths, J. Matthews, J. Ranson, W. Middlehurst, C. B. Johnson, W. Swift, J. Ellison, E. Syder, W. Daine, J. Leatherbarrow, R. Tuson, J. Fisher, W. Tyrer H. Hulme, T. Heald, S. H. Hartley (clerk.) THE MASTER'S REPORT.—The Workhouse Master repor- ted there were 454 inmates of the heuse this week, 452 last week, 435 in the corresponding week last year. There had been 65 vagrants relieved, against 67 in the same week last year. ASSISTANT OVERSEERS.—The Clerk read a circular letter from the Local Government Board, dated the 19th June, containing new orders in reference to the appointment of collectors of poor's rates and assistant overseers, and the filling of vacancies caused by resignation. Poon LAW CONFERENCE.—The Clerk read a circular stating that Mr. Holgate, secretary of the North-Western Poor Law Conference, had recently died, and drawing at- tention to a meeting of the Conference to be heli in the Manchester Town Hall on Tuesday next, to make arrange- ments for the annual conference at Liverpool and to select the subjects to be discussed. He (the Clerk) thought it was desirable the Prescot Union should be represented at the conference.—On the motion of Mr. Fisher, the Chairman and Mr. Tyrer, along with the Clerk‘, were appointed to represent the Board at the conference. THE WIDNES RELIEVING OFFlCrat.—The Clerk reported the receipt of a letter from Mr. John scannel, late relieving officer for Widnes, and who has been appointed to a similar post at London, in which he formally tendered his resigna- tion and thanked the Guardians for the kindness they had shown to him in the past. A SUFFERING AssisreNT OVERSEER.—The Clerk read a letter stating that Mr. Baxter, the newly-appointed assistant overseer for Woolton, was suffering from rheumatic fever, and an assistant was required until his recovery. The Board instructed the clerk to arrange with Mr. Makin, assistant overseer for Present, to render the assistance required. THE RELIEVING OFFICER'S SALARY QUESTION.—Mr. Jackson, in accordance with notice given at the last meet- ing, moved that the resolution passed on May 27th postpon- ing for twelve months the application of Mr. 0. M. Barton, relieving officer,for an increase of salary be rescinded.—Mr. ' Daine and Mr. Middlehurst asked if it was legal or right that after a resolution had been passed at one meeting, a member at the next meeting could give notice that he would move that the resolution be rescinded.—The Clerk replied that Mr. Jackson was perfectly in order in what he had done.—Mr. Jackson then moved his motion, and considered that an injustice had been done to Mr. Barten, after he had fulfilled his duties very satisfactorily for two years, and a hope had been held out to him that if be did so the increase would be made. Each of the relieving officers had had a similar increase. The increase was recommended by 11 members of the Finance Committee. to the increase had come with He thought the opposition. bad grace.—Mr. W. Birchall seconded the veryresolution, and said a promise was held out to Mr. Barton that if he performed his duties satisfactorily for two years, the increase would be given.—Mr. Fisher and Mr. Matthews concurred with this statement.—The Rev. C. W. Wooll said on the last occasion he voted against the increase, but after what had been said he would suppOrt Mr. Jackson's motion.—Mr. Kenwright said Mr. Barton was never definitely promised an increase when he was appointed.—Mr. Middlehurst said they only wished the application to be postponed for in- quiries to be made.—Mr. Johnson objected to the practice of resolutions passed by the Board being rescinded a week or two later.—Mr. Daine did not consider they were doing an injustice to Mr. Barton.—Mr. Jackson replied, and asked his opponents to consider the golden maxim to do unto others as they would like others to do unto them.—The motion was carried by 14 votes to three—the atter being Messrs. Eatock Tuson, and. Johnson.
The officials were :—Judges, Dr. Dobb and R. M`Gill. Starter, J. Cansey. Handicapper, W. Platt. Timekeeper, A. B. Dewhurst.

div.head: LORD HARTINGTON.
div.p: LORD HARTINGTON.

On Tuesday evening, a meeting of the Liberal Council for the Rossendale Division was held in Kay-street Baptist School, Rawtenstall. .There was a large attendance, and Mr. Thomas Brooks presided. Reporters were not present, a resolution to admit the Press being rejected. The meeting lasted over two hours, and the proceedings were very ani- mated. At the close the representatives of the Press were officially informed that the Executive had presented the following report:—" That this Executive. having met on the subject of a candidate for the division as required by the resolution of the Council on the 12th inst., after holding two meetings, hereby respectfully present the following re- port to the Council : (1) Since the first of the two meetings ef the Executive, Lord Hartington has publicly offered himself to the whole of the electors of Rossendale as a can- didate. (21 Your Executive are unable, in the present peculiar circumstances, to recommend any name, and beg to remit the question to the Council. (3) Your Executive would farther respectfully urge on the Council seriously to deliberate on the expediency of no contest, for at the present time a conteq would be probably more successful in sunder- ing our own forces deplorably than in unseating Lord Har- tington." The first part of the report was accepted with- out much opposition, but on the latter portion a protracted discussion ensued. On a vote being taken, 94 voted for the Committee's recommendation and 65 against. A resolution , against a contest in the Rossendale Division was then I passed.

NOTES BY THE WAY.

On Wednesday the Australians, at Nottingham' succeeded in making a draw of their match against the Players of England after it had seemed at one time they Might very possibly be defeated. At the close of Tuesday's cricket the Players had completed a first innings of 334, and the Ans. trafiang had lost six wickets for 174. On Wednesday, in half an hour the innings of the Australians was finished for 205, so that they were left in a minority of 129. The Aus- tralians were placed in the unenviable position of having nothing to play for but a draw, but in this endeavour they proved successful. At the finish tkey were 107 runs to the good with four wickets to fall.

- The match at Lords' between Surrey and Middlesex, was also brought to a close, Surrey winning by four wickets. The Cambridge Eleven suffered their first defeat during the present season at Bramall-lane, Sheffield, when York- shire beat them by seven wickets. Overnight a draw had appeared inevitable, but the University batting broke down comvletely on Wednesday morning. Less than an hour and a half proved sufficient at Derby on Wednesday to finish off the match, Kent v. Derbyshire, Kent in the end winning by no fewer than 173 runs. Over- night Derby had lest four wickets in their second innings for 21 runs, and still wanted 239 runs to win. Though in the end the Middlesex Eleven were beaten by five wickets at Lord's on Saturday, they played a capital game against Nottingham Remarkable cricket was shown in the Gentlemen of Eng- land against Australians match, which finished at the Oval on Saturday. W. G. Grace's cutting was exceptionally fine, and G. Kemp played in admirable style. It was a creditable thing for the Australians to put on 488 after going in against the gigantic innings of 471. The most surprising thing they did was to get rid of eight of oar wickets late on Satm day afternoon, and so leave the match drawn very much in their favour. Mr. Grace enjoyed himself in the Oxford and Marylebone i match on Tuesday. Having knocked up his 100 runs, he then, with the energy and keenness that ever distinguished him all through his cricket career, went on first to bowl, and got rid of the whole Oxford team for 90 runs, little over half of them being from his own bowling. W. G., when be is captain of a side, has a great liking for going on bowling to start with. I believe if ha were asked his candid opinion ' as to what is the proper thing at cricket he would tell you that he ought tn go in first, stop in about a day and a half, ! make a couple of hundred runs or so, then commence I bowling at the other side, put them out quickly, make ! them follow on, and polish them off the second time nice and early on the third day so as to be able to get a comfort- able dinner and catch the train house to Bristol.—Manchester Guardian.

div.head: MIDLOTHIAN CAMPAIGN.
div.p: THE MIDLOTHIAN CAMPAIGN.

Mr. Gladstone opened his campaign in Midlothian on Friday with a speech which was received with un- precedented enthusiasm by an audience which few orators can rouse into that condition. The battle to be fought, he declared at the outset, was the people's, as Inkerman was the, soldiers, and he had confidence in the result. What he had seen on his way north had strengthened that conviction, and he did not think Scotland would be found adverse to Home Rule. Mr. Gladstone dealt with criticisms directed against his policy by the press and by public men, and declared that when the question of Home Rule was settled, men would wonder why they had op- posed it. The Prime Minister remained at his hotel in Edin- burgh nearly the whole of Saturday. In the even- ing, accompanied by Mrs. Gladstone, he drove to the residence of Mr. John Cowan, at Beeslack, eight miles distant, to dine. Along the crowded thoroughfares the Premier was loudly cheered, as also in the vil- lages en route. Leaving Beeslack about ten o'clock, Mr. Gladstone returned by another route, and within a mile of the busier thoroughfares of the city he alighted with his son for the purpose of walking to his hotel. He had not walked far before he was re- cognised and surrounded bY a jostling crowd, which cheered enthusiastically. linable to continue his walk, the Premier sought refuge in a tramcar, in which he procTeded to the hotel, followed by hundreds of persons. It was with difficulty, that Mr. Gladstone, somewhat exhausted, made his way from the tramcar into the hotel.

MONDAY'S MEETING. An announcement baying been publicly made that Mr. Gladstone would at noon on Monday drive to the International Exhibition now open in Edinburgh, a great crowd gathered in Princes-street. opposite his hotel door, and another crowd at the Exhibition, in order to see him ; but the right hon. gentleman found himself too much engrossed with his corres- pondence and with preparations for the afternoon meeting to leave his hotel at noon, and Mr. W. H. Gladstone also remained indoors to assist him with his work. In the afternoon Mr. Gladstone addressed another great meeting of the electors of Midlothian in the Edinburgh Music Hall. Admission was by ticket, and the ticket-holders were in their seats au hour before the proceedings commenced. Those who came later had to stand in the passages. The hour of wait- ing was occupied with a performance on the organ of national and other popular airs. Mr. Gladstone was enthusiastically cheered when he entered the hall. 1 Mr. Cowan, of Beeslack, occupied the chair, and among those on the platform were Mr. Childers, Mrs. and Miss Childers, Mr. C. S. Parker, M.P., Mr. Wallace (candidate in opposition to Mr. Goschen), Principal Rainy. Principal Cairns, the Countess of Aberdeen, and a large number of local gentlemen. ...Mr. Gladstone said it was his anxiety to deal with English, Scot2h, and Irish affairs which induced him to insist at this moment so pertinaciously upon the Irish question, for Ireland blocked the way against all legislation on other subjects, and the whole ques- tion of the election was the question of "clearing the rails." Referring to Mr. Chamberlain's complaint that he had cheered a slighting reference in the Rouse of Commons to the office of Mayor of Birmingham, he declared that a grosser error never proceeded from the mouth of man. Passing to the Carnarvon-Parnell in- cident, he repeated the questions he put on Friday to Lord Carnarvon and Lord Salisbury, and said he thought the country was entitled to full and explicit answers to those questions. The right hon. gentle • man procdeded to refer to the meeting of seceding Liberals in London, at which Mr. Goschen declared that the great object of the gathering was to provide a long purse in order to run as many candidates as Vossible who were opposed to the policy of the Govern- ment and the majority of the Liberal party. Mr. Goschen, he said, would be a most admirable candi- date for a Tory constituency, for his energy for years past had been mainly directed towards stopping the progress of Liberalism. Though the Liberal seceders amounted in the House of Commons to nearly two. sevenths of the party, yet among the masses of the Liberal party 'the seceders were not one-twentieth, perhaps not one•fiftieth of the whole. He objected to the claim of the seceders that they represented Liberalism, not only on the ground that they were a small minority, but also because they had. abandoned the 'generous and wise traditions with which the policy of the Liberal party was associated. The Premier quoted from his autumn manifesto and speeches to khow that he did not at that time conceal the ideas that beheld on the subject of Ireland. He argued, moreover, that the speeches of Lord Salisbury at that time justified the expectation of a Tory measure of Home Rule, in which, had it been brought forward, the, Tories would, he sai4, have had support from many members of the Liberal party. Artful attempts had been made in some quarters to show that the ex- isting Parliament had not declared against the prin- ciple of Home Rule for Ireland ; but he maintained that this Parliament had rejected the principle, and declared that on this principle was based the fresh appeal about to be made to the country. In conclu- sion he entreated the people not to lose this golden opportunity of settling the Irish demand. The result was within their reach, and if they missed it there must be another miserable round of coercion and dis- appointment. (Cheers. GREAT MEErING AT GLASGOW.

Mr. Gladstone left Edinburgh on Tuesday after- noon for Glasgow, where he addressed a large and enthusiastic meeting, convened by the Scottish National Liberal Federation, in Hengler's Circus, Princes-street, along which the right hon. gentleman, accompanied by Mrs. Gladstone, Mr. W. H. Glad- stone, and Mr. Campbell, his election agent, drove from the Royal Hotel. The street was crowded by thousands of people, who cheered him most lustily. Mr. Gladstone acknowledged this by repeatedly rais- ing his hat. A select company assembled on the station platform to wish the Premier "God speed," and the train moved away amidst a hearty outburst of cheering, which was taken up by workmen and others who had assembled along the railway banks. At West Calder, and indeed every station between Edin- burgh and Glasgow, large crow4s assembled upon the platform and cheered as the train rushed at express speed along. Upon arriving at Glasgow, the right hon. gentleman had every reason to be gratified with the warmth of the reception accorded The I streets through which be passed on his way to the 11 residence of Sir Charles Tennant, and from thence to the place of meeting, were occupied by admiring and enthusiastic crowds, who kept up one continued vol- ley of cheering. The circus was inconveniently crowded, and the most unbounded enthusiasm pre- vailed. Mr. Gilbert Beith, MP., occupied the chair. Mrs. Gladstone, the Countess of Aberdeen, and other ladies, occupied seats on the platform, and amongst those present were several members of Parliament, who, upon being recognised, were loudly cheered.
Mr. Gladstone dealt with the Irish question chiefly from a Scottish point of observation. t3peaking iret

div.p: WIT AND HUMOUR.

Noah was an ark4tect. Gentlemen of colour—Painters. Train detention—Treading on a lady's dress. A man who sticks up for his master—A bill-sticker. Which travels the faster, heat or cold ?—Heat; because you can't catch cold. If you wish to communicate with the finny tribes of the sea first drop them a line. He is a miss guided youth who does everything his sweet- heart asks him to do. Why was the Egyptian of olden times a really filial kind of a fellow ?—Because be thought a great ;deal of his mummy! To a certain point we all profit by each other's misfor- tunes, but the man who tells a woman that her babe is not pretty is liable to go home with a bleeding scalp. A HITCH IN THE TESTIMOICY.—" SO, Mr. Witness, you swear that at the time this theft was committed on the south s:de you saw the Prisoner on the north side." "Yes, sir." "Was he going toward the south side or was he coming from that direction ?" "I can't answer that now." "Why not ?" "Because the prisoner's lawyer forgot to tell me which way north is !" , He THOUGHT HE COULD BETTER IT.—Mr. Fauxpas (to young lady) : Ah, Miss Charmante, I have just come froml the side of Mrs. Smith, who has been asking me about the I beautiful young lady at the flower table—Miss C. (appear- I ing to busy herself in arranging some flowers) : Have you never known how I detest flattery ?—Mr. F. (who thinks he may have blundered) : Oh, but really, you know it is dark over where she is sitting. One can hardly see you. CAUSE OF AGITATION.—A specialist in throat troubles was called to treat a Boston lady who manifested BO much , interest in his surgical instruments that he explained their 'uses to her. "This larnygoscope," said he, "is fitted with I small mirrors and an electric light; the interior of your 'throat will be seen by me as clearly as the exterior; you would be surprised to know bow far down we can see with an instrument of this kind. The operation over, the lady appeared somewhat agitated. "Poor girl," said her sister, who was present; "it must have been very painful." "Oh, no, not that, not that," whispered the Boston lady; "but just as he fixed his instrument in place I remembered that I had a hole in my stocking." A day or two before the close of this session at Edinburgh I University, one of the professors appeared with a large fools- cap paper in his hand. The students, expecting that this was the honours-list, were on the alert. The professor com- menced, " Before beginning my lecture this morning, gentle- men, I have something to say with regard to the distribution of "—tremendous cheering, which lasted a considerable length of time—" the remaining tipae at our disposal." The laughter which followed was join eff in by the professor. An Austin coloured man named Jake was very late a few, days ago in getting down to the store. His employer, Colonel Allspice, rebuked Jake in somewhat severe language. "I want you to understand that this trifling will never do. If you can't get down to your work in time, I'll hire some- body who can." "Boss, don't be hard on me ;" and the negro's eyes filled with tears. "Why, what's the matter you? Anybody ill 2" "Ill! I don't know which am' gwinter die fust, my wife or my old mudder" "I am sorry, I I spoke so harshly as that. I didn't know things were so bad. We shall not need you about the store to-day." "Thank you, boss—thank you kindly ;" and off he went.l The next morning Colonel Allspice asked Jake what he meant by saying that his wife and mother were dying, when he had seen both in the street on the day before. " Dyin' !" I exclaimed Jake, elevating his eyebrows in amazement. "Yes, dying—you said they were dying; and, half an hour after you left, your wife came here to see if you had drawn your wages for last month." "I neber• said dey was dyin'. Ef you was ter see de way dey opens dar moufs and takes in chunks of bacon, you wouldn't 'spect dem ob dyin'. I bleve I did say I didn't know which of 'em was gwinter die fast, and , I don't know dat yet; dey's bole got sich good I appetites. I knows one ob 'em's got ter die fust, but—" ' Here Colonel Allspice interrupted the orator with an axe- helve, and the business relations heretofore subsisting be- tween them have been severed. "CRAM."—Under the "cramming" system so religiously pursued by teachers, it is not surprsing to find that the juvenile mind makes a hash of its supposed learning. School-examinations are to a great extent parrot-like or mechanical peiformances. The master or mistress, as the case may he, gets to know by experience the nature of the questions likely to be put, and upon these particular points the children are "ground up" day after day, with little thought or care of their understanding. The result Is serious. "A famine in the land," according to the answer of one bright youth, is what made the Tower of Pisa lean; and "cos the moon is so changin' is the reason why it is of a different gender from the sun. The inquiry, "What comes next to a man in the scale of being?" got for an answer, "His shirt." A young student declared that "chyle flows up the middle of the backbone and reaches the heart, when it meets the oxygen and is purified." Another said, "The work of the heart is to repair the different organs in about half a minute ;" while still another "crammer" comes to the conclusion that the organs of digestion are "stomach, utensils, liver, and spleen."- The remarkable answer on Scriptural matters form an endless catalogue. It was "Daniel in the lions' den" who said, "It is not good for man to he alone ;" and why the Israelites made a golden calf was "because they hadn't enough silver to make a cow." Another instance of these logical conclusions was when a pupil was asked, "What did the Israelites do when they came out of the Red Sea ?" The answer was, "They I dried themselves." A YANKEE TRADER.—" I calculate I couldn't drive a trade with you to-day?" said a true specimen of a Yan- kee pedlar, as he stood at the door of a merchant of St. Louis. "I calculate you calculate about right, for you cannot," was the sneering reply. "Wall, I guess you needn't get huffy about it. Chow, here's half a dozen razor strops, worth two dollars and a half—you may have 'em for two dollars." "I tell you I don't want any of your trash, so you had better be going." "Wall, now, I declare! I'll bet you five dollars if you make me an offer for them , 'ere strops, we'll have a trade yet." "Done," replied the ' merchant, placing the money in the hands of a bystander. The Yankee deposited the like sum—when the merchant offered him a picayune for, the strops. "They're your'n," said the Yankee, as be quietly fobbed the stakes. "Bat," he added, with great appareni honesty, " I calculate, a joke's a joke, and if you don't want them strops, I'll trade back!" The merchant's countenance brightened. "You are not so bad a chap after all; here are your strops— give me the money." "There it Is" said the Yankee, as he received the strops, and passed over the picayune. "A trade's a trade—and now you're wide awake in airnest, I guess the next time you trade with that 'ere plc, you'll do a little better than 0 buy razor strops. And away walked the pedlar with his strops and his wager, amid the shouts of the laughing crowd. - WOMAN !—Dr. Mackay gives in his reminiscences a racy sketch of Sir John Easthope, the principal proprietor of the Morning Chronicle, on which the doctor was at one time engaged. Sir John is descfibed by his old employee as an extremely irascable man, captious and disagreeable in all matters of business connected with the paper, and conse- quently the reverse of popular with the people employed in the office, many of whom habitually spoke of him, with a grim attempt at jocosity, as" Sir John Blast-Hope." But in private and social life he was the very soul of good-fel- lowship, and made his employees forget, at his table or else- where, all the rebuffs he bad made them undergo in the exercise of their vocation. Dr. Mackay had been away from the Chronicle for nine years when he mat Sir John for the last time. It was in 1853, when the baronet had gone to Paris to visit his old friend, the Emperor of the French. Both Mackay- and his former employer happened to stay at the same hotel, and Sir John invited the doctor to his room in the evening to take a hand at a rubber of whist. Dr. Mackay's partner was Lady Wyatville, the widow of a once-celebrated architect, over eighty, sharp, active, intelligent. and still showing traces of a beauty that must in her youth Wave been remarkable. The lady re- voked, and being accused of it, vehemently denied the fact, treating the proofs afforded of it wiith haughty disdain and not very polite contradiction. Sir John lost patience with her, and rising abruptly in his chair, exclaimed," Madam, you are a cheat !" The lady's eyes flashed with almost pre- ternatural fire as she also rose in her chair, and took a step or two towards Sir John, as if. she would inflict summary punishment upon his face with her nails. Sir John, still standing, said, "Yes, madam, I repeat it You cheat abominably! And in the course of a long life," he -added, laying his hand upon his heart," I have invariably noticed that the handsomer a woman is the more she cheats at cards.' The lady sat down •, a smile suffused her ancient but still' beautiful face; and the apparent tigress of a minute before became as gentle as a dove."

div.p: NORTHWICH DIVISION ELECTION- SELECTION OF A CANDIDATE. SPEECH BY MR. BRUNNER. A meeting of the Liberal Three Hundred for the Northwich Division of the County of Chester was held at the Salvation Army Barracks, Winsford, on Saturday afternoon. About 200 delegates were present, including a large number from Runcorn. Mr. E. 11. Moss, the president, occupied the chair, and there were also on the platform—Mr. Jamws Handley, Runcorn (chairman of .Council), Mr. J. Slater and Mr. J. C. Johnson (vice-presidents), Mr. A. Fleteher (hon. secretary), Mr W. Handley (general secretary), and Mr. W. H. Tolfree (local secretary for Winsford). After some preliminary business had been transacted, The CUAIRMAN moved "That the General Council of the Northwich Division L beral Association thank John Tom- linson Brunner, Etci , for the consistent support he has ac- corded to the Government in the present Parliament— (cheers)—and hereby resolves that he be again invited to contest the division—(cheer)—at the ensuing Parliament- ary election in the Liberal interest as a supporter of the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone." (Cheers.) It was only In November last that they had the pleasure of returning Mr. Brunner to Parliament with a very large majority as the representative of the division. (Cheers.) The session, it was true, had been a short but laborious one, and Mr. Brun- ner had worked hard incessantly at his deities in London. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) His name would be found in nearly every divieion list, and he (the chairman) had always found it on the side of freedom and progress. (Cheers.) At the last election they had a great number of Issues before them, but now it was narrowed down. The question was, should they support Mr. Gladstone's policy— (cheers)—or that of Lard Salisbury? (Groans and laugh- ter.) Under these circumstances, all he had to say was that they must vote true to their party. Every vote withheld weakened the Liberal party as a whole, and every vote given for what they called a Liberal Unionist—(laughter)— increased the Tory majority. There was a compact now between the Tory party and the Liberal Unionist, and it re- minded him very much of the monkey and the chestnuts. (Laughter.) Mr. Jamas HANDLEY seconded the resolution. He was sure they were all unanimous in supporting the terms of the resolution. They had, as the chairman had remarked, only one issue before them—conciliation or coercion. If they gauged the majerity aright, he thought they were ou the side of conciliation, and if they were for that policy where could they find a better representative than their present member ? (Cheers.) Mr. Gladstone, in the great speech which be delivered at Edinburgh on Friday night, said the Only pledge- which a Ministerialiet candidate ought to give should be in the following terms, that he was ready in the coming Parliament to support a bill which would give Ire- land a really effective control of her own local affairs. That was all they required, that was all the pledge they required. The bill was dead, but the principle of it was alive. (Hear. hear.) They thoroughly went with Mr. Gladstone, and they believed that the course upon which he had entered would bring contentment, peace, and prosperity to Ireland. They were told in the good old book, "Righteousness exalteth a nation," and he was certain that Mr. Glad- stone had taken this step in the pith of righteousness. (Cheers.) The Rev. W. GULLEY, of Northwich, sueported the re- solution. In the course of his speech he said he hoped they would decide this election with a little more magnanimity and with a little less bitterness and personality than on the last occasion. (Hear, hear.) Mr. J. H. COOKE, of Winsford, spoke amid continual in- terruption against the resolution. Be contended that the Irish faction—(a Voice: "Nation ")—in the House of Commons only wanted to secure for their country severance from England. (Cries of "No, no," "Nonsense," and Never.") These were his views. ("You don't under- stand the question," and cries of "Sit down.") Alter some further remarks in the same strain. A Delegate suggested that tbe Chairman should ask Mr. Cooke to move an an.endment or sit down. His one ob- jection was to sow disunion in the meeting. (Cheers.) Mr. J. R. FRITH (Runcorn): May I ask Mr. Cooke if he supported Mr. Gladstone at the last election? (Cries of " No, ' and "Old turncoat.") Mr. COOSII attempted to speak on the Land Purchase Bill, but he was obliged to leave the platform amid a storm of Ironical laughter and groans; while cheers were given for Mr. Brunner. The resolution WAS then carried unanimously, and Mr. Brunner WAS brought into the room. He was accorded a most enthusiastic reception, the audience rising and sing- ing "For he is a jolly good fellow." Mr. BRUNNER, who, on rising to address the meeting, was received with mace cheering, said it did one' heart's good to find they were the thorough earnest men he had known in the noblest cause they had ever to fight. The re- solution thanked him for the consistent support he had ac- corded to the Government in the present Parliament. He wanted no thanks from them for the work he had done for them in the short time since they last met, for be could as- sure them that it had been to him a heartfelt pleasure. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) The resolution went on to say that he was again invited to contest the division, and right grad he was to see those words. (Laughter and cheers.) They did not know whether their friends on the other side I were going to pluck up couraore to fight—(a voice: "Which of them," and laughter)—nor yet did they know who their champion was to he if they did pluck up cenrage—(a voice: "And we don't care ")—but that there should be a contest he desired from the bettom of his heart. If there was anything he liked it was a good tight in a good cause. (Cheers.) Last year, and not only during the election con- test, but from the beginning of the year to the end, he stood before them as a supporter of their great leader, Mr. Glad- stone—(hear. hear)—and as a supporter of Mr. Gladstone he stood before them that day. (Cheers.) During the last session he had, as they wanted him to do, voted straight. (Hear, hear.) They would bear him described, over and over again, in the few weeks that were to come before the final decision was made, as a servile follower of Mr. Glad- stone. Be had been nothing of the sort. He claimed to have voted straight because he had voted for the principles he laid down last November. He really believed he voted as often against the Government as in their favour. In the most important vote that he gave he voted for the princi- ple of the Home Rule Bill—(hear, hear)—and let him tell them that on the let December they voted for the principle of the bill. (Hear, hear.) No candidate throughout the three kingdoms spoke straighter than he did for the prin- ciple. He then said that he would give to Ireland full power to manage all affairs purely Irish—(hear, hear,)—but that be would consent to no plan which would make the two millions of Irish people living in Great Britain foreigners amonget us. (Cheers.) He would not go for separation. (Hear, hear.) Many a man amongst the 93 dissentient Liberals said he would rather have separation than this bill. He would not. (Cheers.) He wanted a real Union, and for a real Union he had voted. (Cheers.) He had not the shadow of a doubt that they would vote for the principle again, and that they would give him the opportunity of voting for it.—(criespf "We will ")—for no matter what their friends at Northwich decided tat afternoon—(laugh- ter)—he was going to be the member for the Northwich Division. (Cheers.) But after all it did not depend upon him ; it depended upon them, and he knew full well that there was not a set of men throughout the whole length and breadth of the country that were better to be depended upon than were they. (Cheers.) He was not going to discuss the details of the Home Rule Bill, but he wanted to point out to them that in coming to that decision he was following their own ex- ample. They had an organisation, a thoroughly sound and well-grounded organization— (a Voice: "Not a Caucus")— but what did they do when they started it and when they amended the rules by which they had chosen so guide themselves? Did they discuss the details of these rules in full board? No; like sensible men they appointed a com- mittee to consider them, and when the committee—repre- sentative men of their own choice—had considered them they accepted them. (Hear, hear.) You accepted the de- tails by which you bound yourselves together. So on the larger scale the voters of the country decide upon the prin. Ciple and leave it to the Parliament—the small committee-- to settle the details. Nevertheless, gentlemen, with regard to these details what had he said? He said this: "But with regard "—this was his last speech to them—" to the Home Rule Bill, I may say that I don't think it a perfect bill any more than I think the Land Purchase Bill a perfect bill." Though he had had to do with a great many Acts of Parlia- ment, he never yet knew a perfect one. With regard to the latter, lie had told them that the landlords were going to get ten much mosey. They usually did. That was an evil to face in that bill. With regard to the Home Rule Bill, he .did not like the exclusion of the Irish members from the Parliament at Westminster, and he agreed with Mr. Cham- berlain in his reason for disliking that exclusion. He wanted the Parliament at Westminster to be a supreme and Imperial Parliament. He had not the shadow of a doubt they were all absolutely unanimous on that point. It was .a wrong thing to ask the Irish to pay money to ns that we should spend it, and that they should have no voice iD the spending of it; and if England should get into trouble, as she may do some day, he thought that the Irish, who comprise a very large proportion of the namiis which are meat illustrious in war, shoulel be called upon to join us. He claimed to have the courage of his own cenvictiene, aod to be one of the men whom Mr. Chamberlain recom- mended should be sent to the House of Commons. (Hear, hear.) Whether he had the ability to express his opinions or not he left to them. Be wished he had more. (Cheers.) The first objection to the bill was that if passed it would lead to the dismemberment of the empire and the second that it would destroy the supremacy of Parliament. Now pitt,ose of the greatest prime ministers England ever had up to Mr. Gladstone's time, in 179, when Grattan's Parlia- ment existed In Dublin used the words, "Great Britain and Ireland form one empire; they are inseparably connected." He (Mr. Bruonee) appealed from Hertington and Chamber- t ain to Pitt and Gladetone. He pinned his faith upon the greater men, and when they had it that in 179, at the time of the existence of Grattan'e Parliament, Great Britain and Ireland formed one emptre far more would they form one •ernpße when the Parliament that Mr. Gladstone proposed ahoEari have been granted. (Cheers.) And why? Because Mr. Gladstone proposed that the very large powers that were paesessed by Grattante Parliament should he withheld from the parliament he proposed to establish. We had now a paper union with Ireland, and as a paper union a very complete and perfect paper union it was. (A voice "It is perforated," and laughter.) But what did that union lack. It lacked this, that it absolutely prevented a union of hearts. (Cheers.) We were in a time of revolution, and he fished them to recognise the fact that there had been one

BRUNNER AT NORTHWICH. The first public meeting in support of Mr. Brunner, the Ministerial candidate, was held on Wednesday night at Northwich. Mr. C. Green presided over a very large and enthusiastic gathoring.—The Rev.W. Vausa (Runcorn) pro- posed a resolution recognising that the Home Rule pro- posals of Mr. Gladstone were an earnest and righteous en- deavour to no justice to Ireland, and to maintain and strengthen the integrity of the Empire on the basis of con- ciliation instead of coercion.—Mr. Kniveton seconded the motion in a speech which was greatly applauded.—The re- solution was carried unanimously, as also another resolu- tion favourable to Mr. Brunner's candidature. Mr. Brunner, who received an enthasistic ovation, claim- ed that he declared in favour ef Irish self-government in his address last year, when he was returned. He saw the Tory Government, contrary to ' all precedent, retain- ing office. What was the reason ? The reason was the Carnarvon - Parnell interview. (Applause.) He saw also eighty-five Parnellites demanding Home Rule and the Orangemen urging coercion. Now, what was coercion? It was something very different to enforcing the ordinary law. It meant imprisoning men without bringing them to trial, suspension of trial by jury,the violation of homed by police- men without warrant, the expulsion of aliens, the renewal of the Norman laws of curfew and blood tax, and the gag- ging of the Press. Would Englishmen tolerate such things in their own country. (Loud cries of "No?") Then, in God's name, why force them on Irishmen? What was the cause of Irish discontent? It was misgovernment. Eng- land had forced her Church and her laws upon Ireland, and worse, had not reformed them for the Irish when reforming them for herself. The refusal to reform the Irish Corpora- tions had the effect of increasing the death rate. The hor- rible sy?tem of landlordism had starved a million of peo- ple, and expatriated two millions. One of the most ini- quitious Acts ever passed was the encumbered Estates Act of 1847. R4specting the hoped-for results the " Times " wrote :—" In a few years a Celtic Irishman will be as rare in Connemara as is the red Indian en the shores of Man- hattan." Mr. Gladstone had declared that the Act was a gigantic robbery of the tenants' improvements, and so it was. (Cries of 4' Shame.") What was the remedy ? It was that proposed by Fox in 1800—the Irish Government regulated by Irish actions—and that was what Mr. Gladstone pro- posed. Three clrees were afterwards given for Mr. Brunner. UNIONIST CANDIDATE AT RUNCORN. STORMY MEETING.

Mr. Robert Verdin having failed to successfully woo the representative Liberals, and his brother's aspirations for a Parliamentary life having been doomed to disappointment, has now come forward in the character of a" Unionist "with the support and consent of the Conservatives of the Northwich Division. He appeared before the electors of Run- corn on Wednesday evening, when a public meet- ing was held in the Public Hall. Amongst those present, who were far from numerous until after the meeting had proceeded for half an hour, the "Grand Old Man appeared to be a great favourite, and cheers were frequently raised in his favour. Upon Dr. McDougall. the chairman, entering the platform, accompanied by a number of Tories, there were loud groans, mingled with cheers and cries of "Turn coat. On the platform were the Rev. W. Preston, Dr. Mackie (Warrington), Messrs. Robert Verdin (the candidate), W. H. Verdin, Joseph Ver- din, I. Brundrit, J. H. Cooke, F. A. Lake, J. W. Lighthurn, John Paterson (Liverpool), J. W. Alsop (Liverpool), and Captain Clark. Mr. COOKE, who is agent to the candidate, read letters supporting Mr. Verdiu's candidature from the private sec- retary to the Duke of Westminster. Mr. William Hayes, and Mr. Beckett Chadwick. The CHAIRMAN, in a rather lengthy speech, was repeatedly interrupted by groans and cries .of " Tories," " Turncoat," claimed to have been a " passive Liberal "for the last 18 years, and that although now against Mr. Gladstone, he was on the side of such men as Mr. Bright. Mr. Chamberlain, Mr. Trevelyan, and Lord Hartiogton, and he considered himself equally as good a Liberal as any in Runcorn. He argued that by Mr. Gladstone's hill Ireland would be re- duced to a vassal or a tributary state—(loud cries of "no ") —and that, should England become involved in war, he did not believe that Ireland would contribute her portion to- wards the cost. (Hisses ) He asked were they prepared to pay their quota of the 200 millions required for the Land Purchase Bill. (A. voice : "Make Ireland pay as you have always done," and cheers.) He eoncladed by stating tkat be voted for Mr. Brunner last year —(chears)—and that had Mr. Brunner voted against the Home Rule Bill and suppor- ted Mr. Chamberlain in his scheme of domestic legislation for Ireland, they would not have seen him there that night. (" Sit down.")—Mr. J. Pasrmasost, ot Liverpool, moved " That this meeting considers that in all legislation relating to Ireland the following principles mast be maintained :- Ist, the supremacy of the Imperial Parliament (hear, hear) ; 2nd, the maintenance of the union ; and 3rd, the protection of the Irish Loyalists." (Hear, hear.) This speaker was several times brought to a stindstill through the disturbance that prevailed, and the Chairman intimated to Mr. John Ravenecroft, who occupied a seat in the gallery, that unless be behaved himself "they would tumble him out." When Mr. Paterson asked those present to follow such men as John Bright, he was asked amid great cheering why his friends on the platform did net follow him, and three cheers were given for Mr. Gladstone. He was told he was "wast- ing his breath" to talk there, that his remarks were "nothing but bosh,' and he resumed his seat amid groans mingled with cheers, having described the Home Rule Bill as a sham imaginary, fictitious, and fantastical scheme.—Mr. J. W. Alsop, of Liverpool, seconded the resolution, but the greater part of his remarks must have been inaudible to the major portion of the audience, and he was constantly inter- rupted by cries of "Poor fellow," and other interjections.— The resolution was than put to the meeting by the chair- man, who declared it carried. A voice called out, "Let us understand it," and then followed three enthusiastic cheers for the "Grand Old Man. ' "For be is a jolly good fellow" was also heartily sung. Mr. Robert Verdin, the candidate, en rising to deliver his address, was greeted with cries of 'Tory" and cheers and gtoans that continued for some time. He stood, he saiS, as a Liberal, and not as a Radical (" Tory "). He had held the princi- ples of Liberalism during the whole of his life. (Long- continued groans and disturbance.)—The Chairman ap- pealed to the audience not to disgrace the good old town. (Cheers.)—Mr. Verdin, proceeding, said having fought in the Liberal cause in the past, he should continue to fight in the Liberal cause. (Laughter, shouts of" Tory," and other cries of dissent.) He would willingly put Irishmen on the same footing as Englishmen, but if they gave Ireland Home Rule, what would be the consequence. (Cries of "peace," " happiness,"" union," and cheers.) The time was when there was such prejudice against Irishmen that Englishmen did not like to work along with them. That prejudice had gradually died out. (Cheers.) They had become so mingled that they looked upon each other as brothers. (Hear, hear.) He objected to Home Rule because it would sever that brotherhood, and he trusted the people of Eng- land whether he was returned to Parliament or not—(a voice : " Tha'rt nod in id," and laughter)—would say they would not have the union split. (Cheers.)—Dr. Macias proposed, "That thia meeting accepts Mr. Robert Verdin as a proper and suitable Unionist candidate for this division, and undertakes to support him by all legitimate means." Dr. Mackie good humoured's- led the audience in a round of cheering for Mr. Gladstone, and succeeded in gaining a fair hearing. At the conclusion of Dr. Mackie's speech, Mr. CIJRZON wished to ask him a question and he was invited upon the platform. He at once accepted the invitation and took a seat on the platform amid great laughter. When, however, the question came to be put Dr. Mackie was not to be found, having left the platform to drive home.—Captain CLARK, received with cheers and groans, and a voive "Hard a port "—(laughter) —seconded the resolution. He announced himself as a Whig, He bad, he said, been in the division 31 years, and this was the first time he had ever taken part or parcel in potitics, and the candidature of Mr. Verdict was the cause of him putting in an appearance. He was describing Mr. Verdin's personal qualities, when he was met by crtes of "Politics," and much disturbance ensued, during which be s randedeedf eahteids bayeaat—veTryhelarmgeotraioaniorwitays. pcuthetoertshweermee.4eitvinegn for Mr. Brut:incr.—Mr. T. D. LIVESEY asked whether Mr. Verdin, if elected, would support a Home Rule Bill krought in by the Conservative party ?—Mr. VERDIN replied in the negative. He would vote against any measure which did not extend the same privileges to England, Ireland, and Scotland. (Applause.)—The CLNDIDATE proposed a vote of thanks the chairman.—Mr. W. H. VERDIN seconded, and created a violent disturbance by branding his opponents as disloyal ists, cries of shame coming forth from all parts of the hall.—The motion was carried unanimously, and in replying Dr. McDouGALL said he should content himself with mentioning the names of three persons who bad dis- turbed the meeting. The first was Mr. John Daniel Jones, librarian to the Free Public Library. The remainder of his remarks were lost in the tremendous uproar that ensued. Mr. Jones, imme 'lately his name was mentioned, rose to his feet, but the chairman motioned that he could cot be heard. Mr. W. H. Verdin struck up the National Anthem, and his Tory friends to all appearances followed his lead, but the groans and hooting that proceeded from hundreds Pt throats drowned their voices. Mr. :ones went forward to the platform, and was about to address the audi- ence when Dr. McDougall pushed him to the extreme end of the platform. Mr. Jones was loudly cheered, and threat- ening demands were made by the audience for an apology. The excitement was intense, and the audience rushed ot the platform in a body. Most of the AccupAnts of the plat- form made their exit, evidently fearing violence, but the audience contented themselves with expressing strong dis- approval of Dr. McDousall's canduet. At length there was a brief lull, and Dr. McDougall said ' he had no intention of injaring Mr. Jones. Cheers were raised for Mr. JONES, who said that if an ex- planation of his conduct was needed by the audience— (shouts of 'Not a bit of it ")—he could simply say that he exercised his right an a voter. He did not think 'the re.
land found in him a mighty champion; at a time when his just denunciation of wickedness in hich places" earned for Ulm the hatred of the Tory and aristocratic parties all over the country ?._

The cause of liberty and justice will not stand still be- cause some of those who should be leaders lag behind. This generation will witness no greater or grander act than that of lifting from the shoulders of Irishmen the grievous burden under which, alas, they have suffered and greened so long.—Yours, dm, FELIX I:10LT. VOTE FEARLESSLY FOR MR. GLADSTONE AND IRISH HOME RULE. Sir,—l greatly regret to no completely debarred, by con- siderations of health, from taking any public part in the present political campaign, but I am not physically able to stand the excitement of it. The question now before the electors, however, is so transcendently important, and opinion in the ranks of our party is unhappily so conflict- ing, that it Is most undesirable for any supporter of Mr. Gladstone's policy, who holds a position of prominence in the community, to allow his absence or silence to be open to misconstruction. The opponents of Home Rule are so clamorous, and Liberals not s few are so full of nervous , fears lest Home Rule for Ireland should be the death-blow to even English power and prosperity, that it becomes the bounden duty of every Liberal ;who has the courage of his principles to make free avowal of his faith. My object, therefore, in this letter is, by your permission, briefly, but emphatically, to declare my cordially adhesion to the policy of Home Rule for Ireland, and my earnest hope that my fellow Liberals in Warrington will, one and all, " shake off their fears, and put a cheerful courage on," and make Mr. Crosfield's election sure. I advocate Home Rule for Ireland for several reasons, and, among ethers, these :- Ist. Our government of Ireland has hitherto been a most miserable failure, for it has alienated the people whom it should seek to attach and bind closely to our national heart and life, and it has become a reproach against us throughout the world. 2nd. Our government of Ireland has been such that if we saw it pursued by any other Power towards any similarly subject nationality, we should be the first to denounce the injustice and tyranny. 3rd. It England had been under Ireland, as Ireland has been under England, we Britons, who boast that we "never will be slaves," would have rebelled as truly as, and perhaps even more violently than, Ireland has against the many in- justices of our rule. 4th. It is impossible for one Christian democracy to con- tinue to deny popular rights to another Christian democracy. Justice and righteousness must prevail. Home Hula for Ireland, which means simply power for the Irish people to govern themselves by themselves in their own offairs is mere justice to a distinct nationality. And I believe in the maxim, often avowed, but now in this instance unhappily forgotten, by Mr. John Bright, "be just, and fear Lint." sth. The fears of the evil consequences of Catholic as- cendency in Ireland that are being expressed by the Protes- tants of Ulster may be honest, but are hardly honourable to that powerful community, while they are by no means shared by Protestants who live in the midst of the Catholic majority. And such fears should operate least of all upon those of us who believe in civil and religious liberty and equality. For Nonconformists to show cowardice in this respect is a positive disgrace. 6th. Ireland, by her duly-elected representatives in Par- liament, has declared that Mr. Gladstone's proposal will be accepted by her as a final settlement of the long contro- versy between England and herself. She has declared that she will loyally carry out the scheme subject to the conditions which the Imperial Parliament may impose, and that she will do so in fairness and honour towards all classes in her community. We are bound to accept this assurance, and may do so in the full faith that when Ireland is given true Home Rule, she will speedily show that she can rule her 'home to her own credit and our entire satisfaction.—Yours I faithfully,

MESsES. JuSEPH CROsFIELD Sc SUNS AS EXHIBITORS. As the visitor wends his way through the lofty galleries of the Liverpool International Exhibition and surveys the singularly varied objects which are there gathered together in such profusion, he must often feel impressed with the vastness of the busi- ness enterprise of the manufacturers and traders of this and other countries, which has done so much to make the Exhibition what it is. On every hand there are exhibits, the result of amazing skill and efficiency of labour and great cost, which would not have been there but for the enterprise of business firms whose peculiar departments of production they represent. English exhibitors, of course, in .the number of their stands take a long lead, and amongst the English exhibitors those of Warring- ton, as we have previously pointed out in a de- tailed notice of their exhibits, in comparison with the size of the town, take a prominent place. We mentioned that, in addition to the beautiful dis- play in gallery F of the main building, Messrs. J. Crosfield and Sons, soap manufacturers, of this town, were to have a kiosk in the grounds, which at the time of our first notice was only in course of erection. That kiosk is now completed, and it is not too much to say that it agrees with the other exhibit of Messrs. Crosfield in this, that while the latter is one of the most admired of the things that are to be seen in the interior of. the building, the kiosk is equally admired outside. The person who has passed through the various departments of the large building has by no means exhausted the attractions of the Exhibition. There are many notable things to be seen in the surrounding grounds. The grounds in themselves are delightful to stroll through, and in addition they con- tain the remarkable similitucte of the Eddy- stone lighthouse, the model dairy in which butter is made by machinery, and the curiosities of the Indian village. It is in the neighbourhood of this last-named erection that Messrs. Crosfield's kiosk is placed. This kiosk, it will be found, whilst having its business aspect, and indeed affording one of the most striking examples of that business en- terprise to which we have alluded, is also one of the finest embellishments of the exhibition grounds. The structure is of a light and elegant design, and in admirable keeping with its surround- ings. It has been painted in a manner that gives it the appearance, at a first glance, of having been built of the very appropriate material, mottled soap. A closer inspection in this case adds enchant- ment to the view, for the interior has been finished with a kina of Oriental elaboration. The roof is brightly displayed with star-like spangles, and the ceiling and sides are draped with a profusion of handsome hangings, besides various other sorts of ornamentation. That the kiosk has not been erected solely for the purpose of embellishing and adding attraction to the grounds, as from its ornate char- acter might naturally be suspected, is to be seen from the counter—the unmistakeable emblem of business—which it contains, and the striking dis- play of soaps of almost every colour and blending of colours. There are specimens of the common varieties of household soaps used by the lowliest to promote that highly-placed virtue, cleanliness, and likewise a wide selection of the costlier toilet soaps shaped into elegant tablets. It may safely be assumed that this kiosk will not be one of the least visited parts of the great exhibition, and in- deed those who come away without havinc, seen it can scarcely be said to have made the best 7of their visit. It may be explained that the exhibit of Messrs. Crosfield, in gallery F., is one of the most remark- able of the many noteworthy objects surrounding it, and is probably unique of its kind. It consists of a beautiful temple-like structure built entirely of a great variety of soaps. It is oriental in its architectural style, having been designed by Mr. Gray, an artist employed by Messrs. Garnett and Sons, Sankey-st., and is completed, in every part, of soap manufactured by Messrs. Crosfield. Few could have imagined that out of such a common- place substance so beautiful a thing could have been made, and probably fewer still have thought that the soap-maker has such resources as Messrs. Crosfield here display. Some of the parts, one might almost think, were composed of exquis- itchy tinted marbles, while others present the col- ours and appearance of different kinds of building stone. As might be expected, much use is made of the mottled varieties of soap, and the really artistic manner in which they are blended and contrasted with each other makes a striking effect. The minarets or cupolas of the temple are compounded of a special manufacture of Messrs. Crosfield, the Perfection" soap, which is so rapidly getting into favour for ordin- ary domestic purposes thatmmense and increasing quantities are turned out. It is claimed for this soap that it is much superior for its purposes to any other kind, both in regard to economy and effici- ency. Messrs. Crosfield, as. is well known, manu- facture very largely for foreign Markets, and they do not commit the mistake, which is often laid at the door of Englith manufacturers, of not consult- ing the tastes of their foreigh customers. It will be seen from the specimens of the kinds sent abroad that the tastes of foreign users of soap lie much in the direction of bright colouring. Near to this exhibit Messrs. Crosfield have algo a stand at which visitors may procure specimens of their soaps, so that it will be seen that this firm is particularly well represented at the great Lancashire exhi- bition.

div.head: SIR RICHARD CROSS AT NEWTON.
div.p: SIR RICHARD CROSS AT NEWTON.

Sir Richard Assbeton Cross. the Conservative can. ate for the Newton Division, commenced his , electoral campaign on Monday evening, when he ad- dressed a meeting of his supporters in the Town Hall, Newton. The chair was occupied by Mr. 'Marcus Brown Westhead, chairman of the Newton Polling Conservative Club, and among the gentlemen present were Captain Withington, J.P., Mr. John Pearson, J.P., Mr. R. Houghton, J.P., W. F. Gooch, J.P., Mr. T. J. Gillespie, J.P., Mr. R. Pier. point, J.P. (Warrington), Alderman Davies. 'LP- (Warrington), Captain Seton, Messrs. B. B. Glover, W. Valiant (Ashton), T. Stone, C. B. F. Boum., W. Arnott (Golborne), C. F. Clark, T. Sutton, H. J. Longton, D. Mather, R. H. Wright, G. Clarke. J. I Lythgoo, R. Brierley, R. Barton, .1, Thompson, F. J. Wood, J. Patinas, Rev. James Carson, Dr. A. Handy. side, and others. The CHAIRMAN, who was well received, said Sir Richard Cross was asking their support upon one issue—were they or were they not going to submit to the breaking up, in- directly in the first instance, of a part of the Empire ? (‘• No," and applaose.) Sir RICHARD CROSS was received with cheers. Consider- able amusernent was occasioned by an attempt to sing "For be's a jolly good fellow," but the effort was a failure. He said the present Parliament would soon be dissolved, and the misfortune was, a great deal of good work which Par- liament was ready to do would now be for a long time laid aside. They would remember at the last election the pre- sent Premier put forward an authorised programme under four particular heads, saying ,that the subjects were ripe for legislation, and, as he (Sir Richard) said at that time about those four points, there was very little to choose between the programme of one side or the other. Nobody could have believed at the last election that Mr. Gladstone projected bringing in spelt bills, and ha looked upon these as the most startling propositions which any responsible Minister of the Crown had ever made, and he thought the question was one which they would de well to consider. Parliament did consider these measures, and it was put in a great difficulty with them. The bill for the Irish Government was introduced by the Prime Minister in one of his wonderful speeches ; and the second bill, for the purchase of land, was also in- troduced in anOther wonderful speech by the Prime Minis- ter, who tried to impress upon the country the absolute importance of passing these two measures, which he de- clared to ba absolutely inseparable, and he meant to pass them if he could. But, unfortunately, the more these measures were looked at the less they were liked, and Mr. Gladstone had already lost several of his colleagues, who would not join his Government even to make inquiry as to the question of a separate Government for Ireland. The result was that Parliament decided by a majority of thirty to throw out the first measure—and he thought most wisely —for what he called the futute misgo.rernment of Ireland. (Applause.) The country had now to decide one great issue—would they or would they not give Home Rule to Ireland? (" No.') Mr. Gladstone was trying to bamboozle the people of England and Scotland—(applause and hisses) —to go for something they did not know what. He said "Our bills are dead, out the principle is alive." But he (Sir Richard) would ask what principle? (Laughter.) The question they had to ask themselves was—would they estab- lish for the first time, in the heart of a united empire, an ab- solute independent Legislature and administrative body— (hear, hear, and No ")—absolutely independent of the con- trol of the Imperial Parliament ? ("No.") This was the question which he was going to put to the electors of the Newton Division, and he had not the smallest doubt that, if an opponent was brought out against . him, the voice of the constituency would declare it- self almost unanimously for himself. (Applause.) He believed that by gentle and firm dealing they would bring Ireland into habits of prosperity, and they might get capital into the country and develops its industries, and make the people happy and contented. They did not require coercion for Ireland; all that they required was that the same liberties which they enjoyed in England and Scotland should be felt and enjoyed in Ireland. (Hear, hear.) It was not simply to the inhabitants of these islands that they must turn, and it was most essential that this great empire, this anion of three kingdoms, should be maintained unim- paired and undiminished, for if they broke up the great Im- perial Parliament their influence and progress for good throughout the world would be lessened and diminished. (Applause.) Mr. 3. CATHERALL moved " That this meeting, haying heard Sir Richard Cross's address signifying his assent to become a candidate for this division in the next Parliament, hereby promises him its support, satisfied he will do his ut- most to preserve and maintain the Empire."—Mr. 'F. Stre coca (Golborne) seconded the motion, which was supported by Mr. R. Pierpoint, of Warrington, and Alderman Davies (Warrington), and passed unanimously.—Sir R. A. CROSS acknowledged the resolution, and moved a cordial vote of thanks to the chairman, which was passed.

A Suteme.t. FAMILY.—On Saturday morning, a shocking case of suicide was reported to the East Surrey coroner. Mr. Wm. Gage, aged 57 years, greengrecer, Bermondsey, Lon- don, was discovered with his head nearly eevered from his body in the stable at the rear of his shop, a large carving knife being by his side. About 12 months ago one of his daughters committed suicide in the Surrey Canal, and since that time another daughter had twice attempted to drown herself at Ramsgate. TERRIBLE THUNDERSTORM: ONE MAW KILLED.— A. thunderstorm of brief duration, but unusually severe, passed over Earlestown and Newton district on Saturday afternoon. 'Though the sun was shining nearly the whole of the time, rain fell heavily. The peals of thunder were loud and con- tinuous, while the lightning was occasionally very vivid. One man was killed and several persons injured by the lightning at Wigan. The thunderstorm broke over the town, and lightning struck a party of spectators surrounding a booth outside the public park. Seven persons were thrown down, and it was found that one was dead and two others partially paralysed The lightning was very vivid and the thunder extraordinarily loud. At Golborne the church tower was stripped of its slates and some narrow escapes are reported.

Puna IN A COIXTERY.—A fire broke out on Monday in the workings of •Crosby Colliery, near Maryport. A large quantity of wood was in the neighbourhood, and the fire spread rapidly. The whole of the miners had to leave the workings, and they were safely got out. It is not believed that the coal has become ignited, prompt measures having been taken to put out the fire. The colliery is one of three owned by Messrs. Baird and Co., who employ about 300 persons. DEATH OP HOBART PASHA.—Hobart Pasha, otherwiselthe Hon. Augustus Charles Hobart-Hampden, uncle to the Earl of Buckinghamshire, died at Milan, on Saturday, in his 65th year. He joined the Navy in 1836, but after some active service cf the Confederate States from 1861 to 1865, and commanded a blockade runner. In 1888 he was appointed to a command in the Ottoman Navy, and since that time he has, with little intermission, been in the Turkish service. He was the first Christian upon whom the rank of Marshall of the Turkish Empire was conferred.

DREADFUL TRAGIEDY.—A shocking tragedy occurred at Bow, London, on Saturday evening. Walter Wright went to the house of his sweetheart, Alice Clark, and fired a pis- tol at her, and then attempted to kill her mother, after 'which be shot himself through the head. The reason for the outrage is not at present apparent, but it is believed that a case pending in a local court which he had brought against another girl for perjury in charging him with being the father of her illegitimate child had preyed upon his mind, and had rendered him temporarily insane. Dr. Spicer, of Tredegar-road, was at once summoned, and he sent Mrs. Clark to the London Hospital, where she died under an operation. The bullet having entered her head at the nose, passed through the roof of the mouth and tongue, and lodged in the throat. Alice Clark lies in a precarious con- dition, the bullet having entered the left temple, and, pass- ing through the nose, lodged in the cheek. The murderer cannot possibly recover, he having shot himself in the right , temple, whence the bulls, entered the brain. He was de- , tained by Dr. Spicer at the residence of Mr. Hamlyn, in Tredegar-road, and bia :her remained with him awaiting jliB death.

Cricket: Australians, first innings, 354 ; Middlesex, second innings, 83 for one wicket. The National Union of Conservatives Associations have addressed an appeal to electors of the United Kingdom. Sir Wm. Harcourt, addressing a meeting of Midland Railway workmen at Derby, on Friday, said there was al- ways a lot of weak-kneed Liberals or piebald politicians who deserted the ranks when any fighting was to be done. Such Liberals were not worthy of a chief like Mr. Glad- stone. Referring to the Railway Rates Bill, which had been made a local question in Derby, the right hon. bart. said he understood from the Board of Trade that a satisfac- tory understanding had been come to with the Railway Companies.
AIR. GL kDSTONE'S VISIT TO MANCHESTER.

Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone left Ilawarden Castle on Friday afternoon shortly before one o'clock, and, driving to Sandycroft Railway Station, took the train to Chester, and thence through Warrington to Manchester.

On-reaching Manchester a tremendous reception awaited him. His rogress through the city was a 1 great triumphal procession. Mr. Gladstone, in addressing,. monstre meeting in the Free Trade Hall, spoke with regret of the loss of Mr. Bright, whose critic he refused to be ; but urged that during the last fifteen years he had never said one word against the principle of Home Rule. They had lost the upper ten thousand of the party. but happily the Liberal party depended less than some other parties on the upper ten. The Irish members, by moderating their demands, had shown a desire to settle the question, but the oppo- sition had shown no desire, and had altogether dis- regarded the safeguards which the Government had put into the bill. He admitted that the strong feel- ing in Great Britain made it necessary to retain the Irish members at Westminster for Imperial affairs. He challenged Mr. Chamberlain to produce the Land Purchase Scheme he put before the Government last February, and promised that it would be found in curious contrast with his latest views. He claimed that the Government were perfectly free to reconstruct the whole system while preserving the main principle of the bill, but declined to accept the alternative scheme of Lord Hartington. He made a strong appeal to Manchester Liberals who had fought, and not in vain, for Free Trade, to once more set an example to the country.
