LADY-r.] WESLEYAN AND GENERAL ASSURANCE SOCIETY. Sir,—Would you kindly give me space in your excellent paper to say a few words in favour of the Wesleyan and General Assurance Society. My daughter, Margaret Jones, was insured in this society, and paid one penny per week for some years. She left War- rington a short time back to go to Australia, and upon im- forming the office that I wished to discontinue paying, they generously returned me through my agent, J. Procter Jones, of 6, Academy-street, £1 4s Od of the premiums I paid. As many statements have been made contradicting that the Wesleyan does not give a cash surrender value, I can prove these statements to be false, as it is the fifth time that the society has given me surrender value for my children under similar circumstances.
Trusting I am not trespassing on too much of your valua- ble space, I am, sir, yours respectfully, JANE JONES, 85, Winwlck-road, Warrington. Warrington, 23rd June, 1886.
- REV. G. S. REANEY AND MR. JOHN CROSFIELD.

Sir,—Will you allow me to express my hearty hopes that Mr. John Crosfield may win the seat at the coming election. As a Nonconformist, I have tha fullest sympathy with Mr. Gladstone's endeavour to deal justly with the Irish people. Some of my co-religionists seem afraid of what the Irish Parliament may do in the matter of educa- tion and religion. One thing I feel sure they will not do; they will not force an alien faith and an alien system of education upon 'any of the Irish Protestants. In London, two of the shrewdest Protestants of the day, Rev. J.. G. I Rogers and Rev. Hugh Price Hughes, are on the side of the great Liberal leader. The only thing I fear for Protes- tantism is, that it should deny to Catholic Ireland that which we Dissenters have wrung from Protestant England, civil and religious liberty.—l am, faithfully yours. GEORGE S. REANEY. Stepney House, E., June 21, 1886.

div.head: NECESSITY FOR HOME RULE IN IRELAND AND ENGLAND ALSO.
div.p: THE NECESSITY FOR HOME RULE IN IRELAND AND ENGLAND ALSO.

Sir,—The rearobject of Home Rule appears to be almost entirely lost sight of in. the present controversy. Why was the question cf Home Rule ever raised? and how has it beeripessible to create an interest in the question ? There is only one answer, and that is the interest which Irish- men feel, and feel deeply, in the land, in all its aspects and conditions.

The Land League of Ireland has developed the question of Home Rule as a means to secure to the natural sons of Ireland an interest in the land of their birth. And can any man deny them such a right? But right is not the policy of the great men of the earth ; their policy is might and Ibe power to hold in possession. This policy of the rich and the grett is conspicuous in England as well as in Ire- land. Even the birda of the air are not denied the right A f an independent habitation, a place upon which to build their nest ; but man is refused by his fellow nrin the right to build himself a habitation except he first contributes to the support of another, and pays a ground rent which jointly very often amounts to a greater burden than the Imperial taxation of the country. _ . _

It would be interesting to calcnlate for instance the amount which the inhabitants of Warrington pay annually to three or four men who hold the land in possession, and it would be further interesting to discover the first and orieinal title deed to this land, and to ascertain what human being took upon himself the right to sell it. A piece of land about 70 yards square may lee considered to be an acre. How many acres does the town of Warrington stand upon ? Cast this out at an average price of 3d.per square yard and you get a rental of about £6O per acre per annum, or an amount equal to many thousand pounds sterling per annum paid by Warringtoe alone to three or four persons. This heavy burden is carried by the industrial population, who all pay additional house rent in consequence, and pay I also extra prices upon the goods distributed by the shop- keepers from the same cause. There is also the division of agricultural land into smaller farms so as to support a greater number of families, requir- ing immediate consideration. If "three acres and a cow" will not support a family, then multiply it by three ; but is It not monstrous that one man should have the farming and produce of 300 acres ? It will thus be seen that Home Rule and the requirements of borne, with our fast increas- ing population is becoming a necessity, not only for Ireland but for England also, and unless this or some other means are immediately adopted to relieve our unemployed popula- tion, there will be danger ahead.—Yours truly, AN ENGLISHMAN.

div.head: June 24th, 1886.
div.p: June 24th, 1886.
CLERICAL INSOLENCE.

Sir,—l know net whether we are to have a continuance of the priestly interference in political matters or not, but at all events unless the clergy' learn what is due to the people, and that soon, they will be taught that they are looked upon more as a curse than a blessing. In the report given of the Conservative meeting called to select a candidate, I find a true follower of the Ulster Orange faction, the Rev. I Mr. Carleton, of Warrington, giving his opinion as to what course Mr. P. Rylands should take with his workmen dur- ing the coming election. Says this priestly autocrat, " Mr. P. Ryland was a large employer of labour in Warrington, had undoubted interests in Warrington, and they might I count upon that influence if a battle was to be fought." I Does Mr. Carleton clearly understand what he suggests in I the words I have quoted? Would he like to know that Mr. I Rylands, as the employer of the present writer, had inter- fered with that political freedom which is the birth right of her Majesty's subjects? Englishmen have descended to a low depth in asking for and using a ballot box, but its necessity is proved by the existence of such narrow-minded men as the pastor of Trinity. .Mr. Rylands has thought out the Irish subject for him- ielf, and I can promise Mr. Carleton that he not only knows what is due to himself as a gentleman, but he knows what is due to his workmen, and that is what few Tory employers know, and still fewer Tory clergymen. I am reminded by Mr. Carleton's condect of a passage in one of Lord Mac.aulay's essays. Speaking of the Church of England, he says:—" She continued to be, for more than a hundred and fifty years, the servile handmaid of monarchy, the steady enemy of public liberty. The divine right of kings, and the duty of passive obedience to their commands, were her favourite tenets." We have not altered in this one jot; had the Church power to-day it would crush out all thought and all action, and would glory in the return to faggot and stake The description given by the Timee" (Oct. 9th, 1876) of the Church of the past ap- plies equally to it to-day—" The Church of England w 45 in favour of the alliance of continental absolutists against eonetitutional government; it was against the amelioration of the Criminal Cede, and in favour of the principles of vengeance and prevention as against that of reformation; It was against Catholic Emancipation; it was against Par- liament reform and municipal reform." This charge, made by one who had no sympathies with Radicalism mightlhave bad a thousand examples added to it during tbe last election. What is the Primrose League but a band of men and women organised together to intimidate their lesa fortunate fellow- men.; to cajole with bribes in country districts, and to flatter with empty titles those whom they have hitherto kept, to use the words of a Tory candidate, "in a state of intelligence little better than a pig "P Speaking as a workman. I should advise these clericals to keep silent; a reckoning day is coming, and the people will neither forget the whited sepulchres, nor yet the rich men's toadies. CLIFFORD DIX.

div.head: JOHN BRIGHT'S OPPOSITION TO HOME RULE.
div.p: JOHN BRIGHT'S OPPOSITION TO HOME RULE.

Sire—The splendid service rendered by John Bight to the cauee of freedom and justice in days gone by is justly appreciated by every true Liberal. He has engaged in many struggles for liberty, but, I am sorry to say, he ap- pears to have lost touch with modern Liberalism. The views he bolds on Ireland to-day are in striking contrast to the position in which he stood, and the sentiments he held at the time the Church in Ireland was disestablished.

On June 3, 1868, Mr. Bright, speaking at Liverpool, said —" I have never said that Irishmen are not at liberty to ask for, and if they could accomplish it, to obtain the repeal of the Union. . . . I say we have no right—l am willing to say this anywhere—we have no right whatever to insist uporVa union between Ireland and Great Britain upon our awn terms only." Speaking at Limerick, July 14, 1868, he said—" I am one of those who admit—as every sensible man mast admit— that an act which the Parliament of the United Kingdom has passed, the Parliament of the 'United Kingdom can repeal. And, further, lam willing to admit what everybody in England allows with regard to every foreign country, that any nation believing it to be its interest, has a right to both ask for and strive for national independence." With regard to 'Ulster. Mr. Bright, on April 4, 1860, spoke as follows—" The Ulster men have stood in the way of im- provements in the franchise, in the church, and in the land question. They have purchased Protestant ascendancy, and the price paid for it is the ruin and degradation of their . country" __. •

What will be the verdict of history on the statesman who shall succeed in settling the Irish question ? " I say," said Mr. Bright, on December 23, 1867, "the man who, leading the counsels of the Queen's Government, shall grasp this question and conclude it—who shall comprehend the reme- dies, shall administer them, and shall make them law--L-evill do that which in future time the pen of history will delight to trace. He will to the very full gratify the noblest am- bition of his mind, and he will build up for himself a last- ing memorial in the happiness and the gratitude of a re- generated nation." Such were the grand sentiments of John Bright, fifteen or twenty years ago respecting Ireland. While the "Grand Old Man " has been pushing forward in the path of progress John Bright has gone back. Tho Tories, ready to catch at any straw, have placarded the walls of the town with John Bright's latest opinion on the Irish question. What do they think of the above quotations from speeches made at a time when John Bright was really the Eesples Tribune;" at a time when the oppressed in every

div.p: - TO THE ELECTORS OF THE BOROUGH OF WARRINGTON. GErriam EX, Having been unanimously chosen by the Council of the ..14heral Association to contest the borough at the coming elec- u°n. I have with pleasure consented to be the Liberal candi. date. I have lived amongst you all my life, and for the past five and thirty years have taken a warm interest in promoting the Principles of the Liberal party. MY political opinions are well known. am in favour of perfect religious freedom and equality. I am in favour of and will support the voluntary and de- nominational school system. , I love peace and condemn war. I am in favour of the ee.forcement of the strictest and sound- "t economy in all branches of the public serviee. will, to the utmost of my ability, assist in the reduction of the burden of taxation caused by our enormous national ex- . Penditure, which at present falls far too heavily upon the ahuulders of the working clwses. All measures calculated to foster and improve the Trade fir d Commerce of our Great Empire shall have my most cor- dial support. The one great and important political questicn now before the Country is Mr. Glacbaoue's measure of Home Rule for Ire- -1 d, and you will have to decide at the Polling Booths whether you are in favour of giving to the Irish Nation a Domestic Legislature under conditions such as to maintain the honour and consolidate the unity %.,f the Empire, or whether You will support Lord Salisbury's policy of Twenty Years More of Coercion, and the banishment from the land of their ,„hirth of another million of Irishmen at a cost of Fifty Million r ounds Sterling. If you elect me as your Representative, as I hope and believe you will. I shall earnestly support Mr. Gladstene's measure for the Government of Ireland, because. in my °Pinion, it will spread Peace. Contentment, and Prosperity throughout the Sister Isle, and will bind Great Britain and Ireland in an Union stroneer and more real than has ever ex- ° isted before. I remain, Gentleman. TO THE ELECTORS OF THE WIDNES DIVISION OF THE COUNTY OF LA.NOASTEtt. Gentlemen, —lt is much to be regretted that Mr. Muspratt is prevented by family reasons from again seeking your sup- port. Had he been able to do so, he would have asked your votes, as I now ask them, as a warm supporter of Mr. Glad- stone. Home Rule for Ireland, though apparently a novel idea in some quarters, is not so in LitalCatlilire. where many of us have been long waiting with an ever increasing impatience for the time when a statesman of the necessary authority should have the courage to recognise the actual facts and necessities of the case. Ireland's great want is good and steady government. How is she to get it? Is it to be imposed upon her from outside, and maintained by legislation of a repressive and exceptional chtracter, which cm only be obtained in the face of a fierce opposition in Parliament. and after contests and struggles whieh perpetuate hatred and breed fresh discord, or may we not reasonab'y hope tbat if Irishmen are made responsible for the maintenance of order and the well-being of their country, we shall live to see them at last entering upon the long untrod- ' den paths of peace and prosperity? Mr. Gladstone believes we may be confident of this. Lord Salisbury, on the other band, finds it impossible te believe aaything of the kind. Iriaimen, in his opinion, are not fit to ' be trusted to this limited extent. I ask you to support Mr: Gladstone. Difficulties there may be ahead of us, but it is surely better to pass through these than to dwell amongst them for ever. Mr. Gladstone's policy may be difficult; Lord Salisbury's is plainly impossible. The twenty years of firm government Lord Salisbury advocates would be twenty years of bullying and coaxing, and of constant and discreditable intrigue with the Nationalist Party in the British Parliament. •Sueh a policy, so far frcm strengthening the Imperial Parliament, would disgtace and might destroy it. Home Rule has never failed yet, and I rejoice that the only available course open to us is one which has so fair a chance of success. At the present time the question of Ireland overshadows all else; but, without alluding in detail to other subjects of politi- cal importance. I may say that lam an earnest and unfaltering Liberal, and, therefore, confidently rely upon your support in the ensuing contest. I remain, Gentlemen, Your obedient Servant, AUGUSTINE BIBRELL. 37, Addison-gardens North, NV., June 19, 1886.

iTO THE ELECTORS OF THE NORTHWICH PARLIAMENTARY DIVISION OF CHESHIRE. GEXTLEMEN, You took me into your service last December as an appren- tice. I wish to remain in that service as a journeyman. I ask no higher wages, but only a renewal of your confidence and a continuance of your kindness. Two years ago, Irishmen living in Ireland were, for the first time, put on an equality with you in respect of the power to send men to Parliament to represent their opinions and their feelings. Last year they returned to Parliament 85 men, out of a total of 1,3, pledged and determined to demand at your hands a restoration of their ancient right to a Partiament of their own in Dublin, and Great Britain elected a large majority ot men anxious to do battle for the well-being of the reople against the privileges of a class. The statement has been made that the Irish Proposals would , never have been submitted for consideration. if Mr. Gladstone had been returned to power with a sufficiently large Liberal vote ta support him against the vote of the Irish party. Let truth prevail.. Mr. Gladstone in the November of last year thus warned his countrymen: "If such a matter comes forward at the outset of the proceedings of the new Parliament as I have described, namely, a demand made constitutionally by the vast majority of the representatives of Ireland. for the concession of large local powers of self-government, accompanied wt 0 the ad- mission that the unity of the Empire is not to be impaired, the magnitude of that subject will sweep into the shade for the moment, all those subjects of ordinary legislation on which I, or on which others, have addressed you, and the satisfactory settlement of that subject, which goes down to the very roots and foundations of our whole civil and political constitution, will become the first duty of Paniament.” When Parliament met, the leaders of the Tory party, dis- appointed in their hopes of support from the new electors, de- clared once more for the old bad policy of government by force, and were ousted trom office. Mr. Gladstone, Prime Minister for the third time, then sailed upon the House of Commons to satisfy the national as- pirations of the Irish people, and to declare for government by consent of the governed. A vo'e of the House of Commons rejected Mr. Gladstone's proposal; and the manhood of the three kingdoms is now called upon for a decision. I am confident that the verdict will be given in favour of a generous and a trustful Irish , policy. Depend upon this, that when Ireland shall once be governed by a Legislature chosen by her own people, intent upon devel- oping the resources of the land and fostering the prosperity of the nation, It ishmen, with their homes and the fruits of their labour secure, will make their native island a prosperous, a happy, and a progress"ee portion of the British Empire, and contentedly will stay in their own land. The Protestant religion, which the ma jority of us held so dear, has for many a day gone by been associated in the minds of the Irish people the world over, with a long and sad story cf oppression and wrong-doing. You, whose highest aspirations and holiest thoughts have been ever inspired by its teachings, know lull well that it rests upon the charity which believeth all things and lispeth all things, and that every day it urges you to do onto others as you Si ould they ehould do unto you. Upon you it now lies, as a solemn duty, to re- deem the character of that religion before the eyes of these people. The performance of this duty will bring its own blessing. You will steady the Irish leaders with the weight of respon- sibility. You will add another to the magnificent group Of self-governing communities which form at once the strength and the ornament of the Britiah Empire. You will set free the Imperial Parliament to grapple with the great problems of legislation which await solution. Again I say, that while holding myself at liberty to look beyond the programme set forth by our venerated leader, Mr. Gladstone, I avow myself, now as heretofore, a warm sup- porter and a devoted follower of him who, more than all living statesmen, is entitled to our affection and our gratitude. • I remain, Gentlemen, Your faithful servant, JOHN TOMLINTSCN BRUNNER. Winnington Old Hall. Northwich, June 188.3.

TO THE ELECTORS OF THE NEWTON PARLIA- MENTARY DIVISION OF TELE COUNTY og LANCASTER. GENTLEMEN,—Her Majesty has been pleased to appeal to the sense of her people on the gravest issue of modern times. You are called on to select a policy for dealing with Ireland, on which will depend the tranquility—perhaps the safety of the Inspire; to say whether that policy is to be one of prudent concessions and just reforms, the policy of Mr. Gladstone, con. sonant with the best traditions of the Liberal party, or one based on the incoherent projects of our opponents, powerless alike to subdue or conciliate Ireland, while teeming with im- mediate anxieties and future dangers. At this critical juncture, it is the duty of every true Liberal to go forward in support of our principles; and it is on this account that I venture, eveis at the eleventh hour„ having only just landed from a distant voyage. and though compara- tively a stranger among ydu, to accept vs ith gratitude your selection of me, in my absence, to mtest your division at the approaching election. We can hardly doubt what the verdict of the 'country will be, and if you honour me w.th your support you will find in me an unflinching defender of the Crown and Constitution, de- I termined to preserve through thick and thin, the Unity of the Empire, while cot cedins; to Ireland that due measure of Home Rule without which I believe Unity can no longer be maintained. But there are many other questions of the utmost impor- tance, such as that of Local Gaverment aril Administration, the Reform and Simplification of the Laws connected with the Ownership, Occupation, and Transfer of Land, the advance- ment of our depressed Commercial and Agricultural interests, and, closely connected with these, the Consolidation and Development of our Great Colonial Empire ; also, as matters of special urgency, the amendnient and extension of the Em- ployers Liability Acts, and the proposed Legislation, with re- ference to theßegulation of Mines; especially as to the selec- tion of checkweighmen by the miners themselves. Further, as a Catholic. I warmly support our National system of De- nominational Education. But, vital and urgent as all these matters are, they are dependent upon and must await the settlement of the Irish Difficulty ; till that question is disposen of the legislative Arm of England is pantls sad. It rests with you, gentlemen, and with the constituencies of the couLtry, by supporting Mr. Gladstone, to restore to Par- liament its freedom of action, without which all further Liberal progress is impossible. I hope to have the honour of laying my views before you in detail on all these subjscts, and I remain, in the meanwhile, Your very faithful Bavant. GEORGE ERRINGTON.. The Hall, Rainhill, June 25th, 1886.

TO THE PARLIAMENTARY ELECTORS OF THE BOROUGH OF BT. HELENS. GENTLEMEN, At the unanimous request of the 1C341 Liberal kesociation, acting on the equally unanimous recommendation of the Council of the same body, I have consented to become a Can- pidate for your suffrages at the approaching Election. I deeply regret the early Dissolution:of the first Parliament elected on the popular basis of the Reform and Redistribution Acts of last year, not only on account of the differences of opinion which have rendered an appeal to the country inevitable, but,, because Parliament had so much useful work before it in the too-neglected region of Domestic Legislation, and a majority of its members were evincing such earnestness and lspacity for performing it. I have also the more personal regret that Colonel Gamble should not have felt himself at liberty again to come forward as a Candidate; and that the state of the health of Lieut.-Colonel Richard Pilkington, -who was gener- ally looked upon as Colonel Gamble's natural successor, should not have permitted the question of his Candidature to be enter- tained. Apart from these eonsiderations, lam proud to have been thought worthy of a place in the front of the impending battle; and I appeal to you with every confidence for your support. Of myself, I will say but little, I have been too long and too intimately associated with the progress of the town not to be known to the majority of you, or for there to be much doubt on the subject of my political opinions. I have always been a Liberal; and have never swerved he my allegiance to Mr. Gladstone as, at once, the most enlightened and most conscientious of political leaders. , I am in favour of reforming the Procedure of Parliament, so as to make it a thoroughly efficient medium for the prompt and perfect execution of the wishes of the people. I am in favour of further amending the law on the subject of Registration of Voters, by patting on responsible public officials the absolute duty of enrolling and retaining on the register all duly qualified persons. lam in favour of such a reform of the English Land laws as shall render all land marketable, encourage extended cul- tivation and give all who till land such a reasonable oppor- tunity of acquiring some fixed interest in it as shall wed them more closely to the soil, and so avoid any preventible increase in the flow, to such towns as our own, of labourers for whom there is no remunerative labour, and whose presence only serves still further to impoverish both themselves and others. I fully sympathise with the movement for amending the Employers' Liability Act, and would loaf at that no contract should be allowed which would not secure to any workman injured in his master's service, either from his master or from a mutual Insurance fund to which the master had contributed, the full measure or compensation fixed by law. I congratulate the Miners of the constituency that legisla- tion is already in progress for the improvement of the regula- tions under which they work. I heartily support their claim to an absolute range of choice in the appointment of their checkweighman ; and I shall oppose, if again brought for- ward, the proposea restriction on the employment of women on pit-brows. If elected at your hands to Parliament. my best efforts shall be directed to a careful scrutiny of the details of our enormous Rational Expenditure, with a view to the accomplishment of all reductions c.nsistent with perfect efficiency. The incidence of Taxation should also have my earnest attention, with a view to that re-arrangement for the relief of the working-classes and correction of the existing inequalities between the landed and other interests of the country, which is, in my opinion, very urgently required. I will be no party to any disturbance of the system of De- nominational Education, which in Bt. Helens, at all events, has woiked so admirably and is, in my judgment, best suited to the religious freedom which is one of our proudest boasts. I am a warm supporter of Mr. Gladstone's proposed Irish legislation. I never could and cannot now see any reaeon why the principle of Local Autonomy, which has been so successful in other countries. should be inapplicable to the United King- dom. On the other hand, I believe that its establishment, guarded as Mr. Gladstone has said it must be guarded, is the only chance of converting our present irksome and almost in- tdlerable connection with Ireland into that beat of all unions ; one based, that is to say, neither on prescription nor on power, but on justice and mutual goodwill. The alternative objections to the details of MR Gladstone's proposal seem to use to be destructive of each other. One class of objectors say that the scheme is too large ; the other protest that it reduces Ireland to such an undignified position that she is sure to ask for relief from it. I confidently sub- mit to you that to cut down the scheme would be but to give Ireland an excuse for furtiser agitation; while the Irish people, both at home and abroad, have plsdgesi themselvet be- fore the world to accept the limitations of the present settle- ment a. final. The remaining alternative of a repeal of Coer- cion Laws, after twenty years of "resolute government." is surely not the inspiration of a far-sighted statesman, but the panacea of a politician in despair. I hope to have opportunities in Public Meettngs and other wire, during the progress of my Candidature, of laying before you in greater detail my views on the various questions to which I have referred, and of noticing many others which cannot be suitably comprised within the limits of a written Address. I believe, if elected as your representative, that my extended acquaintance with the development and present condition of your town and its various industries wilt very materially as- sist me in looking after your local interests as you would wish them to be looked after. In matters political. I shall strive to prove a loyal member of that great party of Peace, Retrench- ment and Reform, for whose success in this boron h and county I have so long laboured; and, in all other matters, it shall be my constant study to ascertain and, so far as practic- able, advance, without reference to politics, to religion, or to class, the legislative requirements of my fellow-townsmen. I have the honour to be, Gentlemen, Your obedient servant, ARTHUR BINCLAIR. Waterdale, Bt. Helens. 18th June, 1886.

SKIN DISEASES Are of two kinds: firstly, those which are only skin deep (which are not now to he considered) ; secondly, those which are caused by a bad btate of the blood, and which attack various parts of the body in different ways. E kin disease shows itself in the HEAD, sometimes in the form of Dandruff, which no amount of brushing and combieg will get rid of ; and some times in the form of scaly eruptions. In the NECK, by an enlargement of the glands (commonly called Glandular Swell- ings), which, if unchecked, become very uesightly wounds. In the ARMPITS, and the inside of the ELBOWS, by an in- flamed roughness of the Skin, which is very paintul when washed. In the HANDS, b.", deep cracks or fissures, which, if healed fcr a few days, speedily open again, or by horny-look- ing patches. In the ',BUS, by hard, shiny, and inflamed swellings, or by wounds mare or less deep; and on the BODY, in red scaly patches, which, as often as rubbed off, form again, or in the discharge of a thin watery fluid of a very disagreeable nature. In all these cases the treatment must be twofold. An Ointment is required to relieve Itching, and to heal the surface, and medicine most be taken to change the state of the Blood and render it pure. \ Both these requirements are supplied. by Dr. ROBERTS' CELEBRATED MEDICINES. .
